ASRS:1766062.n: During boarding we had a guest come on board with no mask on. The A FA was in the midst of making a PA, so I went back to talk to him. I politely asked this guest if he had a mask, if not I could provide him with one. He responded, that he indeed had one. I let him know that he had to put it on. I stood to the side while this guest put away his carry-on bags and got into seat and buckled up. At this point, I informed him that he needed to put his mask on at this time, and I walked up front to inform the A about our interaction. I went back closed some bins and saw that he still had no mask on. This time the A FA went back to this guest carrying some extra masks and asked him if he needed one. He responded to her saying he had one. So she politely asked him to put it on. In a stern and harsh voice, he told her 'I heard you the first time.' The A FA came forward. The Customer Service Agent (CSA) was by the boarding door, and the A informed her on what was going on and the CSA automatically knew who we were talking about. She already had a discussion with this guest about wearing a mask on the plane. He put it on in front of her, but took it off before he got on the plane. We decided that a Supervisor needed to have a talk with him. The A FA informed the Captain on the situation and he went to the back of the cabin, and noticed that this guest was still not wearing a mask.A CSA Supervisor, came onto the plane and removed the guest who was non-compliant with the company's face mask policy. Passenger in XX4 boarded the aircraft last, with no mask. I was making a PA while the FA D had just started closing bins etc. I noticed he was not wearing a mask after he passed me. D FA asked him to put a mask on and if he needed one. He said he had one. She asked him to put it on and thanked him. He stowed his bag and she again asked kindly to please make sure your mask is on. He did not. The FA walked away. After waiting approximately 5 minutes and no compliance I, the A FA walked backed back to his seat bringing extra masks. I tried to hand him one. He said I have one. And I said, please put it on. He then said sternly and harshly, I heard you the first time. I walked way. He did not put a mask on. Our Captain walked by to introduce himself to the FAs in the back, the passenger still did not comply. I asked the agent about him. She said, yes I had to tell him to put it on in order to board. He complied, so I let him board. He obviously took it off after passing her. He was asked 4 times to comply. I decided giving him a warning before we closed the door was only going to escalate the situation. We decided to ask the agent to deplane him. As he deplaned with agent he still did not have a mask on nor was he trying to put one on. The crew did not feel comfortable with him going with us.
ASRS:1766062.s: Flight attendants and a captain reported a passenger boarding without a mask who refused to comply after four requests. A CSA Supervisor subsequently removed the non-compliant passenger from the aircraft before departure.

ASRS:1766068.n: I fell victim to the dirty dozen, complacency. I was reading the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) to perform the leak test of the P1 and pitot S1 system when, in the middle of the test, I realized the airspeed indicator was not indicating correctly. I went back through the manual to realize that I had read it incorrectly. I saw that the circuit breakers needed to be 'opened' instead of 'closed;' which conflicted with what I thought I read. When I inspected the left and right pitot probes I saw the inner sleeve of our test equipment had melted around it and entered the probes, which caused the erroneous readings. After removing the damaged sleeves I realized that the test equipment, DPS1000, had a maximum limit of 60 HZ and should not have been plugged in to the aircraft galley outlet;which exceeds that limit. I did not see the limit on the test device due to it being on when I plugged it in. It booted up and tested normally so I did not look at that part of the device. I detected the problem by realizing the airspeed indication was not lining up correctly with the test equipment.It was my first time doing any work on pitot probes so I wanted to move slowly and read the manual, after being on the task for 6 hours and at the final stretch to finish it I began to lose focus. After I found the problem I began talking to my partner about writing a report and doing damage control by removing the damaged equipment.When I was looking through the manual my eyes went right to the breakers, glossing over the warnings and cautions. Maybe having those color coded, since we no longer have to print out papers due to the electronic systems in place, would be beneficial and more eye catching.
ASRS:1766068.s: A mechanic performing a pitot system leak test on the ground misread the maintenance manual and plugged a DPS1000 tester into an incompatible galley outlet. This caused the test equipment's inner sleeve to melt and enter the probes, resulting in erroneous airspeed indications due to complacency and fatigue.

ASRS:1766071.n: The NEF 52-40c, requires a Door Verification for the integrity and condition of the metallic speed tape application PRIOR TO EACH DEPARTURE. The grand majority of the AMT are not documenting this verification in logbook, because the (M) procedure instructions in this NEF are very confusing. The AML is classified as the major historical record of the aircraft since it contains records of pilot reported irregularities, 'ACTION TAKEN'. Every Action Taken must be documented in the AML as required per GPM section 05.01. To make this situation more complicated for the MOC-MCTs the MOCPM section 03.06.5 (A) 1. Requires that a Maintenance Hold will be applied to an aircraft when MOC has identified a task that must be accomplished prior to flight departure, The MCT is required to remove Maintenance Hold and release the aircraft when 'POSITIVE' confirmation that the task has been accomplished. the problem with this is that we cannot do a positive confirmation if the verification Action Taken required per the NEF was not documented in the logbook. This MEL verification procedure must be corrected to ensure traceability with the FAA/CASS DEPT, and the safety of our flight crew and passenger. In order to correct this issue a logbook entry signifying verification of the tape, must be required to be in compliances with the GPM section 05.01 and FAR 14 CFR 121.701.
ASRS:1766071.s: Maintenance personnel reported that confusing NEF 52-40c instructions prevent proper logbook documentation of pre-departure door speed tape verification. This lack of recorded action blocks Maintenance Control from removing maintenance holds and releasing aircraft, creating a traceability and safety issue requiring procedure correction.

ASRS:1766072.n: This is a SAFETY concern. In order to issue the B737 MEL 35-XXX for the Passenger Oxygen Complete System inop, Boeing MEL 'M' procedure, step 'e' requires portable oxygen units to be provided for at least 10% of the passengers. Our 737 NG aircraft is configured for 160 passengers. If we multiply this number by 0.10%, [it] is equal to 16 portable oxygen units that are required to be in compliances with the MEL instructions. During the last MEL Rev 60-XX, a note was added to the 'M' procedure for clarification. This note reads the following. 'The B737 NG is equipped with sufficient portable oxygen CAPACITY to provide for 10% of the passengers, provided that no more than one bottle is inoperative or missing.' The information provided on this note contradicts the 'M' procedure and requirements to issue this placard. The 737 NG is not equipped with sufficient portable oxygen units for 10% of the passengers in accordance with our emergency equipment configuration. There are only 6 portable oxygen units available in the cabin for the passengers. The amount of oxygen available for the passengers should not be measured based on the CAPACITY of oxygen available in the aircraft, but the AMOUNT of units available to assist multiple, different passengers in the event of an emergency.This MEL is a SAFETY hazard for our passenger and flight crew, and should be corrected as soon as possible due to compliances.
ASRS:1766072.s: A mechanic reported a safety hazard regarding the B737 NG MEL 35-XXX for the inoperative Passenger Oxygen Complete System. The report states the MEL note contradicts requirements by citing oxygen capacity instead of the actual six portable units available, which is insufficient for the required 10% of 160 passengers.

ASRS:1766075.n: The AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) calls are very specific tooling required to do this job it does not give us any way to deviate from the tooling required. A tooling part number was given. There are none in ZZZ. Referencing this MM, what other tooling can I use that is acceptable with this AMM. Others suggest that I make my own tooling.Please do not ask technicians to make up tooling just to accommodate the task. Use the correct Tooling as listed in the AMM.
ASRS:1766075.s: A maintenance technician reported that the Aircraft Maintenance Manual requires specific tooling unavailable at ZZZ, with no approved alternatives listed. The reporter requested that technicians not be asked to fabricate tools, emphasizing the need to use only the correct equipment specified in the manual.

ASRS:1766080.n: Aircraft X arrived in ZZZ with a PIREP (Pilot Report) 'AMBER ECAM MSG COND FWD CRG ISOL VALVE'. A history check revealed that the aircraft had the same fault on [the day prior] and MEL 21-XXX C/N 11XXXXX was applied. The MEL (Minimum Equipment List) was cleared by ZZZ1 Maintenance on the RON (Remain Overnight) and the fault repeated during [the] flight to ZZZ. Since it didn't complete 1 flight cycle before faulting again I re-opened the MEL 21-XXX C/N 11XXXXX. About 1/2 hour later began researching for a TSM (Trouble Shooting Manual) and parts to update the item and that is when I found that the aircraft does not have a FWD cargo isolation valve installed. The MEL does not contain any effectivity information and the aircraft was clearly faulting a FWD cargo isolation valve. I had never heard of an Airbus displaying an ECAM (Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor) fault of a component that is not installed in the aircraft and had no reason to question that MEL 21-XXX was not an acceptable deferral for the fault.If aircraft effectivity was contained in the MEL this would have been avoided.
ASRS:1766080.s: A mechanic at ZZZ re-opened an MEL deferral for a recurring forward cargo isolation valve fault on Aircraft X after discovering the component was not installed. The error occurred because the MEL lacked effectivity information, leading to an unnecessary deferral of a non-existent system fault.

ASRS:1766084.n: I work in a contract tower at EDC, Austin Executive. The tower cab does not have a field lighting panel nor the ability to turn on/off runway lights other than activating with a microphone. This allows the lights to stay on for 15 minutes. We may call the FBO to ask an operations person to turn the lights on but it may take several calls before we are successful.This evening it took three phone calls before I was successful in getting the lights manually turned on by the airport operations. In the meantime I had activated the lights using my microphone hoping that Ops would turn them on before the lights turned off. Aircraft X had just landed Runway 13 and exited the runway when the lights turned off. Had they timed out a minute before when they were in the landing phase it could have been an accident. I have also had the lights time out when a Cessna was taking the runway for departure roll on Runway 31. Again, had the lights timed out 10 seconds later it could have been horrible if they had been committed to departure roll and the lights turned off.I have many decades in both control towers and approach controls. I have never been in a control tower that does not have control of the lights. Airport management apparently does not want to pay for the install. I don't think they have factored in the amount of a lawsuit if, God forbid, there is a fatal accident because the lights turned off when an aircraft was in a critical phase of flight. Please help bring this to the attention of an authority that is able to address this situation before we have an accident.
ASRS:1766084.s: An air traffic controller at Austin Executive reported that runway lights timed out during landing and departure phases because the tower lacks manual control and relies on delayed airport operations support. The controller warned that this equipment deficiency creates a risk of accidents if lights extinguish during critical flight phases.

ASRS:1766091.n: I coordinated my annual recurrent training with the instructor to take place yesterday. The instructor was Director of Training for Company for many decades, and even still provides insurance-required recurrent examinations, etc., and I have been flying with him since I purchased Aircraft X in 2006. The instructor is also a recipient of the Wright Brothers Award from the FAA for 50 years of safe flying. With the weather situation, we decided to fly out of ZZZ. I met the instructor about noon after flying in from ZZZ1, and by the time we got Aircraft X started and taxied to Runway X for departure, we heard Aircraft Y announce 'downwind'. It took a few minutes to get to the approach end of Runway X, and we came to a full stop so we could carefully check for traffic before taking the active. In fact, the instructor and I examined just about every place we could look, including downwind and approach trying to locate any traffic, especially given the previous call. No traffic was depicted on the ADS-B (Automated Dependent Surveillance Broadcast) either. I specifically asked the instructor, 'do you see any reason we cannot take the active', to which he replied he saw no reason not to. At the time, I even commented seeing what appeared to be either a large bird or an aircraft, but whatever it was it seemed to be moving out of the area and was therefore not a factor. Accordingly, I announced taking the active and departing Runway X for local air work with a northwest departure. After establishing Aircraft X on the runway and starting to advance the power, we suddenly heard Aircraft Y report 'short final', after which Aircraft Y passed over Aircraft X and landed on the same runway in front of us. I aborted the departure and we watched Aircraft Y land far down the runway (it appeared to be well over halfway down from where we were sitting) at what seemed to be a very high speed, and then, after touchdown, generating all sorts of smoke in the aircraft's wake, either from the engine or from the brakes/tires. It appeared as though there wasn't much runway left and it eventually cleared the runway at the end, apparently using almost all of the 6,704 ft. runway. The instructor observed the smoke to be more 'whitish' in color, meaning it may have been coming from the tires (notably, the instructor provides recurrent training events in the TBM and Jet-prop aircraft as well).Following our recurrent event, the instructor and I thoroughly debriefed what had transpired. We could not understand why we had not visually observed Aircraft Y, given the careful examination of the area surrounding the airport we did prior to taking the active. We were in no hurry whatsoever, and would not have taken the active runway unless we were completely certain there was no conflicting traffic approaching, and we observed none. We examined the FlightAware record as well, but it did not become more obvious as to what may have transpired until today when the instructor and I were discussing the event. For example, Aircraft Y climbed to a cruising altitude of 30,000 ft. enroute from Columbus, Ohio to ZZZ. We believe the pilot may only possess a private pilot certificate, which brings into question whether he could legally be operating at that altitude under IFR (Instrument Flight Rules) conditions or on an IFR flight plan. The mysterious track Aircraft Y flew descending into ZZZ commenced with Aircraft Y descending to 12,500 ft., presumably VFR (Visual Flight Rules), while still a significant distance from the destination airport. For whatever reason, Aircraft Y pilot apparently elected not to execute one of the three IFR approaches available for that airport at the time, including an ILS (Instrument Landing System) and two GPS (Global Positioning System) approaches. According to the FlightAware data, Aircraft Y first circled the area at 12,500 ft., completing a 'racetrack' pattern in the immediate vicinity of the airport, while at the same time descending.After flying the racetrack pattern, Aircraft Y continued to descend in an even tighter circular pattern around the airport. It then commenced a base leg turn as it descended out of 5,300 ft., and then, as it was approaching the airport, it completed an even tighter 360 degree turn at approximately 3,700 ft. As it descended out of that exceedingly tight turn onto final, it was closing on the airport very quickly at an altitude of 2,100 ft. Given our familiarity with the weather at the time, some of the cloud bases of a scattered to broken layer were approximately at 2000 ft. MSL (Mean Sea Level) or even slightly lower, with multiple layers above. In other words, it appears as though the pilot was descending in the vicinity of the airport in what was essentially a 'cloud break' procedure, instead of flying one of the three available instrument approaches. He apparently only relocated the airport visually when he was on a very high approach path already, which would explain the extended touchdown point and the use of most of the runway. It would also explain why we did not see him, as at 2,100 ft. Aircraft Y was likely obscured by the clouds at that point, when Aircraft Y would be located approximately a mile south of the approach end of Runway X.First, the airman made no callouts on Unicom other than flying 'downwind', not mentioning he was at or above 6,000 ft. while on the downwind leg. Nor did the pilot tell anyone on Unicom he was orbiting the airport and descending trying to locate the runway visually. He made no callouts whatsoever between the original 'downwind' call we heard while taxiing Aircraft X initially, and then just the 'short final' call before Aircraft Y overflew Aircraft X, landing far down the runway in front of us.As the conditions were very similar when I arrived approximately 30 minutes previously, there was no problem maintaining VFR conditions in order to make a visual approach to runway X, and those conditions continued 45 minutes later when we concluded our flight. Visibility was at all times in excess of 10 miles. There appears to be a significant amount of desperation exhibited by the pilot in landing over Aircraft X after we had initiated the departure, as it seems he might have been in somewhat of a panic to get Aircraft Y on the ground, when the only prudent course of action at that point, given that neither of us visually located Aircraft Y, despite an extremely diligent search, and after announcing that we were taking the active runway for departure purposes, was to immediately go around and reenter the pattern.Quite a few of the preceding flights for Aircraft Y available on FlightAware appear to be training type missions, and it is unclear what put so much pressure on the pilot to complete the approach and landing, imperiling all involved, instead of merely executing a prudent go around and reentering the pattern, which the weather would certainly permit at the time. Quite frankly don't know what else we could have done to prevent this situation from occurring, as we used all due diligence before we took the active runway. Aircraft Y was likely above the clouds when we searched for traffic before departing. The two pilots on our flight deck at the time had over 100 years of [combined] flight experience, without incident or accident.
ASRS:1766091.s: A pilot and instructor in Aircraft X aborted a departure from Runway X after Aircraft Y overflew them on a high-speed, late touchdown. The reporter attributes the near-miss to Aircraft Y's pilot descending through clouds without proper callouts or an instrument approach, obscuring the aircraft until it was on short final.

ASRS:1766096.n: On climb, I tried to start moving fuel forward with the gravity flow valve open and noticed that it didn't work. Then I tried the normal transfer valve and nothing happened, my last resort was the rapid transfer system and it didn't work either. I then tried to open the crossflow valve and nothing happened. I checked the circuit breakers and noticed the crossflow valve breaker was out. I asked my FO (First Officer) to start looking for an airport to land since we were not going to use our fuel from the fuselage tank. The airplane was not showing any indication of any of the fuel valves working, I notified my company of the incident while I was looking through the airplane manual to try to reset the circuit breaker. After I tried it once and noticed it didn't solve the issue, it kept popping out, I commanded my FO to notify ATC and initiated a descent and turn towards our closest suitable airport. Our fuel from the wings kept getting low and after great coordination with controllers we were able to get safely to the ground. Possible power surge changes in such an old and poor maintained airplane lead to crossflow valve to fail also causing other valves and indications to malfunction.
ASRS:1766096.s: During climb, the pilot and First Officer experienced a total fuel valve failure caused by a tripped crossflow circuit breaker on an older aircraft. They descended to the nearest airport after reset attempts failed, landing safely with low wing fuel due to suspected power surges.

ASRS:1766099.n: I had an uneventful pre-flight, run up and departure from ZZZ1 enroute to ZZZ2. Approximately 2 hours into the 3.5 hour flight, my left turbine inlet temperature spiked and while trying to diagnose the problem, I heard a grinding noise from the engine. I had just been switched from ZZZ Center to ZZZ1 [Center] and while reporting in, told them that I may [need priority handling]. They immediately located ZZZ airport 20nm at 12 o'clock so I immediately pulled power to 50% to try to preserve my engine. The grinding noise occurred one more time but I was able to land uneventfully under normal landing conditions. The mechanics have diagnosed a potential problem with the alternator and left magneto that could have caused the runaway temps and noises. The aircraft maintenance is being performed and will be certified before I fly it.
ASRS:1766099.s: The pilot experienced a left turbine inlet temperature spike and grinding noise during cruise, prompting a priority landing at ZZZ airport. Mechanics diagnosed a potential alternator and left magneto issue, and the aircraft is undergoing maintenance before recertification.

ASRS:1766132.n: I was flying with my husband a student pilot. I am a flight instructor. He was sitting in the left seat, I was sitting in the right seat. We were heading northeast bound at a VFR cruising altitude of 3500 feet. Our airplane is equipped with ADS-B in and out. We had VFR flight following with a distinct squawk code and were on frequency with Approach. I looked at our GPS map screen. I periodically check the screen for traffic that I may not see outside. I saw a target moving directly towards us, southwest bound, showing the same altitude. I looked outside, and did not see the aircraft. I listened to Approach and the controller was busy vectoring other airplanes. According to our GPS screen, the target was approximately 4 miles away from us. We had a strong tailwind and were moving 140 knots over the ground. I immediately told my husband to turn to the right and put us into a climb. He did the requested maneuvers. As we climbed to 4000 feet we saw the airplane pass under and to the left of us. If we had not made an evasive maneuver we probably would have hit each other. According to my ADS-B information, the airplane coming towards us was from a flight school. After we cleared the airplane, we again descended to our VFR cruise altitude of 3500 feet. Approach did not mention anything about the traffic or altitude change.
ASRS:1766132.s: A flight instructor and student pilot in a VFR flight at 3,500 feet used ADS-B to detect an opposing flight school aircraft at the same altitude. The instructor initiated a right turn and climb to 4,000 feet, causing the other aircraft to pass below and left, avoiding a collision while Approach remained unaware.

ASRS:1766139.n: I often fly late-day or evening, and routinely use the associated pilot-controlled airport lighting both to fix my position and for terminal guidance. Sky Manor has MIRL but does not have an airport beacon, so I often also turn on the lighting for Alexandria (N85), located approximately 2NM northwest, which has both MIRL and a rotating beacon. The frequency for this at Sky Manor is 122.975 (which doubles as the CTAF frequency), at Alexandria, 121.8 (with 122.975 as CTAF).On at least two separate occasions, coming from more than one direction, I have turned the airport lighting on for Alexandria and ended up momentarily distracting pilots and/or ATC by doing so. Alexandria is not very far away from Newark Liberty (EWR), or Lancaster (LNS), both of which use 121.8 as a Ground Control frequency and are apparently well within radio range and altitudes at and below 2000 ft MSL. Further research indicates that McGuire (WRI) may also be affected, as it's a similar distance as Newark.While I don't want to keep distracting others in the ATC system - and I've resolved the issue for myself by increasing familiarity with the airspace, which has reduced the necessity of me using the Alexandria airport beacon for guidance - I also realize that this has the capability to reduce my situational awareness, and at any event, aircraft intending to land at Alexandria at night must necessarily turn the airport lighting on, potentially distracting operations at the airports previously listed.I propose that the lighting frequency at Alexandria be changed, either to CTAF or to some other discrete frequency, with the intention of minimizing possible adverse operational implications for local controlled airports.
ASRS:1766139.s: A pilot reported that activating Alexandria airport lighting on frequency 121.8 while operating near Sky Manor inadvertently distracted pilots and ATC at nearby controlled airports like Newark and Lancaster. The pilot attributes this interference to the shared frequency and proposes changing the lighting frequency to prevent future operational distractions.

ASRS:1766140.n: M54 is an untowered airport with recent heavy flight instruction activity from a nearby college, 2 local flight schools, an active flying club, and flight instructing originating from a nearby Class C airport. Local custom is Runway 19 is used for light and variable or no wind take off and landing because there is an open field just south of the airport. Just north of the field is a college. When recently flying I politely mentioned the local custom over the radio trying to turn the airport traffic back to using the preferred runway. A few minutes later I was informed that the AFD (Airport Facility Directory, Chart Supplement) did not mention a preferred runway. There are still many aircraft on the field flying without radio communication. I think it would be a good idea to publish this local custom in the AFD and post on signage at the departure point of both runways. Several years ago I had to leave the runway onto the grass while rolling out on 19 to prevent a twin aircraft broadcasting on the wrong frequency landing on Runway 1 from landing on top of me. Had we executed a touch and go we might have had a mid air on climb out.
ASRS:1766140.s: The pilot reported high traffic at untowered M54 and a past incident where they exited Runway 19 onto grass to avoid a twin aircraft landing on Runway 1 while broadcasting on the wrong frequency. The pilot noted that executing a touch-and-go might have caused a mid-air collision and recommended publishing local runway customs.

ASRS:1766145.n: While practicing an ILS approach on A/P I went missed at the FAF and reengaged A/P at 1,800 ft, at that point Aircraft started pitching in an unusual high nose up attitude, tried to disengage A/P by pressing A/P on the yoke, additionally on the A/P disconnect on autopilot panel, and finally disconnected circuit breaker, none of this disengaged it and aircraft continued pitching up and down with elevator trim running up and down on its own.Was able to land after 90 second approximately from when event started, very difficult to control but landed safely.Reported the incident to NTSB and sent them the data card of the aircraft flight, awaiting for results back. While practicing an ILS approach on A/P I went missed at the FAF and reengaged A/P at 1,800 ft, at that point Aircraft started pitching in an unusual high nose up attitude, tried to disengage A/P by pressing A/P on the yoke, additionally on the A/P disconnect on A/P panel, and finally pulled A/P circuit breaker , non of this disengaged it and aircraft continued pitching up and down with elevator trim running up and down on its on.Was able to land after 9 seconds approximately from when event started, very difficult to control but landed safely.Reported the incident to NTSB and sent them the data card of the aircraft flight, awaiting for results back.After 30 minutes on the ground and shutting off avionics 1 and 2 and master switch decided to fly back to base with A/P breaker off. The 20 mins Flight was uneventful. Problem is definitely with pitch trim and or A/P.
ASRS:1766145.s: The pilot experienced uncommanded pitch oscillations and trim runaway after re-engaging the autopilot at 1,800 feet during a missed ILS approach. Despite multiple disengagement attempts, the pilot manually landed safely and attributed the cause to a pitch trim or autopilot malfunction.

ASRS:1766177.n: We were conducting a long cross country for the student's commercial pilot requirements. This required us to deviate west and south of course due to not being cleared into the Class Bravo airspace and Class D airspace. We had a near miss with a powered parachute. The other operator was slightly below us, heading westbound. Our altitude at the time was 3500 feet eastbound, with flight following. Weather conditions were VMC, clear and unrestricted. Both I and the student were actively scanning for traffic outside due to the busy Bravo environment and using ADS-B to aid us. Since he was slightly below us, we did not see him until close, less than 1 mile separation and probably closer. I directed the student to immediately turn left to pass behind, but he started turning slowly, so I took controls to avoid the situation. The powered parachute passed behind, and we continued without further incident. The parachute's color caused it to really blended in until we were close. We were attempting to spot all traffic visually, but did not see them until late. I'm unsure if the parachute operator ever saw us, as we would've been coming out of the sun off his roughly 3 to 4 o'clock. I did not report this to Approach, mainly since we ourselves were getting into a high workload environment since we were close to our destination. Additionally, with the traffic was behind us, I was more concerned with flying the airplane and watching for other traffic, especially since it is a busy general aviation airport. That was probably my biggest self recommendation, is trying to report that if able to approach to warn other aircraft. The only other recommendation for myself is to be a little clearer when I need to assume controls.
ASRS:1766177.s: A commercial pilot and student conducting a cross-country flight at 3,500 feet experienced a near miss with a powered parachute while deviating around Class Bravo airspace. The pilot took control to avoid the low-visibility aircraft after late visual detection, attributing the incident to the parachute's color blending with the background.

ASRS:1766242.n: We were departing ZZZ to ZZZ1 after dropping our passengers off at their personal hangar. As we began taxiing out, we made a call on the CTAF that we were taxiing out and planning to takeoff on RWY XX. We heard an Air Force C130 on CTAF doing work in the pattern. We made a second call as we rounded the hangars on the NE side of the airport. At that time we heard a very faint radio call of a tail number (we could not make out the N#) saying that they 'were entering the pattern, ZZZ' That is all that we heard. I made a radio call asking for the aircraft to repeat the call, and heard nothing. As we were taxiing to the hold short line, I as the PNF (pilot not flying) called for our release from Center Radio. the PF (pilot flying) was monitoring CTAF the entire time, and heard no additional radio calls from the unidentified airplane in the pattern. We stopped at the hold short line and made another radio call that we were holding short and were going to be departing RWY XX. The C130 radio'd that he would extend his orbit so that we could take off. We heard no other radio calls during that time. We crossed the hold short line and I looked and verified the final approach area for RWY XX was clear, the PF looked and verified that RWY XY Final was clear. As we were taxiing into position we heard a very faint 'you guys hold up a minute' call over CTAF. We did not know who it was for and I called over the frequency 'say again' We heard nothing. We started our takeoff run. About 5 seconds later we saw a Cessna landing on RWY XY and aborted our takeoff at a speed of about 100 knots IAS. We called out on the radio that we had made radio calls saying that we were taking off. I do not recall the exact words but we were getting chewed out for taking off while a local was trying to land. We taxed clear of the runway, reset everything, checked our brake temperatures, made another radio call and proceeded to take off uneventfully.We try to be hyper vigilant operating a high performance jet out of uncontrolled fields. It is possible, but I believe unlikely that we missed radio calls from the aircraft in question, but it is possible that we did. I believe the problem arose from a weak transmitter on the Cessna, and non standard phraseology and lack of position report calls on the CTAF. I believe that we followed the AIM guidance for operating on an uncontrolled field, by making several radio calls stating our intentions, and listening for other traffic. We heard no other position reports from the Cessna such as 'entering downwind or turning base' etc. I am not saying the other pilot did not make the calls, I'm saying we did not hear them if he did. There is also a dip in the runway that prevents you from seeing the end of RWY XY from the end of RWY XX. In addition the pilot of the Cessna did not have his landing light on, which would have helped to identify him sooner. We asked for a repeat of his initial radio call, but heard nothing. We also heard no other radio reports from any aircraft other than the C130. In addition, this could have been avoided if a proper radio call such as 'ZZZ Traffic Aircraft Y short final, landing RWY XY ZZZ' had been made instead of 'You guys hold up a minute'. We can always be more vigilant in our actions. Taxiing out while getting a clearance and setting up the FMS is a very busy time, monitoring 2 radios can be distracting. Careful attention to detail and vigilant use of the checklist and PF/PNF duties all need to be done to ensure that nothing is missed, inside and outside the airplane while operating on an uncontrolled field.
ASRS:1766242.s: A high-performance jet crew aborted takeoff at 100 knots from an uncontrolled airport after a Cessna landed on a crossing runway. The reporter attributed the near-miss to the Cessna's weak transmitter, non-standard phraseology, lack of position reports, and a runway dip that blocked visual contact.

ASRS:1766245.n: While conducting a CFI checkout in a Grob-103C, the canopy came open and separated from the aircraft during final approach with a forward slip.This was my second training flight in the glider, the purpose of the checkout was to allow me to provide flight instruction in the Grob-103C. I normally provide instruction in Aircraft Y. The Grob-103C we were flying was recently inspected - 100-Hour and Annual - and was flying frequently at the flight school. Before flight, we performed our standard pre-flight inspection and pre-takeoff checklist which included ensuring both canopies were closed and locked. I was seated in the front seat, having flown side secured canopies often, [I] closed the canopy latch and tested the canopy by pushing up on the side to ensure it was securely closed. I noted no problems during closing and locking the canopy.After executing our pre-takeoff procedure, my Instructor and I proceeded on aerotow to 3,000 AGL, released, and performed some basic maneuvers - stalls, slow flight, and thermalling. After gliding for approximately 15 minutes, we elected to enter the pattern on the downwind leg. While turning from base to final, we decided to slip the aircraft to practice flying without airbrakes. After slipping for approximately 8 seconds, the front canopy suddenly opened and departed the aircraft. I immediately came out of the slip, nosed down for approach speed, and opened the airbrakes. I was able to land the glider with normal maneuvers and noted no change to the controllability of the glider.Upon examination of the glider, there was no structural/significant damage. There were no injuries to either crew. There was a slight score to the fiberglass on the right wing and damage to the canopy hinges. The canopy was later recovered in a field where the fiberglass appeared to have shattered on impact. Analyzing the situation, I am still unsure why the canopy separation occurred, but if I could improve my process, I would have examined the canopy all along its edges after securing the latch to insure there were no gaps or leaks. In addition, I probably would have looked closer during preflight at the edges/seals of the canopy from the exterior to ensure there were no abnormalities on either canopy when closed and locked.
ASRS:1766245.s: During a CFI checkout in a Grob-103C glider, the front canopy separated during a forward slip on final approach despite a pre-flight check confirming it was locked. The pilot landed safely with no injuries, though the canopy shattered upon impact, and the cause remains unknown.

ASRS:1766260.n: I was working the CIC position in Are a X when the controller on Sector XY told me that Aircraft X reported seeing a drone above him about 3,000 to 4,000 feet above him. Aircraft X was at FL240 orbiting over our wild fire TFR'S. No further information was received about type. Since this drone could potentially been at FL280 the controller quick looked sector YY/ZZ to see if there were other aircraft in the area before calling the high altitude sector. He did notice a air carrier aircraft about FL340 about 20 miles north of Aircraft X position but no other aircraft. No primary target was noticed and no ADSB information noticed.I did advise the OMIC of the situation.Aircraft X did not see the drone any other time while orbiting.I felt we did all we could do in reporting the possible UAS.
ASRS:1766260.s: An air traffic controller in Area X reported that Aircraft X at FL240 sighted a drone 3,000 to 4,000 feet above while orbiting a wildfire TFR. No radar or ADS-B targets were detected, the drone was not seen again, and the incident was reported to the OMIC.

ASRS:1766262.n: An aircraft was doing practice approaches. The aircraft requested the VOR A approach to join the arc to start the approach. It isn't an approach that is normally used. I cleared the aircraft to maintain 3000 ft. until established and they got into the small 032 MVA area at 3000 ft. No recommendations. I should have looked at the MVA prior to clearing.
ASRS:1766262.s: An air traffic controller cleared an aircraft performing practice approaches to maintain 3000 ft for a VOR A approach, resulting in the aircraft entering the 032 MVA area at that altitude. The controller attributed the incident to failing to check the MVA before issuing the clearance.

ASRS:1766266.n: While approaching the initial fix (IF) TNNER for the San Juan, Puerto Rico ILS Runway 10, we heard a commercial airline pilot ahead of us report that his cockpit had been illuminated by a green laser near TNNER. Approach Control warned us of this laser strike. We asked for clearance to proceed to waypoint REMSY (IAF) instead of TNNER (IF) to allow us to avoid the area where the green laser strike had been reported. Immediately after being cleared to REMSY, our cockpit was illuminated by a very bright ground based green laser coming from the 1:30 clock code position at about six to eight miles from our position. We reported the green laser strike to ATC at approximately (XA:33) Z. The Approach Controller asked if either pilot had sustained any eye injury. We responded that we did not believe we had sustained any eye injuries. I estimated the laser to be approximately four miles southeast of TNNER, or 260 degrees at 8 NM from the SJU VOR. I estimate the source to be on the ground between the 436 feet tall tower and the 489 feet tall tower (shown on the SJU ILS Runway 10 Approach plate). The green laser was an unnecessary distraction during a critical phase of flight (approach, configuration change, visually searching for arrival traffic, attempting to locate the runway visually, conducting the landing checklist, landing, etc.). Law enforcement never met us at the airport to take a report. It did not appear that anyone at the FAA or law enforcement were interested in gathering facts immediately after the event in order to pursue the perpetrators. The San Juan, PR, TJSJ/SJU-1, (date), Station Information Page (SIP) 3.0, Note 6 says, 'Numerous LASER events have been recorded in area' as a warning to pilots. It seems like laser strikes have become so common in the area of the San Juan Airport that officials just accept this fact. Is law enforcement aggressively investigating these laser strikes in an attempt to hold the perpetrators accountable? Fortunately, tonight, the laser strike caused only a momentary distraction to the pilots. What happens when a persistent series of laser strikes causes the pilots eye injury, disorientation, and/or loss of aircraft with all passengers onboard. Will the FAA and law enforcement treat the event more seriously after such a catastrophic event?Will the FAA, FBI, NTSB, and/or law enforcement aggressively investigate and pursue the perpetrators who are pointing high intensity green lasers at commercial airline cockpits flying into San Juan Airport.
ASRS:1766266.s: While approaching the TNNER initial fix for San Juan ILS Runway 10, the flight crew was illuminated by a ground-based green laser from the 1:30 position. The strike caused a momentary distraction during the approach, but the pilots reported no eye injuries.

ASRS:1766276.n: Day 5, while enroute to the ZZZ layover hotel I received a message from a Captain I had dinner with on Day 0. I'll put this message in context by mentioning my First Officer and I met this Captain and his First Officer for dinner that evening.The message stated on Day 2, this particular Captain was notified by the company that the First Officer he flew with had tested positive for COVID. The First Officer had sent a message to this Captain confirming such. The ZZZ1 Chief Pilot was subsequently notified and a request was made for that office to contact my crew of this matter (I never received any communication about this event). This Captain was tested on Day 2, became symptomatic on Day 3 and obtained a positive test result on Day 5 prompting the message.Upon reviewing the message, I contacted my First Officer and the company On-duty Manager to notify each of the situation. Per company and CDC COVID protocol both the First Officer and I have been quarantined for a 14-day period commencing Day 0. As I compose this report, I am quarantined at the hotel, unable to travel home.The intent of this report is to question why didn't the company notify my crew of the COVID encounter? Apparently protocol wasn't followed or if it was, it should be modified to address this particular or similar scenarios. Flight crews should not be placed in a situation where they must quarantine away from home while on company business, especially if the company was previously notified to contact a crew which was exposed to a COVID positive employee. Had I not been received said message I would still be flying the line with the potential to infect others with this virus.
ASRS:1766276.s: A pilot and First Officer quarantined after learning via a third-party Captain that they had dined with a crew member who later tested positive for COVID. The reporter states the company failed to notify them of the exposure despite being alerted, resulting in unnecessary quarantine away from home and potential virus transmission.

ASRS:1766284.n: On approach to 35R, we were direct FRONZ, cleared visual approach. We were on an angled intercept to final. Captain asked 7,000 ft. be set for FRONZ, I did and after leaving 8,000 ft., tower advised our callsign and low altitude alert. I replied to ATC that we were ok, meaning level and clear of terrain at 7,000 ft. We intercepted the glide path to a normal approach and landing. During the low altitude alert we had finished slowing from 190 to 170 knots assigned. Several runway changes and speed changes preceded this event. I believe the Captain was trying to have the airplane, on the assigned speed, desired configuration and omitted the class B floor as I did.
ASRS:1766284.s: The flight crew received a low altitude alert while descending to 7,000 feet on a visual approach to runway 35R. The pilot attributed the alert to the captain and first officer omitting the Class B floor restriction during speed and configuration changes.

ASRS:1766287.n: I received an ACARS message from the crew in flight that they are returning to ZZZ due to a cracked windshield and also notifying ATC. I saw that they were at an altitude of 7000 feet and decided that it was best to just make changes to release and monitor flight untill it was safely on the ground to get details as to what occurred. I got word from the ATC Coordinator who contacted ZZZ Center that the flight encountered a hail storm while climbing out. There were some scattered to broken CBs (cumulonimbus clouds) east of the ZZZ area at the time. The flight landed safely back at ZZZ. I did talk to the Captain briefly who said about 20 miles east of ZZZ they encountered a hail storm.
ASRS:1766287.s: The ATC controller managed a flight returning to ZZZ after the crew reported a cracked windshield caused by a hail storm encountered 20 miles east of the airport during climb-out. The aircraft landed safely at 7,000 feet while the controller monitored the flight and coordinated with ZZZ Center.

ASRS:1766393.n: This was a training flight. Occupants included student in left seat and instructor in right seat. ATIS reporting winds 300 degrees at 8 knots, SKC, visibility greater than 10 miles. Student confidently performed all preflight, taxi, and run up procedures. After run up, advised complete and cleared to hold short of the runway and monitor Tower. Takeoff clearance was north turnout approved cleared for takeoff. No additional wind direction or speed was given in the clearance. Student lined up appropriately and commenced takeoff roll. Once rolling, the plane veered towards the left of the runway while student continued the takeoff. As speed continued to increase, the student was unsuccessful in aligning the plane with the centerline and began to prematurely rotate in what appeared to be a moment of panic. With an excursion inevitable, instructor called 'abort my controls' retarded power and struggled to regain control. The aircraft may have momentarily became airborne. As the aircraft settled back onto the surface, a violent porpoising action proceeded. Instructor discovered student was applying full pressure on the brakes. Instructor demanded 'off the brakes' and eventually brought the aircraft under control towards centerline. Instructor canceled flight and taxied back to the ramp without further incident. Factors leading up to this event included too much confidence placed in student's ability as he done exceptionally well leading up to the takeoff, reported a very successful flight with a previous instructor, as well as having previous aircraft type experience. Additional factors would include lack of control inputs to counter the reported direct crosswind. Typically, a direct crosswind from the left would tend to cause a right deviation of centerline. It is possible the student inadvertently or over corrected the beginning takeoff roll with differential left brake after feeling the plane go to the right and did not transition to rudder steering once airspeed increased. It is also possible the 300 degree wind direction and runway assignment seemed coincident causing a lack of correction for winds. Regardless, lesson gained for instructor is to stay on the controls with student until student demonstrates safe takeoff procedures. Additionally, instructor should identify early on a rejected takeoff scenario that leaves enough space to safely recover.
ASRS:1766393.s: During a training takeoff, a student pilot veered left and panicked, causing the aircraft to porpoise after the instructor took control. The instructor attributed the incident to the student's overconfidence, failure to correct for crosswind, and inadvertent brake application, leading to a flight cancellation.

ASRS:1766414.n: My aircraft engine started having a loss of power at 1000 ft. AGL I was too far from the airport for what I considered a safe return. I circled a remote road twice planning on how I would accomplish an off field landing with partial power. I executed a safe landing on the road and on rollout a mailbox contacted the left forward strut and dented the strut and a slight dent in the wrap around cowling. I then taxied up the driveway and parked in the grass to tie down the aircraft. I returned the next day and disassembled the aircraft and returned it to its hangar at ZZZ.
ASRS:1766414.s: The pilot experienced an engine power loss at 1,000 feet AGL and executed a safe off-field landing on a remote road. During rollout, a mailbox contacted the left forward strut and cowling, causing minor damage before the aircraft was parked and later returned to the hangar.

ASRS:1766415.n: During departure from ZZZ, the lavatory service door apparently opened inflight and departed the aircraft. During climb out, the crew noticed an 'Ext Door' light illuminated in the cockpit. Note that this light is not incorporated into the Master Caution Warning system. It is also located up underneath the cockpit glare shield and not readily visible to the cockpit crew during normal instrument scan. This light has historically been associated with the air pressure on the fuel service door switch causing light illumination and was assumed by the crew to be in this case. Upon post flight, the crew discovered that the lavatory service door was missing. Crew was not aware until this time that the door had been lost inflight. Loss was immediately reported to company.
ASRS:1766415.s: During climb out from ZZZ, the lavatory service door opened and departed the aircraft. The crew missed the non-master caution 'Ext Door' light, assuming it indicated fuel door pressure, and only discovered the missing door after landing.

ASRS:1766439.n: On arrival into ZZZ, descending via on the ZZZZZ3 Arrival just before the ZZZZZ waypoint, we checked on with approach, and they responded 'Company XXXX, cleared ILS X.' I had programmed the ILS X for our arrival, but didn't select any transition on the approach. The ZZZZZ3 STAR has the note to cross ZZZZZ at 6,000 feet, expect ILS or LOC Runway X. On receipt of the clearance, I paused for a moment as there was a discontinuity in the box after ZZZZZ and before ZZZZZ1 [waypoint], and the remaining points on the ILS X. ATC had not given us a heading or guidance for after the last fix on the STAR, just cleared ILS X. I looked at my EFB to see what the text of the STAR said, and my Captain seeing my confusion, said 'you're cleared for approach, how about direct ZZZZZ1?' He had also queued up ZZZZZ1 in the box, and was poised to execute it. I still wasn't sure, but he seemed positive. I said 'OK;' he executed it and we began direct to ZZZZZ1. Within a few seconds, Approach queried us 'I show you left of course, what [are you] doing?' The Captain replied, 'we're direct ZZZZZ1 cleared for ILS X, is there something else you would like?' ATC responded that there was a ZZZZZ transition to the ILS X, and in future that is what he meant when he cleared us ILS X - to fly the ZZZZZ transition on the ILS from the STAR. Had I looked closer at the approach plate, and not just the STAR chart, after the issuance of the clearance, the ATC clearance intention would've become obvious to me. I let my Captain cause me to second guess my hesitation, and disregard my uncertainty over our clearance. I should have requested he ask for clarification from ATC instead of allowing him to execute a path I was unsure of. I have felt a bit slow in the cockpit lately, due to having flown very infrequent this year (light schedules/hindsight/scheduled time off) and I believe I made the false assumption I was missing something and he was correct. A simple query to ATC would have cleared up the matter.I should have taken a moment longer to review the appropriate charts to clarify the appropriate flight course, and failing that answering my question, I should have queried ATC for clarification. When programming the approach, closer examination of the plate would have shown the available lead in transition from ZZZZZ. I should have trusted my hesitation upon receipt of the clearance and not assumed I was wrong in needing clarification.
ASRS:1766439.s: The pilot and captain deviated left of course while descending on the ZZZZZ3 STAR after the captain executed a direct to ZZZZZ1 instead of the required ZZZZZ transition to the ILS X. The error resulted from the pilot's hesitation to query ATC for clarification due to low recent flight experience and deferring to the captain's incorrect assumption.

ASRS:1766458.n: Move Team dispatched to take 777-300 from Gate XX to the hard stand. Upon arriving to the gate they saw that when you put the 777-300 on Gate XX the entire tail of the aircraft hangs over the VSR (Vehicle Service Road) and anyone driving has to break the company policy and drive under the aircraft or go around and drive into the active taxiway, both of which are against company's SOP (Standard Operating Procedure) and city driving regulations. I know there has been a SRA (Safety Risk Assessment) done on this ongoing problem and they have decided to take the risk rather than move the aircraft to a gate that can accommodate it. The 777-300 aircraft parked at ZZZ on Gate XX places the tail beyond the VSR (Vehicle Service Road). When this aircraft type is positioned on this gate it leave the drivers of GSE (Ground Service Equipment) two options: to drive equipment directly under the aircraft, [or] leave the VSR and enter the alley where aircraft are actively taxi or under tow.
ASRS:1766458.s: Move Team reported that parking a 777-300 at Gate XX causes the tail to overhang the Vehicle Service Road, forcing Ground Service Equipment drivers to violate SOPs by driving under the aircraft or entering active taxiways. Management acknowledged this risk in a Safety Risk Assessment but decided to maintain the current gate assignment despite the safety conflict.

ASRS:1766480.n: It was from ZZZ1 to ZZZ IFR flight. Our flight plan and clearance was from ZZZ1..ZZZZZ5. ZZZ. On the ground, [the] Captain, and I reviewed the route including every fix in the arrival and programmed [the] FMS for Runway XXL in ZZZ. From takeoff until descend via ZZZZZ 5 Arrival, flight was uneventful. Captain and I took off from Runway XXL at ZZZ1 and then instructed to go direct ZZZZZ shortly after instructed go to direct ZZZZZ1 which is [the IAF] of [the] arrival. We were instructed to descend via ZZZZZ5 Arrival in to ZZZ with both altitude and airspeed restriction as stated in the STAR. During the descend, the ZZZ Approach Controller gave instruction to switch our runway to XXR. Captain and I programmed [the] FMS and switched our planned runway to XXR as well as review the fixes along the route. However, as we approach the fix ZZZZZ2, LNAV autopilot was switched to lateral mode [and the] airplane was late to turn to [the] final [approach] fix which is ZZZZZ3. As soon as Pilot Flying noticed the mode change in autopilot, Pilot Flying used heading bug to make a left turn to rejoin the course for the rest of arrival. After the arrival, flight crew flew rest of flight uneventfully and land safely at Runway XXR. Next time, we will review the fixes more carefully after making any changes on the runways or arrivals and make sure if there are any fixes that are duplicated, we will deleted it. On arrival to ZZZ we were descending via ZZZZZ5. Our dispatch release had planned [Runway] XXL and we had already briefed our approach prior to the beginning of the arrival as is common for preparation and safety. As an LCA (line check airman) I have been flying our route structure for over X;XXX hours in the left seat and this is common practice for myself. However, I am still trying to understand the traffic flows in ZZZ and as time progresses I am positive the other crews and I will get better at selecting runways based on flow and approaches utilized over time. ZZZ Approach Control gave us instructions for XXR somewhere after ZZZZZ5 I believe. I was the pilot monitoring. So I immediately went to work resetting FMS verifying ZZZZZ3 had now changed to ZZZZZ2. Altitudes were correct at said waypoint. Getting new landing data. Resetting both navigational aids for the correct runway. And since my FO (First Officer) was fairly new to the plane I began briefing his approach to him out loud, highlighting changes and re-briefing all pertinent information. It was in the middle of this brief that I heard the lateral NAV disconnection chime. The plane had entered ROL mode and within a second I and the FO were both reaching for the heading bug. He made the correction on the FGC (Flight Guidance Computer) about as quickly as anyone could. We recaptured the LNAV course to ZZZZZ2 and were given a number to call.I have been operating with this company for over X years, almost Y are as an LCA. In all my time I have never seen what I described above. After the fact I am aware of exactly what happened and I will explain and make suggestions to correct. Upon loading the runway change to XXR the FMS duplicated the ZZZZZ fix. I know this because the pilot observing told us when we got on the ground what he had witnessed and told us it was a current trend within our airline and they were trying to troubleshoot. I understand why that might happen in the mind of the FMS as it is trying to separate the arrival into parts. Initial arrival segment versus approach segment. However, reloading approaches or fielding runways changes are common in our route structure and not once in four years has this happened anywhere else. ZZZZZ4 in ZZZ2. Landing north transitions to ZZZZZ6 at 7000. Landing south your next fix might be ZZZZZ7 at 7000 for XXC. But never in four years has a reassigned runway and a reload of the approach caused ZZZZZ4 to duplicate. This is specific to ZZZ2. This is why we are just now seeing this throughout the pilot group in this airspace. I know there is verbiage within our books that states duplicated points must be removed for this very reason. However, in this event I was unable to catch the duplicated fix due to workload and I had never seen the issue before so my mental radar so to speak was focused on threats I have seen: monitoring our descent rate, monitoring speed control for arrival compliance, re-briefing navigational aid frequencies, briefing go-around and missed approach for the new runway. All the things I have seen cause errors in our flight on a normal day. So when this lateral break happened I was as stunned as the FO. I will say to his credit he corrected in the quickest fashion and made the correct adjustment for the situation. There was nothing more we could have done. I did not feel safety was at stake nor that the violation was hugely significant. I however do see that as a systemic issue the implications of this are massive and need to be corrected ASAP which is why I have my recommendations. I spoke with a sim pilot who was able to recreate the event and he confirmed what I had already suspected. Pilots need to be aware that this is common in ZZZ2. When receiving a new runway or a change to the approach. Look for duplicate fixes!
ASRS:1766480.s: During an IFR arrival at ZZZ, the crew switched the FMS to Runway XXR, causing a duplicate ZZZZZ fix that triggered an LNAV disconnection and late turn. The Pilot Flying manually corrected the heading to rejoin the course, and the aircraft landed safely, though the crew identified the FMS duplication as a systemic issue.

ASRS:1766489.n: I was Captain and the flying pilot for arrival into IAH. We were descending in VMC conditions on the LINKK1 Arrival for the assigned Runway 27. We had completed our Approach to Landing above the line and as we were approaching 10000' we were running our Approach to Landing checklist Below the Line when we were cleared by the Approach Controller for the ILS 27 Approach and to maintain 240 knots.I put on the appropriate lights and we finished our checklist. However I did not - in hindsight - set the lower 1500' at which we were to cross the FAF at REDOC. Between RDFSH and GEYGR we were queried as to whether we were going to make our crossing restriction of 4000 at GEYGR. We realized the error and started to descend on the approach. Shortly after not complying with the crossing restriction at GEYGR, we were broken off the approach and vectored back around-slowed to 210 and descended to rejoin the approach. We were given a phone number to call HOUSTON TRACON. We then completed the approach and landing. The error started when I did not select the lower altitude for the FAF of 1500. The timing of our clearance was a contributing factor but the error was in the failure to set lower FAF altitude. Typically we are double checking each other and we missed it. Greater vigilance would have eliminated this error. We were also discussing the fact we were at 240 as assigned still inside of RDFSH was also a factor. We debriefed this all on the ground in detail. I later spoke with TRACON about this. They informed me that there were no separation issues and he did note the timing of the clearance when they reviewed the tape. We were flying the LINKK 1 Arrival, runway 27 to IAH. We confirmed all points in the MCDU and set the altitude down to 6000 we both confirmed the altitude we were then given a speed of 240kts with a clearance of descend via the STAR. I believe we were between RDFSH and GEYGR and the controller asked if we were going to make the crossing restriction at GEYGR which was supposed to be 4000, at this point I looked at the distance to GEYGR and it showed 4.2 miles and we had 2000ft to lose. We both looked at each other to confirm everything before we started to descend down immediately. There was not enough time to report that we were not going to make the crossing restrictions at 240kts and also the altitude. We both realized at this time that the altitude had not been changed for the lower altitude of 1500ft. at REDOC. The controller gave us a 360-degree turn back on course as we lost our altitude. At this point we realized our error. The controller called back with a number to call Houston for TRACON, we completed the approach and landed. Timing of the clearance was a factor, as well as not selecting lower altitude for the FAF of 1500 or double checking each other. Also should have discussed that we were inside of RDFSH and still at 240. We talked when on the ground in detail.
ASRS:1766489.s: The Captain and crew failed to set the 1500' FAF altitude for the ILS 27 approach at IAH, causing a missed 4000' crossing restriction at GEYGR. They were vectored for a 360-degree turn to rejoin the approach, though TRACON confirmed no separation issues occurred.

ASRS:1766491.n: During the landing rollout, after all three wheels were firmly on the ground and brakes were being applied, the airplane began to yaw to the right. At the same time, the right suspension settled down and the left wing rose significantly. I could not steer the airplane back towards the center line. I then brought the airplane to a stop via braking. Upon coming to a stop, I applied power to attempt to move and steer the airplane with neither being successful. The entire event was felt the same as a blown tire would. I then told the tower we had blown a tire and requested to shut down engines. After gaining permission, we shut down the engines and awaited city employees. After a city car arrived and circled the airplane to inspect the damage, I alone exited the airplane to speak with him and inspect the airplane myself. He informed me there appeared to be no damage, and I verified this with my own inspection of the tires and landing gear struts. I then decided to start the engines and attempt to move the airplane. Upon advising the tower, I started engines and applied power. The airplane moved normally. We then taxied to the gate with no further incident. It is my opinion, after observing no bald spots on the tires, that a gust of wind from the left lifted the left wing significantly and at the same time the right brake locked up or would not release from an applied position. After letting the airplane rest for a few minutes, the sticky brake may have released itself allowing movement as normal.
ASRS:1766491.s: The pilot reported a right yaw and left wing rise during landing rollout, suspecting a gust of wind combined with a locked right brake. After stopping and inspecting the aircraft with no visible damage, the brake reportedly released, allowing normal taxi to the gate.

ASRS:1766493.n: While cruising at 38,000 feet in VFR conditions the TCAS RA alert sounded. The First Officer and I performed the memory items and initiated the commanded climb. I advised ATC of our situation and was told by the controller that no other aircraft were observed in our area. TCAS then commanded us to descend and we also complied while looking outside for any intruding aircraft. The alert then said we were clear and went away. We regained our original altitude with no further conversation with ATC. All appeared normal and we determined the alert was false. The TCAS gave us 2 more false alarms. The 2nd was level at 30,000 feet and the 3rd was at 3,000 feet. While being vectored for the ILS Approach. Once on the ground the faulty TCAS was written up. Maintenance and Dispatch were made aware of the problem. After talking to Maintenance I was informed the TCAS system had been a continuing problem with multiple write-ups. I believe we were the first to get an RA alert, but it would've helped if someone had given us a heads up.
ASRS:1766493.s: The flight crew received multiple false TCAS RA alerts during cruise and approach, including at 38,000, 30,000, and 3,000 feet, despite ATC reporting no traffic. The faulty system was grounded for maintenance, revealing a history of recurring issues that had not been communicated to the crew.

ASRS:1766495.n: Before departure I randomly decided to look at the L1 door. I noticed that there was daylight coming from the aft vertical part of the door. I walked down from the upper deck to inspect the status of the door and noticed that the daylight was a 2-3 inch gap. The door handle was in the down and locked position and the forward part of the door was latched. Being that we were in a BCF (Boeing Converted Freighter), we had no way of knowing that the door was not secure because the BCF had no doors synoptic. I informed the Captain and he came down to inspect the door right about the time the ground crew personnel noticed the door was ajar. The door was then closed properly and we went on our way. The safety concern that we had as a crew was that we had no checklists or instructions to verify the L1 door was closed on the BCF, and without a doors synoptic page, we wouldn't of known it was still ajar. [Recommend incorporating] a check before departure from the crew to verify the L1 door is closed on BCFs that do not have door synoptic pages.
ASRS:1766495.s: The flight crew discovered a 2-3 inch gap at the L1 door on a Boeing Converted Freighter before departure, despite the handle being locked. The lack of a door synoptic page and specific checklist prevented detection until ground crew noticed the issue, prompting a recommendation for a manual pre-departure verification.

ASRS:1766504.n: When we arrived at the aircraft, there were three MEL items. Two were in reference to recent maintenance work on the aircraft. One of those required an inflight APU restart, and the second was in reference to work done on both engines that required a flight before the aircraft could be returned to ETOPS status. The specific MEL was 72-XXX, ETOPS In-flight Verification Required. Enroute to the destination, we performed the APU restart, and of course monitored the engines. The Captain was getting a line check, with the Check Airman sitting in the jumpseat. After the successful APU restart, the Check Airman volunteered to do the logbook entries. Although the engine MEL didn't give specific items that we were supposed to check, I did not realize that no logbook entry was made to this MEL. MEL 72-XXX is very generic and, in our case, was unclear [with] what specific checks needed to be accomplished. Also, whether causal or not, there were several distractors on this trip. The Captain was getting a line check, there was an unrelated maintenance problem that caused a two-hour departure delay, and our sequence was being broken up after our arrival at ZZZ.For MEL 72-XXX, in the DP (Departure Procedures) section, the Dispatcher is supposed to 'discuss the ETOPS verification requirements with the Captain.' I'm not aware that this discussion took place, which left us unsure exactly what we were supposed to do to clear this MEL. There should be a line in the 'O' section that says something like, 'The Captain will discuss with the Dispatcher what specific checks need to be accomplished.'
ASRS:1766504.s: The crew encountered an unclear ETOPS MEL (72-XXX) requiring engine verification and an APU restart during a line check flight. The reporter attributed the failure to log the engine MEL to ambiguous procedures, lack of dispatcher discussion, and operational distractions.

ASRS:1766540.n: Apparently I was exposed to the COVID on this flight. I received a call from Flight Attendant G that Flight Attendant A has tested positive. I wasn't too concerned at the time. My time with her was minimal. But I heard from Flight Attendant D that she too had tested positive. So I called the company to set up a test. After the testing I was informed I could not fly until I received the results. Just an FYI, we flew the aircraft with the XX-day spraying using Product X. The cleaners in ZZZ were very rushed because we arrived late. I do know they did not spray, which they didn't need to. But they also didn't wipe down any of the tray tables. I am unsure what else they did or did not do.
ASRS:1766540.s: A flight crew member reported potential COVID-19 exposure after two flight attendants tested positive, resulting in a temporary flight suspension pending test results. The reporter noted that while the aircraft received a scheduled disinfectant spray, cleaners in ZZZ were rushed and failed to wipe down tray tables.

ASRS:1766550.n: I was positioning for a take-off at ZZZ. AWOS noted that the preferred calm wind runways are X for landing and XX for takeoff (with pilot discretion). Also announced was the fact that taxiway A was closed between A-2 and A-4 so all traffic should be aware of back-taxing aircraft on the runway. Winds were about 3 knots and a slight cross wind. The plane in front of me taxied to XX for takeoff, including the back taxi from A-4 to A-2. I was stuck at A-4. The amount of incoming traffic began to increase, with all of it calling for a landing on [Runway] X. So it made sense for me to switch to taking off on X to keep with the traffic direction for better safety. I decided to taxi on the runway from A-4 to A-5 since I could not turn around where I was. Then I could proceed down A to the end at [Runway] X.Sitting at A-4, I waited for a plane to land and clear my position at A-4. I called my intention and then proceeded onto the runway to move down to A-5. Seeing a plane on final (est. 3/4 mile), I added power for more speed. I arrived at A-5 sooner than I thought and with too much speed. I pulled back the power (too late) and applied the brakes (too hard) and entered the turn into A-5 with too much speed, skidding off A-5 several feet until the prop hit and destroyed a taxiway light. I immediately proceeded to the closest parking spot, with no noticeable prop vibration or noise, shut down the avionics and engine, inspected the plane, and went into the FBO to discuss the incident.In the very brief amount of time I had to make a decision, I rushed to decide to speed up on the runway to get well out of the way of the incoming traffic I could see on final. Even though I had announced my intentions and had the right of way, I should have maintained a safe speed and warned the incoming plane to watch out for me and be prepared for a go-around if I didn't get off the runway at A-5 in time for him to reach my position. I often visualize different scenarios that might occur in flying, but I obviously didn't envision this one so that my instincts might have been better in that very small window of decision-making time. So now our club has to not only replace the prop, but have the engine disassembled, inspected, tested, and reassembled after the prop strike, with all the associated costs and plane downtime.
ASRS:1766550.s: The pilot, while back-taxiing on the runway at ZZZ to switch from Runway XX to X, accelerated to avoid an aircraft on final but entered a turn at excessive speed. This caused the aircraft to skid off the taxiway and strike a light with the propeller, resulting in significant damage and required engine inspection.

ASRS:1766564.n: Upon landing on Runway XXR at ZZZ, I exited on Taxiway 1 and turned left at Taxiway 2. The Controller asked my parking spot. I replied 'Company X.' Controller gave me taxi instructions and I replied 'Taxiway 3, Taxiway 4, cross Runway Y, into parking.' At intersection of Taxiway 2 and Taxiway 3, I turned left instead of right and taxied across Runway XXL. There was Aircraft Y on departure from Runway XXR already past me. Once I realized my mistake of turning left on Taxiway 3 instead of right, I stopped and told the Ground Controller. Most of the 1 hr and 40 minutes I had been on position with positions combined during moderate to busy traffic. I had been held over for 2 hours and a Supervisor was working LC with Tower in-charge on a single runway, so we were not using LUAW (Line Up And Wait). Additionally Runway XXL was closed as well (which we use to offset small arrivals to allow for more departures on XXR) and all these factors were adding complexity to an already busy session.Aircraft X exited Runway XXR and was given taxi instructions 'Taxiway 2, Taxiway 3, Taxiway 4, cross Runway Y and taxi to park' (Runway Y is a closed runway in my control). The pilot read back the instructions correctly. I had other aircraft taxiing and needed a runway crossing between the steady stream of arrivals and departures. I coordinated for the crossing with LC and after Aircraft Y went through the intersection on takeoff roll, I cleared the aircraft waiting to cross Runway XXR at Taxiway 5 to cross. I watched him cross, checked another plane taxiing to the runway, checked the printer for clearances, checked back on my crossing, and informed LC the Taxiway 5/XXR crossing was complete. At that point Aircraft X keyed up and said something like 'Uh, GC? I think we took a wrong turn.' I did a quick scan of the runway and didn't see him initially because one of the poles was in the way. I started to key up to ask him where he was and stepped back to re-scan and realized he was on the north side of XXR half on the runway and half off. I immediately informed LC of the situation. I turned Aircraft X around and held him short of XXR and told local I was too busy to find a hole to cross him and to just call me when he had a place for me to cross him back over. I informed the pilot of his possible pilot deviation and gave him the phone number and then moved on to other planes and clearances. This is an intersection we have had multiple issues with for runway incursions and last I knew is identified as a hot spot on the chart. Recently the airport added wig-wags to make it clear that it is a runway intersection to help stop pilots from doing this. ZZZ needs some sort of ground radar because even with the new safety lights installed they still cross. Some sort of early warning from an ASDE would at least give us a chance to catch this sort of thing.While the Supervisor was doing a very good job of working LC, I was still trying to keep my eye on him because of how little pro-time they need, the regular decrease in traffic from COVID slowing our skills, and the high volume of traffic he was working as well. If the traffic is regularly that volume at that time of day, it's imperative that three people be in the Tower, not two. The only way I could have caught this aircraft would have been if I was staring directly at him as he made the turn. The distance from Taxiway 2 to Runway XXR on Taxiway 3, is very short and I was focused on verifying the completion of the runway crossing Taxiway 5.Recommend 3 people in the tower from XA-XC pm.
ASRS:1766564.s: A pilot deviated from taxi instructions at ZZZ, turning left instead of right and entering active Runway XXR while another aircraft departed. The controller attributed the incursion to high traffic volume, a known hot spot, and insufficient tower staffing, recommending a third controller during peak hours.

ASRS:1766568.n: As part of my job as a CFI for a local flight school, I was looking to add tailwheel instruction to my list of instruction services I provide. I have about 15 total tailwheel hours, but very little recent experience. In order to improve proficiency, I went up with an instructor the day before the ground loop to get tailwheel current and get some additional training. We flew for an hour and did four full stop landings on the airfield's grass runway, and all were straight, and no issues came up during any of these landings that would suggest I needed additional training.
