On the day of the ground loop, the winds had shifted to be about 8 knots directly down the asphalt runway so I chose to use that one rather than the grass which would have had a 90-degree crosswind. During my first approach, I made a low pass to verify the sight picture in my mind and double check any wind correction that may need to be done. I executed a go around and came around for another uneventful approach to a planned 3-point landing. After a smooth touchdown with the airplane rolling down the runway, a gust lifted the right wing and a yaw to the left. My corrective actions did not prevent the airplane from ground looping. Upon reflection, there was a moment where I should have applied power to try to stop the yaw and execute a go-around. However, I believe my ego got in the way since I've been flying more than I ever have that I could 'save' the landing despite teaching my students to default to a go-around when things aren't looking right. My overconfidence in my skills, combined with ego resulted in me trying to save the rollout rather than going around. I also believe more than an hour of recurrent training prior to flying a tailwheel airplane is required, even though I have been flying a lot lately.
ASRS:1766568.s: A CFI with limited recent tailwheel experience ground looped a tailwheel aircraft during a 3-point landing on an asphalt runway after a gust caused a yaw. The pilot attributes the incident to overconfidence and ego, which led to attempting to save the rollout instead of executing a go-around.

ASRS:1766598.n: We departed on the RNAV Departure. The Captain was flying. I was Pilot Monitoring. Shortly after takeoff, while in a turn on the assigned lateral profile, Tower asked if we had helicopter traffic in sight at approximately our 2 o'clock position. I responded that we had the green helicopter in sight. The helicopter was slightly higher than our altitude. Shortly thereafter we received an Amber TCAS TA alert followed immediately thereafter by a Red TCAS RA alert instructing us to continue our climb rate. The helicopter had made a left turn directly toward us. We responded according to the RA guidance to climb even though the helicopter was slightly higher than us. Additionally we added a turn to increase visual separation with the helicopter traffic as we climbed above them and they passed below us.Because I don't know what clearance the helicopter traffic had, I don't know what could have been done to prevent this incident. It does strike me as odd that the helicopter was flying so close to the charted SID lateral profile that low to the ground and that close to the departure runway.
ASRS:1766598.s: During an RNAV departure, a helicopter turned toward the aircraft, triggering TCAS TA and RA alerts. The crew climbed and turned per RA guidance to pass above the helicopter, noting the incident was likely caused by the helicopter's proximity to the charted departure profile.

ASRS:1766629.n: The first 3 flights were uneventful and on arrival in ZZZ we were swapped into Aircraft Y - a broken airplane for ZZZ - ZZZ1. We were then swapped into Aircraft X - an airplane coming from the hangar that was a first flight and had a deferred APU. There was no ground air available at the gate and we were now an hour late. We boarded 30 passengers and had a Company Dispatcher Jumpseater. We started one engine at the gate and taxied out and performed a cross bleed engine start for #1. ATIS was reporting wind shear and we used wind shear numbers for takeoff on XXR, [Taxiway] XX, with ignition ON.On the takeoff roll I noticed an intermittent IDG 1 caution message, followed by an intermittent CONFIG SPOILERS warning message, a BTMS 3 that was dashes and two probe/window heat messages. I called abort and should have executed an abort procedure. I believed the message to be associated with a MEL on a previous flight, and I said, 'Associated, continue;' and continued the takeoff. The winds were very gusty. After takeoff we had a GEN 1 caution message and I ran the QRH for GEN 1, and in the process I accidentally switched off GEN 2, resulting in the ADG deploying. We [requested priority handling] and returned to ZZZ, landing on XYR. CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) was there and escorted us to Gate XXX. No injuries or complaints were reported. We were met by Maintenance and then had a 5-way call with Company, Maintenance, [another person], and one or two other people. I explained what had happened and told them of my mistake. I and the First Officer said that we were done flying and we were taken off our schedules. We then had a call with Maintenance and wrote up the airplane, including the #1 IDG, ADG deployment, and spoiler warning message.I called abort and should have executed an abort procedure. Once airborne, and running the QRH, I should have confirmed that the GEN1 switch was selected and confirmed with the flying pilot prior to actuating the switch. The day began early with an XA45 wake up to accommodate an XB45 van and [an] XC15 show. We completed the first three flights of the day without issue. Upon landing in ZZZ and swapping our good airplane for the plane we were taking to ZZZ1, we found out that that aircraft had maintenance issues and would require us to swap aircraft again. We were informed that there would be a delay in getting a new aircraft from the hangar. After waiting for about an hour the aircraft was finally coming from the hanger and we found out that it had an inoperative APU and it was its first flight of the day. Additionally, we would be having a Company Dispatcher in the jump seat. We were able to complete our first flight of the day items, acceptance checklist to include the first flight of the day items, complete an air start, push back, single-engine taxi out, and complete the cross bleed start without incident. We were set up for a wind shear takeoff with continuous ignition on.We were given a lineup and clearance and taxied onto the Runway of XXR at [Taxiway] XX. After a momentary wait, we were then given the takeoff clearance with a turn to the north. I was the flying pilot at the time, so I was given controls upon completion of the takeoff checklist. I pushed the thrust levers up and commanded for thrust to be set, the CA (Captain) confirmed thrust set and guarded the thrust levers. Shortly after this, a caution message appeared and the CA called out 'IDG 1' and called for the abort initially, but then said, 'Wait, that's associated.' The CA did not perform the abort, so I continued to fly the plane to ensure the positive control of the aircraft. Shortly after this, a warning message appeared momentarily, and the CA called out, 'Config Spoilers;' and the message disappeared. We continued the takeoff normally and began our turn to the north per ATC instructions.I was initially hand flying but shortly after reaching acceleration altitude, I called for the autopilot to be engaged. I called for the after takeoff checklist and noticed the caution messages that were present and called for the QRH. The Captain began to run the GEN 1 caution message QRH for the caution messages that were present. We noted the associated probe and window/windshield heat messages. While he was running the QRH he called out, 'GEN 1 off/reset, then on;' and reached up to perform this action. It appeared that he accidentally reset GEN 2 and the aircraft went dark momentarily, our EICAS and instrumentation screens went dark momentarily, and we heard the ADG automatically deploy. The CA immediately acknowledged his mistake and I continued flying by hand to maintain positive control of the aircraft while we sorted out the generator issue. The CA turned GEN 2 back on and communicated with me that we should return to ZZZ, I agreed.The CA then communicated to ATC that we needed to return to ZZZ and [requested priority handling]. The CA then communicated to Dispatch, the FA (Flight Attendant), and passengers that we were returning to ZZZ and to expect a normal landing. He did mention that there would be emergency vehicles near the aircraft, but that they were just a precaution and not to worry. We were then given vectors for the approach to Runway XYR, giving us time to brief our approach and landing, complete our in-range, approach, and landing checklists. We completed a normal landing, taxied back to our departure gate of XXX with an emergency escort, and arrived at the gate without issue.It would have been wise to perform the takeoff abort procedure at the earliest possible indication of an abnormal situation while the airspeed was still low and safe to do so. This would have prevented handling the aircraft issued in the air. Additionally, it is important to always confirm guarded switches with our fellow crew members to avoid making a stressful and abnormal situation worse.
ASRS:1766629.s: Pilots on a first-flight aircraft with a deferred APU continued takeoff despite multiple caution messages, then accidentally switched off Generator 2 while running the QRH, causing ADG deployment. The crew returned to ZZZ for a safe landing with no injuries, attributing the incident to failing to abort early and misidentifying a guarded switch.

ASRS:1766664.n: While on visual approach for 24R visual backed up by the RNAV approach in visual conditions we received terrain warning and pull-up between HIBAN and WUDAG between 3300-3450. We were cleared for the visual approach at 4000 feet when abeam the airport. I stayed at 4000 until between HIBAN and prose where I then set 3700 ft at 180 knots and flaps 20 had already been selected. I then set 3200 feet to not go below WUDAG and turned the autopilot [off] and hand flew I was above 3300 between WUDAG AND HIBAN when we got the ground proximity terrain and then pull up. We verified we were above 3220 at WUDAG in visual condition I climbed up 100 ft from [our] current position and the warning didn't last more than 3-4 seconds. Once leveled off and confirmed 100% there were no terrain clearance issues we continued the approach to landing.
ASRS:1766664.s: The flight crew received a terrain warning and pull-up alert between HIBAN and WUDAG at 3300–3450 feet during a visual approach. The crew climbed 100 feet, verified terrain clearance, and continued the approach to landing after the warning ceased.

ASRS:1766684.n: After sorting out an issue in ZZZ of not getting a cargo load report (CLR) notes on ACARS on any live animals. The flight crew simply asked [the] ramp agents to resend it. They were unable to do so so we simply asked for a paper CLR. The Ramp Lead became flustered with his scanner and went to go ask a manager for help. The manager came back about 10 minutes later after we had closed and gave the flight crew the notice to Captain form (first time we discovered there was dangerous goods onboard) and resent the CLR with the notes on DG (Dangerous Goods) and live animal (I noticed the bird and medical boxes on my walk around but didn't notice any markings on the medical boxes pertaining to DG). Already delayed pushing back we then became saturated with a runway change. Reaching cruise we became talking more about the lack of NOTOC (Notice to Captain) and an impending incident report. After talking for a few moments at cruise. I realized that we are not allowed to be carrying both dry ice and any live animals in the forward cargo bin together. After bringing that to light I began inquiring about possible diversion options. Including the destination of ZZZ1 40-45 minutes out. After the Captain messaged with Dispatch we decided to divert to ZZZ2 as that was the fastest option to separate the dry ice and live animal. Landing and taxing in we made sure we had a ramp crew that was informed of the situation and needing to open the fwd cargo door asap and remove the live animal. As well as a gate in ZZZ2. I went down to check as soon as the jet bridge was pulled up. And when I got down there the bird was out of the fwd cargo and in good health. The live bird was ok and the ramp agents took the bird into the office to be in the air conditioning and off the loud ramp environment while the ramp crew and flight crew figured out a new bag count. Cargo count. And any other required paperwork. I began calling for fuel. Loading in the new flight plan from the release while the Captain went down to talk to ramp managers as to what cargo is staying or going. A new and confirmed bag count after ZZZ2 rampers recounted bags and cargo (which did not match the original bag count out of ZZZ even though we only removed the DG) was received.After getting everything all figured out in ZZZ2 we calmly talked to the passengers and gave them a timeline of when we would expect to be pushing back and going to ZZZ1. After getting to ZZZ1. And finishing the flight. Deplaning. And, making sure the live animal was ok and in the possession of ZZZ1 Ramp Operations. The Captain and I began debriefing today's events. We reconstructed a timeline. No cargo load remarks. Called OPS. They began to get flustered about their system. We then just asked for a paper cargo load report to remedy the glitch in the system. The Ramp Manager came and threw though the window a notice to Captain. This was the very first time we realized we had any DG onboard. We then hyper focused on the problem of closing without a NOTOC and making sure to talk to OPS and Ground. When talking about this in the air. I realized the problem of the DG and live animal in the same compartment. We quickly then realized that this was not a situation that could continue. We began looking at diversion options. Talking to Dispatch and ZZZ2 OPS. We diverted and handled the situation at hand going forward. We talked about how there are numerous safeguards to never let a situation like this happen before it even gets to the airplane or airport/cargo processing counter for that matter. And how this is a prime example of reasons [for the] swiss cheese model. Starting early this morning with 3 runway changes and a wrong turn on a taxiway resulting in the first ASAP. Airline's ramp scanning system and software letting these be scanned together or a safeguard overridden to let this happen. Us hyperfocusing on discovering DG was onboard after closing with no NOTOC. And resulting in missing the combined DG and live animal in the same cargo compartment until cruise flight. Going forward and learning from this. This is a prime example of how to simply complete tasks and move on without hyperfocusing on the previous threats or errors. Today I, while operating Aircraft X from ZZZ-ZZZ1, made a grave mistake and allowed myself to depart ZZZ with dry ice and a parrot in the forward cargo bin. Upon discovering my mistake I contacted Dispatch and subsequently diverted to ZZZ2. The parrot was alive and we got some gas and continued onto ZZZ1 without further incident. While in ZZZ my FO (First Officer) noticed a big parrot and some medical looking boxes sitting outside cargo bin during preflight. He brought it to my attention. I was focused on making sure we had one or the other listed on load remarks. We got our baggage data but it did not generate a load remarks message. I released parking break while talking to [the] Ramp Lead via interphone. I inquired as to why we did not have a load remarks message. I asked if he could resend it. He was unsure of everything and went to find his supervisor. At this time I could not confirm if we had an animal or DG or both. I called Dispatch to see if he could look at stuff for me and he confirmed we got bag total the weight of some cargo thru close out but no load remarks. As a side bar I spoke with Name1 on the Hazmat hotline and he stated that company had to manually override scanner to allow for DG and animal at same time. Could this be why we didn't get load remarks? After about 10 minutes, [a] ramp agent returned but paced. He did not get back on intercom during most of this but when he did I explained he had a couple options. We could do a return to gate or they could give me a paper CLR (Cargo Load Report) thru [the] window if they could not fix it with [the] scanner. He radioed someone and a minute or so later a supervisor came out of an office and did not look happy. He had a wad of paper. He came to FO side and tossed the wad of paper thru window which ended up being the NOTOC for the dry ice. At about the same time we received the load remarks and I was focused on the DG the live animal got past me. I did not do this on purpose. At the time I was more upset with blocking out without the knowledge of DG on board and focused on making sure I had all my correct paperwork and it matched since I had DG. We also had the remark 'EXST:9A'. This threw me for a loop because I didn't know what it meant. We figured it out to be that a passenger had bought a seat onboard a raft for an animal which I already knew about because of gate agents and flight attendants. We had wasted enough time so I decided to continue with the push. We had a runway change on taxi out so I focused on getting thru that and we as a crew focused on operating safely until we were in a low workload environment to talk about it again. At cruise I was filling out incident report for not getting NOTOC when I was talking my narrative out loud the FO was looking at [the] FOM and said we have both an animal and DG on board and he just realized it as he was reading and telling me. We immediately contacted Dispatch who advised us to go to ZZZ2 or ZZZ3 and divert. I chose ZZZ2. I alerted [the] flight attendants and we landed in ZZZ2 without further incident. There was confusion on [the] ground in ZZZ2 as to which item should continue with us. The bird or dry ice. I called Dispatch again and they chose the dry ice and while I was talking to ramp they said company wanted to keep bird to ZZZ1. While checking packages manually in cargo bin I discovered the DG also contained Blood. UN3373. After OPS and company agreed, we departed to ZZZ1 without further incident. After landing I called Hazmat hotline and submitted pictures of bird and DG and ACARS remarks to company.I did not purposefully depart without NOTOC or depart consciously knowing we had dry ice and a bird in same bin. I know it's one or the other. I was just hyper focused on being legal that I missed connecting the two together. I believe I realize now that I can take as much time as I need to make good decisions. No need to rush. I did and it got me nowhere. I hope someone can imagine getting a wadof paper thrown into flight deck and the distractions of finally realizing the gravity of I had almost departed without knowing what was in cargo bin. I had always believed there were safeguards in place to prevent this from happening. This is the first time in 15 years of safe flying I've had to divert for a bad decision I made. I feel horrible and I'm glad the animal was still alive. I know it could have been much worse. I believe this flight had a happy outcome because of Dispatch and my crew. I tried to thank them but I cannot thank them enough.
ASRS:1766684.s: Flight crew of Aircraft X departed ZZZ with dry ice and a live parrot in the same forward cargo bin due to a missing NOTOC and scanner override. The crew diverted to ZZZ2 at cruise to separate the incompatible items, then continued to ZZZ1 after the bird was removed and the dry ice retained.

ASRS:1766685.n: During pushback, we experienced an intermittent, loud and clear radio station broadcast over the push crews headset. We had to repeat our communications several times due to the loud interference. The push operator stated that this has been a problem for 'several years' and nothing has been done to solve the problem. Communicating an emergency situation with the push crew could prove to be difficult and time consuming.
ASRS:1766685.s: During pushback, pilots and the push crew experienced loud radio interference over the headset, requiring repeated communications. The push operator stated this issue has persisted for years, creating a potential safety risk for emergency communication.

ASRS:1766707.n: During my compliance check I noticed Passenger X did not have a mask on. Passenger X's face was covered with a hoodie. I asked Passenger X to put a mask on and the reply was 'no I will not.' Passenger X was going to use the hoodie because it was a barrier. Passenger X started to shout at me and continued to tell me the hoodie would stay on. Passenger X started to go on about how a mask doesn't protect anyone, so at that point I said I would be back right back. Because he wanted to escalate the situation I went up to tell the A Flight Attendant, she came back and explained to Passenger X the company's policy. Passenger X's wife [also] added that the mask doesn't protect anyone. In the middle of flight, he then again put a blanket on his head and the mask was completely off.
ASRS:1766707.s: A flight attendant reported that during a flight, a passenger refused to wear a mask, claiming a hoodie or blanket provided sufficient protection. The situation escalated when the passenger shouted and his wife supported his refusal, leading the crew to reiterate company policy while the passenger continued to cover his face with a blanket.

ASRS:1766713.n: Captain didn't wear a mask throughout the airport, on the plane, in the [hotel] van, nor in the hotel. When asked by the flight attendants, he said he can't wear one. This puts us all at risk and with a higher chance of having to be pulled from the line if he tests positive for COVID.If crews cannot wear a mask, they should not be at work.
ASRS:1766713.s: The Captain refused to wear a mask in the airport, on the aircraft, in the hotel van, and at the hotel despite requests from flight attendants. The reporter states this behavior risks crew exposure to COVID-19 and potential removal from the flight line.

ASRS:1766718.n: The station received an e-mail to correct the logbook of Aircraft X. Contract maintenance, NAME, (NUMBER), at ZZZ replaced the SPCU on DATE. He failed to enter the item in the logbook. Upon further investigation, I found NAME unqualified on Company planes and logbook in Software.DATE, TIMEUpon clarification from tech, the SPCU was documented in the logbook. However, the galley battery meter module was not documented in the logbook. We're confirming the part number and performing ops check for the module.
ASRS:1766718.s: Contract maintenance technician NAME replaced the SPCU and galley battery meter module on Aircraft X but failed to log the latter. The technician was found unqualified on Company aircraft, prompting a part number confirmation and operational check for the undocumented module.

ASRS:1766725.n: While conducting 'pattern work' at ZZZ, during a touch and go landing, the aircraft began an initial climb. The out of currency private pilot stated 'Did you mess with the trim.' I, the instructor, replied 'No. What's wrong?' The pilot stated 'I can't get the nose to come down, the yoke is stuck.' I took control of the airplane, applied forward force on the yoke and it was stuck. With no usable runway remaining, I decided to leave power in and continue the takeoff. The aircraft was climbing at 65mph, above Vs1 and below Vx. I used elevator trim to attempt to get the nose down and stabilize the climb at a safe airspeed. The aircraft pitch decreased, airspeed increased. Shortly after, the controls suddenly popped, the aircraft pitched down due to the excess nose down trim, and control was returned to the yoke. I adjusted the trim and continued the climbout at Vy, we landed immediately and terminated the flight without further event. Upon inspection of the aircraft, all control cables appeared to be free and unmolested. Upon a post flight walk around, it was observed that a tail section screw had backed out and lodged itself between the stabilator, causing the control surfaces to be restricted. A preflight inspection of the aircraft was conducted by myself and the student, however neither of us noticed this issue.
ASRS:1766725.s: During a touch-and-go at ZZZ, a student pilot and instructor encountered a stuck yoke caused by a loose tail screw jamming the stabilator. The instructor continued the takeoff, used trim to stabilize airspeed, and landed safely after the screw dislodged and restored control.

ASRS:1766728.n: Loss of control during student simulated soft field takeoff involving Diamond Aircraft Industries DA20 aircraft, began to depart from Runway XX, by practicing a simulated soft field takeoff. On board the aircraft were an instructor and student. The primary focus of this dual exercise was for the student to refine the skills needed to perform a simulated soft field takeoff required as a private pilot task for FAA-S-ACS-6B. Prior to the flight the instructor thoroughly briefed the student on the proper exchange of flight controls through several exercises and it was clear to the student. After practicing the takeoff the first time, where the student made the mistake of keeping the stick fully aft, instead of slowly reducing back pressure once in ground effect, the student kept the stick in a full aft position creating a takeoff stall. The instructor was able to recover the aircraft by taking the controls and breaking the stall by lowering the angle of attack and regaining airspeed appropriate for a positive rate of climb. After the unsatisfactory performance of the soft field takeoff, the instructor decided to give the student another chance exercising a simulated soft field takeoff after completing several traffic patterns. Prior to taxiing Runway XX for takeoff the instructor asked the student how are you going to perform the soft field takeoff. The student responded with the proper procedure and the instructor reminded the student of his mistake last time he attempted a soft field takeoff. The student properly taxied to runway centerline using constant back pressure on the stick and increased throttle to full power. The student then used the proper right rudder pressure to compensate for P-factor. Once 500 feet down the runway, the airplane was able to get into ground effect however the aircraft was too slow pitch for Vx and after the instructor stated 'release the back pressure slowly' the student increased the pitch up and kept constant right rudder (stalling the airplane again). At this point the instructor took the controls and said abruptly 'my flight controls!' twice. The student failed to positively exchange flight controls to the instructor and locking the grip and control inputs contrary to the instructors. This lead to the plane striking the right wing on the runway pointing and losing control of the aircraft over the grass field to the right of Runway XX. The instructor then overpowered the students control movements to counter a possible cartwheeling right prop strike, banked left while reducing the throttle to idle which caused the airplane to strike its left wing on the grass where it landed. The instructor immediately secured the aircraft, preventing any chances of an onboard fire. Both the student and instructor survived with no injuries. It is unclear what total damage was done to the plane however there was visible damage to both wings.
ASRS:1766728.s: During a simulated soft field takeoff in a DA20, a student pilot stalled the aircraft twice by maintaining excessive back pressure despite instructor warnings. The student failed to release controls when commanded, causing the plane to strike both wings on the runway and grass, though the instructor recovered the aircraft with no injuries.

ASRS:1766737.n: I was scheduled to complete 3 takeoff and landings for currency. The flight was completed uneventfully. Today, I was contacted by a manager that it was discovered the aircraft registration had expired. Typically we would be flying this aircraft frequently, but all of the passenger flights had been cancelled the remainder of the year due to COVID concerns. Crews (myself included) are scheduled at various times to complete currency takeoff and landings. While we checked to make sure the registration was on board during our preflight, we did not notice that the date had expired. When this was just discovered by management and maintenance of the expirations, our company self-notified to the appropriate agency.There are several factors that contributed to this. I had my own contribution to this error by not verifying the date on the registration was current. It was determined the paperwork got mailed to a central location to the company and not directly to our hangar location. With COVID causing a reduced workforce in the location of mail delivery, we never got the paperwork forwarded of renewal and it wasn't until the second notification (delayed by a several weeks) that we got the notification. We have also been shifting different service providers for flight/trip planning and never was a flag raised that we were close to expiration on this document. We also discovered this wasn't tracked specifically on a maintenance program. Lastly, we would typically fly an international trip several times a year (but haven't flown any in 2020) that the registration would also be copied and verified current. There was not just one, but several contributing factors to this error. All these actions have already been corrected to prevent a future re occurrence. I have also learned from this that I made an assumption when checking to make sure the registration was on board that it was current, and that I didn't verify the date because I assumed it was tracked by several methods. The take away that I have from this, even if I assumed somebody else has tracked and checked some of the items that was included on our interior inspection preflight, I need to be more detailed on some of my checks. This is even more prevalent in the current times when the flight hours are drastically reduced. I flew an aircraft with an expired registration for landing currency. I ensured that the document was on board, but am guilty of not checking the date. It is my understanding that the registration is addressed to our corporate headquarters, not the hangar, and due to COVID restrictions limiting staff at headquarters, the reminder postcards never made it to our team. This is not an excuse for my actions, but I do believe it is a contributing factor in this event happening.We have already implemented corrective actions to ensure this never happens again. All of our registration certificates are now being tracked on our maintenance tracking software. We hired a company to automatically renew our registrations and have them delivered directly to our hangar. Additional training and language will be added to our company manuals to emphasize the need to ensure that we have valid and current documents on board for every flight.
ASRS:1766737.s: The pilot flew an aircraft with an expired registration for currency takeoffs and landings, failing to verify the document's date during preflight. The error resulted from mail delays due to COVID, lack of maintenance tracking, and the pilot's assumption that the registration was current.

ASRS:1766750.n: I was departing ZZZ1 and going northwest toward ZZZ2 with a slight jog to the east to avoid the ZZZ3 Class B. My plan departing uncontrolled ZZZ1 was to turn out to the south to climb above the ZZZ4 Class D and call TRACON for flight following and transition through the ZZZ Class C. I have done this dozens of times and never had any trouble getting TRACON to respond. However, I failed to consider that TRACON controllers are handling multiple sectors because of the pandemic. Presumably because of this I did not get a response from TRACON, and I hadn't properly planned for this possibility, and I flew into ZZZ's Class C without ATC communication. As [soon] as I realized that I had done so, I turned and descended to exit the Class [C] (while still avoiding the ZZZ3 Class B. Once I was sure I was clear of the ZZZ Class C, I turned back on course, and was able to establish flight following with the ZZZ5 sector of TRACON.I was assuming that I would get a response from TRACON and thus be cleared through the Class C, because that is what has always happened before, but I failed to plan for the possibility of what actually happened.
ASRS:1766750.s: The pilot departed uncontrolled ZZZ1 and inadvertently entered ZZZ Class C airspace without ATC communication due to assuming a response based on past experience. The pilot immediately turned and descended to exit the Class C, then re-established flight following with the ZZZ5 sector.

ASRS:1766761.n: Aircraft Y was at 2,000 feet MSL, and issued a climb to 3,000 feet to avoid converging VFR traffic who I was not talking to (squawking 1200) observed at approximately 1,700 feet MSL. Sector complexity was high due to IFR/marginal VFR conditions as well as an increase in usual volume we have seen over the past months. I was working 2 different frequencies as well. When I issued a climb to 3,000 feet to Aircraft Y, he read back 3,000 feet, and then I moved on to other priorities. The next time I observed Aircraft Y's altitude, I observed 3,400 and told him to stop his climb and issued a turn away from conflicting IFR traffic (Aircraft X at 040). I also turned Aircraft X away from Aircraft Y and issued traffic. I did not issue a Brasher warning.This was the busiest session, both traffic and complexity wise I have worked in many months due to decreased traffic volume due to COVID-19. I feel like if I had scanned better I would have caught Aircraft Y's altitude bust before I did. If my workload increases to this level in the near future, I feel asking for a split from the departure sector, or even calling someone over to act as a coordinator, or a '2nd set of eyes' when I feel task saturation is causing my scan to break down would be beneficial. I feel that both of these actions could prevent this from occurring again.Another important take away from this event in preventing [a] re-occurrence is to not have an expectation bias assuming a pilot will comply with your instructions, even if he reads it back correctly. A constant scan is absolutely critical at all times, (busy or slow) to ensure pilots are doing exactly what you told them and to prevent separation/deviation errors due to complacency and/or expectation bias.
ASRS:1766761.s: An air traffic controller issued a climb to 3,000 feet to Aircraft Y to avoid VFR traffic but observed the aircraft at 3,400 feet due to high workload and expectation bias. The controller subsequently ordered Aircraft Y to stop climbing and turned both it and conflicting IFR traffic away to restore separation.

ASRS:1766762.n: I was working Ground 1 & 2, CD/FD, combined for the COVID operations. There were quite a few aircraft taxiing out with arrivals interspersed. When I heard Aircraft Y call for pushback, I had three to go behind them, so I spoke to all other aircraft before getting back to them. When I got back to them, I corrected their climb via SID since they were only filed 11,000, and the LOA is initial 10,000. I gave them pushback on A west ok K after the last in line, [behind] a second company aircraft. About this time Aircraft X was rolling out to T on Runway XX Left with Gate XX. I was planning a left turn on B to D, then A when they called. A few other calls were done first, then I observed Aircraft X taxiing straight in K to A without having called. I told them that was a bad plan since I had Aircraft Y with pushback clearance at K and A, and I would have liked to be able to exchange that traffic. I concluded that Aircraft Y had not even started to push back, and simply gave Aircraft X taxi A for Gate XX. I received nothing further from Aircraft Y.Do not taxi clear [off] the runway further than is necessary, until instructed to do so.
ASRS:1766762.s: An Air Traffic Controller managing Ground 1 & 2 observed Aircraft X taxiing from Runway XX Left to Taxiway A without clearance, conflicting with Aircraft Y's pending pushback at the same intersection. The controller instructed Aircraft X to stop, citing the risk of collision with Aircraft Y, and subsequently issued a revised taxi clearance to Gate XX.

ASRS:1766771.n: I took over from the previous controller who didn't build what I considered enough space for the ZZZ1 arrivals. I started vectoring and building space between them. I had a lot of other things going on with most of the aircraft in the sectors needing approach services and help with rides icing. Aircraft X was overflying the ZZZZZ mountain range and ZZZ2 which is the IAF (Initial Approach Fix) for the active runway at ZZZ1. He was picking up ice so I tried to climb him out of the conditions. He came back and said that he couldn't continue the climb to 17000 ft. and would need to go back down to 15000 ft. He then had said he needed lower and I told him I had opposite direction traffic at 14000 ft. so if he needed lower I would need to turn him to the south. He said okay so I turned him to a 160 heading and gave him 14000 ft. He then said 'I stalled' and I noticed he began a rapid descent. I still had other aircraft and did a quick traffic scan and thought he was in a dive to regain airspeed to pull out of the stall. I thought the most helpful transmission I could give was to tell him what my MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) in the area was so if he was IMC he would know roughly what altitude he would impact the ground so he could plan his stall recovery dive accordingly. I decided in that moment to say only that and not use radio time/overwhelm him with the low altitude alert. I also wanted to leave the frequency open so he could make any requests like is there a road nearby to crash on or ask for a pilots assistance or recommendations. I thought he had seconds to a minute to live and felt like I needed to leave the frequency open. I also looked around for a topographical map of the ZZZ1 area which has disappeared or our atlas which is hard to locate so if he made a request of where the lowest possible terrain area or roads were. He pulled out of the dive, came back up on frequency, mentioned he didn't want to climb back into the clouds so I instructed him that I couldn't leave home IFR under the MIA. I asked if he was VMC, he said yes so I quickly gave him the option of canceling IFR and switching to VFR flight following so he could stay below the clouds and remain clear of ice. He lived.
ASRS:1766771.s: An air traffic controller vectored Aircraft X, which was icing over mountains, to 14,000 ft after the pilot reported a stall and rapid descent. The controller provided the Minimum IFR Altitude, and the pilot recovered, subsequently switching to VFR flight following to avoid clouds and ice.

ASRS:1766783.n: I was working Ground 1/2, CD-FD for COVID staffing. Local Control and FLM were separate. I had an aircraft pushing off of Gate XX/YY area which is right in the intersection of Kilo and Alpha. Aircraft X exited Taxiway Tango, and had to make a hard left turn onto Taxiway B to go around towards the Alpha gates. When I gave Aircraft X the instructions, they read it back and began a slow turn of about 135 degrees to go east bound onto Taxiway B. I thought nothing unusual of it. Then to my surprise I heard Local Control cancel Aircraft Y's takeoff clearance. My first thought was that they (Local) did not remember that Aircraft X had to go left onto Bravo and was anticipating the runway separation. At the time, it was clear that Aircraft Y was not rolling, and shortly after Aircraft X cleared completely they once again cleared Aircraft Y for takeoff.Well after the event the FLM and I were in an annual review discussion and they said that I probably did not notice it, but that I turned Aircraft X left on Bravo causing the departure delay of Aircraft Y probably saved an airborne VFR to IFR event that would have been significant. They explained to me that during this same time frame, while they were monitoring Local Control, a [group of] VFR aircrafts had called and were transitioning the airspace northwest bound. The first problem was that the UHF frequency got deselected and so when the Local Controller did not respond [the group of] VFR aircrafts returned to TRACON. While this was going on, and the frequency was subsequently selected, the Local Controller was trying to beat the Aircraft Z flight and I am guessing from the structure of the conversation that when all was said and done they told the Local Controller they should probably report the event.I have a few pieces of input:1. The FLM is one of the newer FLMs and extremely solid operationally, as well as very strong in communicating with people. I am not aware of how the interaction went between them and Local to get the cancellation of the takeoff clearance, as there were no words spoken above the volume only the two of them could hear. 2. The Controller working is a newer check out to the facility and a breath of fresh air operationally. I cannot say enough about them, from the perspective of being here to learn the job and become more proficient, in the times that I have worked with them. 3. The rest of the facility could learn from this event, and chances are there may be a briefing made from it, to express the importance of awareness of operational equipment, performance expectation bias, and not rushing when we are in a COVID traffic level, where there is really no need to push anything out of the ordinary.
ASRS:1766783.s: A Ground controller directed Aircraft X to turn left onto Taxiway B, causing Local Control to cancel Aircraft Y's takeoff clearance. The Flight Line Manager later stated this delay likely prevented a significant VFR-to-IFR event involving other aircraft due to a UHF frequency deselection issue.

ASRS:1766784.n: Aircraft X departed originally VFR under IFR conditions. TRACON was able to give IFR clearance. Aircraft X was level at 5000 ft. Upon entrance into the sector, they encountered icing conditions. Aircraft X was [issued a] climb to 8000 ft. and got out of the icing. Enroute to original destination, pilot asked for a diversion to ZZZ airport due to fuel. I cleared and gave aircraft pilot's discretion clearance to 5000 ft. That put aircraft back into icing conditions of which then icing equipment malfunctioned. Pilot asked for a descent out of the icing conditions. I issued a descent to 4900 ft. which was the lowest MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude). Pilot took the descent but continued to descend. Pilot was not able to maintain altitude and continued descending. We were looking for a safe place for the helicopter to land. Also, wanted to keep aircraft out of the clouds due to icing. Aircraft X requested priority handling. I tried to assist the best way I could due to the conditions. Pilot reported being in moderate to heavy icing conditions and was unable to maintain altitude.
ASRS:1766784.s: Aircraft X, a helicopter, encountered icing and fuel issues while en route, leading to a diversion request. After an equipment malfunction during a climb, the pilot could not maintain altitude despite ATC issuing a descent to 4900 ft, resulting in a continued descent and priority handling request.

ASRS:1766785.n: This is now the 4th Practice Approach (PA) issue we have documented in the past 30 days. ZZZ1 (TRACON) continues to not coordinate PA according to our LOA. They are introducing risk to the NAS by leading pilots to believe they are cleared for a PA and creating uncertainty. LC (Local Control) would have time to anticipate and better accommodate this pilot if ZZZ1 would have simply coordinated this procedure. Due to ZZZ1 not following their requirement in the LOA they are jeopardizing safety and not providing a good service to the flying public. We must get the answers to the following questions before we can move forward. Why did ZZZ1 issue a Practice Approach Letter to Airmen (PALTA) about 3 years ago? What are the reasons for it not reinstating the PALTA? Why was the workforce not briefed or trained on this change? What are the pros and cons of not having a PALTA?On (date), our General Manager signed the now expired PALTA in question. There were many requests from HQ for PA clarification and interpretations on this very topic throughout the past decade.Since the LTA expired on date, we have gradually started to see a thread of confusion among pilots and controllers. The very purpose of having a PALTA was to prevent this from happening. This has led to misinterpretations of many rules within the 7110.65 and the 7110.3. ZZZ ATCT has compiled over 10 falcon replays over the past 10 months that references this very trend and ZZZ2 ATCT has been experiencing similar issues as well. I would like those who review those replays to listen to the disappointment and frustration from the pilots. We are wasting their valuable time and not providing them with the best possible service. It must be clear there are only 3 possible separation rules that can be applied when handling a PA request. These rules are not to be applied by CPC choice at any given moment. 2 out of the 3 rules are defined on whether or not there is an effective LTA that lists your facility. With that being said, CPC and pilots must be trained and aware of these differences. Separation Rules (7110.65) a.1 [states that] IFR aircraft practicing instrument approaches must be afforded approved separation in accordance with Chapter 3, Chapter 4, Chapter 5, Chapter 6, and Chapter 7 minima until the aircraft lands, and the flight is terminated, or the pilot cancels the flight plan. For this argument we have not discovered any issues when complying.[Section] a.2 [states that] where procedures require application of IFR separation to VFR aircraft practicing instrument approaches, IFR separation in accordance with Chapter 3, Chapter 4, Chapter 5, Chapter 6, and Chapter 7 must be provided. Controller responsibility for separation begins at the point where the approach clearance becomes effective. Except for super or heavy aircraft, 500 ft. vertical separation may be applied between VFR aircraft and between a VFR and an IFR aircraft.The issue we have is some CPC are still following a.2 and some a.3. We must train our workforce on which they are to follow, which is dictated on whether or not we have an LTA. We can't allow them to apply a mixture of both these rules. For 2 years our effective LTA has dictated and conditioned pilots, instructors, students, examiners, and CPC that we must follow a.2. This basically implied to all users that they were going to be treated as if they were IFR doing a VFR PA. This was implemented to give VFR pilots and instructors the full experience so they can perfect the instrument approach procedures they are trying to practice. Various air traffic incidents have indicated the necessity for adoption of measures to achieve more organized and controlled operations where practice instrument approaches are conducted. Practice instrument approaches are considered to be instrument approaches made by either a VFR aircraft not on an IFR flight plan or an aircraft on an IFR flight plan. To achieve this and thereby enhance air safety, it is company policy to provide for separation of such operations at locations where approach control facilities are located and, as resources permit, at certain other locations served by ARTCCs or parent approach control facilities.We need to understand that a.2 is simple for all users involved and reduces risk to the NAS. Not to mention it provides a great and safe service to the flying public. The experience we afford the users when utilizing a.2 enhances safety, achieves a more organized and controlled operations where practice instrument approaches are conducted.[Section] a.3 [states] where separation services are not provided to VFR aircraft practicing instrument approaches, the controller must instruct the pilot to maintain VFR, advise the pilot that separation services are not provided, and provide traffic information or advise the pilot to contact the appropriate facility.The implementation of a.2 and the LTA requirement was to detour facilities from using this rule if they have existing resources. This rule creates confusing and is why we are now seeing unsafe trends since our LTA expired about a year ago. Some CPCs are following this rule and are lead to believe that no coordination is needed because they are not clearly them for the approach as they would when utilizing a.2. Some CPCs are still following a.2 and some are doing a mixture of both. We must train our workforce on which procedures must be followed when handling PA. We also need to brief the flying public as well. If ZZZ1 is not going to reinstate the LTA, all the LOAs with the towered airports listed in the LTA must be amended with detailed procedures on dealing with PA approaches, which include coordination requirements. I'm certain Mission Support would support my argument that we should follow a.2 and reinstate our LTA to achieve more organized and controlled operations where practice instrument approaches are conducted. The volume of VFR traffic in the ZZZ1 is on an upward trend and the last thing we need is uncertainty. We also must ask ourselves, why do most all other major approach control facilities in the NAS choose to issue a PALTA to enhance safety? Having the ability to issue a PALTA was given to us to migrate the very issue we are now having. By not choosing to issue a PALTA, ZZZ1 is jeopardizing safety by not creating a more organized environment where PA are being conducted. We understand that the approach control ATM has the discretion on whether or not they need to issue a PALTA however it is important that the workforce understands why they are making this decision. Especially when the data shows that we are now having mass confusion among pilots and CPC. A PALTA will mitigate this confusion immediately. Choosing to not reinstate an LTA on the sole purpose of pilot and CPC complaints is ludicrous and negligent. We did not see this chaos when the LTA was effective. Over the past 2 years ZZZ ATCT has noticed and documented a trend with PA and other facility are starting to notice as well. Our workforce and all the users involved deserve the best possible service and training. Why are we choosing not to provide pilots with a.2 service and waste their valuable time with a subpar service (a.3) instead? I'm asking that the national recurrent training team design a course on this very argument.
ASRS:1766785.s: Local Control reported that ZZZ1 TRACON failed to coordinate Practice Approaches per the expired LOA, causing confusion among pilots and controllers. This lack of coordination and inconsistent application of separation rules created safety risks and service delays in the NAS.

ASRS:1766786.n: This was the second leg of the day. I was the First Officer on my last day of a three-day reserve pairing and was assigned a ZZZ turn from ZZZ1. I have flown with this Captain before. During the initial briefing we briefed that a lack of proficiency due to reduced hours was an additive condition and that we needed to be extra vigilant to keep each other out of trouble. In my case, it had been 40 calendar days since my last flight. We were preparing to push back from the gate in ZZZ. We were on time. I called Ground for clearance to pushback, received it and notified the Captain. He gave the standard talk to the ground crew and I was clearing the right side of the aircraft for pushback. I did not noticed that the parking brake was still set. Ground Crew commenced pushback and the shear pin in the tow bar broke.More attention to switch position, avoid expectation bias and more flying wouldn't hurt. We were not rushed and there were not additional threats. I just stated to the push crew that the brakes were released and cleared to push, but I must not have pushed hard enough on the brake pedals. I should have verified the red Brake Released light was out. Since the brakes were still set, the tow bar pin broke and we swapped for a different tow bar. I just didn't verify as I should have. We are flying less, so we need to be even more attentive. Better attention to detail.
ASRS:1766786.s: The First Officer cleared pushback without verifying the parking brake release, causing the tow bar shear pin to break when the ground crew commenced the maneuver. The incident resulted in a tow bar replacement and was attributed to the pilot's failure to confirm the brake status due to expectation bias and reduced flight hours.

ASRS:1766821.n: On Arrival, ATC left us high. We were setting up for the approach and dropped in at the same time. I used flight spoilers on the descent due to being kept high by Approach Control. Pilot Monitoring was aware that we were dropped in and was monitoring my usage of spoilers the whole time. There were no checklist errors or airspeed errors and because this was at night into surrounding high terrain I made sure to observe altitude constraints and intercept the ILS approach outside of FAF. I briefed the FO and there were no questions. The approach went very well. Airspeeds were normal and so I believed were aircraft configurations. Though we had been rushed by being kept high. At no time did I or my FO ever notice anything out of the ordinary nor did my FO announce that we were not configured. On short final we received a spoiler deployed caution message. This occurs at 300 ft. AGL. The spoilers were only partially deployed still. They should have been stowed by 1000 ft. AGL per company policy. I stowed the partially deployed spoilers immediately and the message went away. The remainder of the approach was uneventful and I touched down in the touchdown zone normally and it was a nice landing. At no time was the aircraft unstable on the approach. Afterwards I was congratulated for the nice landing by the FO. At no time did the Pilot Monitoring alert me that the spoilers were still partially deployed. I noticed the caution message at the same time. I took the corrective action and stowed them as the aircraft completed the approach and landing without incident. At no time before, during, or after the event was I alerted by my FO that there was a problem. At the debrief after the flight, he made no mention of his part in also not noticing the flight spoilers were partially deployed. My error was to leave the flaps partially deployed due to a high workload. I stowed them once alerted and at no time was the aircraft unstable or in a dangerous position regarding airspeed or control on the approach. It has been brought to my attention that this was reported by my FO without sharing his concerns or any concerns with me regarding this event even though he also was at fault in his Pilot Monitoring duties. I feel as though while this was a configuration error per company SOP's it is not a safety report and should not have been filed as such by my FO. I had concerns over my FO's performance over the course of our two trips together. He had programmed an earlier approach incorrectly which I had to correct [while] turning final. He had read back incorrect headings to ATC on one occasion and had failed to stow the thrust reversers after landing at the end of one flight. With all that being said, I worked those things through with him and talked about them with him. Perhaps he felt a little insecure about those issues and this was his way of 'getting back' at me. I certainly wish he would have discussed this occurrence with me as I had with him out of a sense of mutual and constructive support and respect. Communication is always the best policy. I wish my FO had brought his concern to my attention, as I did with his previous errors, constructively. Configuration of Flight Spoiler Caution message was received at 300 ft. on short final at ZZZ. Captain was flying and forgot to stow flight spoilers after ATC left us high on arrival. At 11,000 ft. and 20 miles west of the airport, we had to hustle down. Captain forgot to stow flight spoilers after turning final for Runway 24. Caution was noted by both crewmembers. Flight spoilers were stowed and an uneventful landing was made. I believe a good possibility for this error was because of not ensuring the 'IM SAFE' checklist was satisfactory. At the end of our trip last week, the Captain received sudden notice that a fellow co-worker passed away that he was close to. I observed the impact to the Captain's emotional state, confronted the Captain and asked if he was safe to complete the rest of the trip. He insisted that he was. Finishing our last few legs, I could tell the Captain wasn't into the game and I was pointing out minor errors and missed tasks which he thanked me for and acknowledged. The Captain concluded our trip but stated he would be spending the next several days traveling to the coworker's funeral and would be back in time for our next trip, which commenced today. After the first trip I contacted professional services to report my concern for the Captain's safety condition for our next trip that was quickly approaching. Today, the Captain and I greeted at the gate and he indicated he had gone to the funeral, as well as traveled home, and also traveled back to work within a span of 3 days. I was hopeful the Captain might take some time off. However, he did not and showed up for work today, still contending with the death of our coworker. Our flight to ZZZ was uneventful until short final, which is when we received a Caution Flight Spoiler Configuration message at 300 ft. AGL. The Captain stowed the spoilers and we landed uneventful. I am filling out this safety report because I feel I did my due diligence to show my concern for my Captain in a respectful and professional manner, hoping he might excuse himself from a trip to ensure his safety condition was back to 100%. That may have been a contributing factor to forgetting the flight spoilers on a VFR approach and landing tonight.
ASRS:1766821.s: The Captain forgot to stow flight spoilers after ATC left the crew high on arrival, resulting in a configuration caution at 300 ft AGL. The First Officer reported the event, attributing the error to the Captain's high workload and emotional distress following a coworker's death, though the landing remained uneventful.

ASRS:1766829.n: Departed ZZZ following radar vectors and assigned altitudes. We entered IMC (Instrument Meteorological Conditions) conditions and shortly thereafter we received erroneous readings on airspeed and altitude from both primary flight displays. I assisted the FO (First Officer) in attempting to keep the plane under control, but quickly had to take control of the plane due to large pitch changes taking place from bad information from the flight directors. After disconnecting the autopilot and auto throttle I was able to get level pitch and a thrust setting for straight and level. I was able to determine the standby instrument was the most reliable and used that while the First Officer ran the QRH (Quick Reference Handbook) for airspeed unreliable to maintain a safe level flight. There had been prior to me taking control altitude deviations of 2,000 ft. and the airspeed was rolling back on my PFD (Primary Flight Display) to speeds from 0-162 kts, while the First Officer's ranged from 250-320 kts.The flight exited the clouds and we were VMC (Visual Meteorological Conditions). To assist the First Officer, I completed radio transmissions. I demanded lower altitudes to remain clear of IMC conditions. Once below the clouds, I was able to work with the First Officer for completion of the QRH, setting up an approach, and completing necessary checklists. The speed brake would not arm, during the approach, so at touchdown I had to manually deploy the speed brake. This all happened very quickly and I never was able to formally advise ATC due to excessive workloads. I was provided priority handling by ZZZ Center and ZZZ Approach. The approach was a visual with a successful outcome.[Causal factors], failure of one or both air data computers or associated systems. It is unknown by the pilot what those might specifically be.
ASRS:1766829.s: The pilot and First Officer experienced erroneous airspeed and altitude readings on both Primary Flight Displays while in IMC, causing 2,000 ft deviations and unreliable flight director data. After disconnecting automation and using standby instruments to maintain control, they completed a visual approach with manual speed brake deployment due to suspected air data computer failure.

ASRS:1766837.n: The aircraft had been sitting for the previous 5 days. When we got to the aircraft there was a new maintenance item which they were working on and 2 items to be verified during our flight to ZZZ. This was MEL XX-XX. The APU restart was accomplished and the other was an in-flight verification of engines. We discussed and did not find an entry for monitoring engines and made no entry after everything remained within parameters. I was getting a check ride from a check airman and he offered to make the entries (including a new write up) in the logbook for me since we were now on approach to ZZZ.Main factor was the flight plan was supposed to be locked out, so I could discuss the engine check and any entry needed with Dispatch. That didn't happen as well as on the following flight when it could have been accomplished again. Delays and distractions with the ongoing maintenance item which kept us out of our seats for 2 hours and feeling rushed to get things going quickly, having passengers already on board, once we could sit down. My complacency having a check airman there in case I missed something.If flight plan needs to be locked out make it automatic for Dispatch, so distractions or human error don't play a part. MEL XX-XX needs to be more specific as to what items need to be accomplished. A placard in the logbook would be helpful.
ASRS:1766837.s: A pilot and check airman conducted an in-flight engine verification for MEL XX-XX on approach to ZZZ but failed to log the entry due to distractions from maintenance delays and reliance on the check airman. The reporter attributed the error to a flight plan not being locked out for Dispatch coordination and personal complacency.

ASRS:1766851.n: While enroute in cruise at FL 370, the aircraft displayed a 'DRIVE' discreet caution light for the right engine generator and associated 'R GEN DRIVE' EICAS message. This was not necessarily a 'startle event' to us because we had experienced the same malfunction in the same aircraft on the previous flight to ZZZ1 that morning, and it had an MEL for this flight. At the beginning of the flight, upon pushback, we had to block turn back in when we had an 'L GEN OFF' EICAS message associated with a left engine generator that was cycling on and off. Following the block turn back, we had assisted local maintenance with extensive troubleshooting for the generator(s) which, I believe, resulted in swapping the GCUs (Generator Control Units) between left and right engines to render one generator (the right generator) operable for flight. At cruise, upon recognizing and identifying the 'R GEN DRIVE' malfunction, we ran the appropriate QRH checklist. We then gathered weather information for potential diversion airports in the area and ultimately decided that continuing to ZZZ was our best option for ceiling and visibility conditions. We requested priority handling as a precaution and turned directly to ZZZ. Arrival, approach, and landing were uneventful. We did not find any QRH guidance for the left and right generator off in the electrical non-normal section. While this situation is extremely [un-]likely to occur, it may be worth considering adding guidance for dual generator failure. Flight dispatched with right engine generator inoperable. After block, left engine generator became intermittent. Flight crew ran QRH and cycled the generator but that was no help. Flight returned to the gate and contacted Dispatch via ACARS.
ASRS:1766851.s: The flight crew experienced a right generator drive failure at FL 370 and an intermittent left generator issue after pushback, following a GCU swap to enable the right generator. They diverted to ZZZ with priority handling and landed uneventfully, noting a lack of QRH guidance for dual generator failure.

ASRS:1766874.n: Day 1, leg 1 of a 4 day trip from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was the pilot monitoring on this leg. Had not flown much in the last few weeks. Captain was PF. We flew to ZZZ1 at a pretty low altitude, I believe it was 14,000 feet cruise altitude. After starting the descent, we did not realize we had passed 10,000 feet so quickly, and noticed our speed was beyond 250 knots. The Captain immediately slowed the descent rate and airspeed, in order to return to 250 knots.We were distracted. We were on the first leg of the trip, had woken up pretty early, and the fact that we cruised at such a low altitude were possibly all factors. We did not pay enough attention in the descent.I should have kept better monitoring skills during the descent and avoided distractions.
ASRS:1766874.s: The Pilot Monitoring and Captain exceeded 250 knots below 10,000 feet during descent to ZZZ1 due to distraction and low cruise altitude. The Captain immediately reduced descent rate and airspeed to comply with speed restrictions.

ASRS:1766906.n: After takeoff from ZZZ, I went to pull the power back into climb power. Upon doing so I noticed severe engine roughness with the left engine, and the throttles were split several inches. I applied full power as I thought the left engine was going to quit. When I contacted departure, they advised that an Airport Operations vehicle witnessed billowing black smoke from the left engine as I entered the clouds. I left the power full as any time I brought the power back it felt like the left engine was going to quit. I notified ATC. They vectored me for the ILS XX, when i did bring the power back to fly the approach and land, the engine was smooth and did not quit. As a precaution I had the airport fire trucks come over and make sure there was no sign of fire or further smoke upon landing. They advised they didnt see anything unusual. I then taxied to the gate and wrote the airplane up.
ASRS:1766906.s: The pilot reported severe left engine roughness and split throttles shortly after takeoff from ZZZ, with ground observers noting black smoke. Although the engine ran smoothly during the ILS approach and landing, the pilot wrote up the aircraft as a precaution after fire trucks found no signs of fire.

ASRS:1766916.n: Cleared to 'cross ZZZ at or above 14,000 feet, cleared for the ILS Z XX approach.' Inattention to what mode the descent was in and tied with teaching on an OE, I descended to approximately 13,000 feet before realizing the error. We were in VMC conditions and had terrain in sight. ATC did not mention the error.Performing OE for new FO and inattention to cleared altitude. Pay more attention during training on OE. PM on OE and cleared to cross ZZZ at or above 14,000 feet, then cleared for the ILS Z Runway XX approach. VMC with terrain in sight, descended below 14,000 feet prior to ZZZ. Noticed the error, but ATC did not say anything. Continued the approach and landed without further incident. Probably inexperience with the plane mostly, and also recency/currency, this was my first flight in an actual plane in about 7 months. It was a new plane (I was on OE) and an unfamiliar airport. The Check Airman and I had discussed the arrival/approach and how he was going to fly it during cruise but at the time were reviewing how to use the different descent modes to fly the approach and were momentarily distracted.More active monitoring and attention to what the plane's programming is doing, also experience in the plane will likely help.
ASRS:1766916.s: A Check Airman and First Officer on an Operational Evaluation descended below the cleared 14,000 feet crossing altitude at ZZZ due to distraction while reviewing descent modes. The error occurred in VMC with terrain in sight, but ATC did not intervene, and the crew landed without further incident.

ASRS:1766940.n: During pre-flight review of the logbook, I noticed the Oil Temperature had been written up multiple times, and OCF (Operational Check Flight) had failed, and the right engine had been replaced. I brought this to the CA's (Captain's) attention so we could both monitor the engine oil temperatures during the flight. After we joined the departure, and were passing through 10,000 ft., I observed the oil temperature at 130 degrees. I brought this to the CA's attention and had requested me to review the High Oil Temp QRH. While I was reading through the QRH, we both watched the oil temperature continue to climb. Even as the CA was complying with the QRH and reducing power on the affected engine, the oil temperature would not stop rising. By the time we finished the QRH, the right engine was at flight idle and the oil temperature was still climbing. At that time, the CA called for the Intentional Shutdown QRH. We worked through this checklist and complied with all items as well as the subsequent, single engine descent and single engine landing checklist. The landing was uneventful. We taxied to the gate. With the oil temp having been written up multiple times, we were concerned about this being an issue on the flight. But having recently been brought from [maintenance], there was nothing to refuse. Also the engine had been replaced and ops checked with a ground run. The CA and I decided the continuous monitoring of the oil temp was our only available mitigation tool.
ASRS:1766940.s: The First Officer and Captain monitored rising right engine oil temperatures during climb after a recent engine replacement and failed operational check flight. Despite reducing power and executing the Intentional Shutdown checklist, the temperature continued climbing, resulting in a single-engine landing that was uneventful.

ASRS:1766946.n: Unable to locate Jefferson Hospital heliport, orbited multiple times, eventually located roof top pad and landed.Landing pad markings are faded, weathered, and need to be repainted. The pad itself is located in a high density of other buildings and structures not easily identifiable. Possible high intensity strobes could be added, such as the runway-end identifier type.
ASRS:1766946.s: A pilot orbited multiple times unable to locate the Jefferson Hospital heliport due to faded markings and surrounding structures before landing on the rooftop pad. The reporter recommends repainting the pad and adding high-intensity strobes to improve visibility.

ASRS:1766998.n: I was forced to deliver [aircraft type] differences class using Distance Learning to mechanics in ZZZ & ZZZ1 while I was in ZZZ2. X mechanics in ZZZ sat in a common area together with nonstudents. 5 mechanics in ZZZ1 sat in a common area together with nonstudents. The mechanics in ZZZ each had their own laptop, camera, microphone & speakers. The mechanics in ZZZ1 had one TV screen, one camera, one microphone and one speaker. Throughout class all the mechanics had to be muted due to poor audio quality, this made it impossible to tell if non class related conversations were occurring. Throughout class the mechanics in ZZZ cameras were not always displaying their face, making it impossible for me to observe their comprehension. Throughout class the mechanics in ZZZ1 were too far away from their shared camera, and often not visible on camera, making it impossible for me to observe their comprehension. Throughout class there was a lengthy delay in the audio to video, making class interaction difficult to the point it was nonexistent. During the test there was talking amongst students that the proctor was not controlling, and most students failed the test. The students were given a retest by the proctor without receiving remedial training. Based on these events I was not able to follow company policy and not able to accomplish the objectives on [the training].During the class the internet connection was not reliable enough to promote class participation. After class was over I received an email, and later a phone call from one of the AMTs that attended class. He had some questions regarding one of the systems on the [aircraft type] that were discussed during class. I explained the system in depth, to a level that goes above and beyond [the training], but I am concerned the other mechanics may also have questions and whether they fully comprehended the objectives of [the training].The company has a desire to have a large number of mechanics trained on the [aircraft] and to save money, the company is forcing me to teach utilizing Distance Learning.Stop teaching the [aircraft type] via Distance Learning and return to in person classes.
ASRS:1766998.s: An instructor conducting remote [aircraft type] differences training for mechanics in ZZZ and ZZZ1 reported that poor audio, video delays, and unreliable internet prevented effective monitoring and interaction. Consequently, students failed the test, received unauthorized retests, and the instructor concluded that distance learning failed to meet company policy or training objectives.

ASRS:1767001.n: I issued MEL XX-XX to Maintenance Technician Y, after he had accomplished the MEL maintenance procedures, an MEL placard was placed in the logbook. But I forgot to generate an XX-XXXX, follow-up/repetitive inspection form. Out of Practice: Have not actually worked a desk since the X type aircraft were parked [several months ago]. Stress: Presently going through personal issues. Provide a review/refresher class for technicians that have been idle during the pandemic. Add a step to the X procedures of all MELs that states to generate an XX-XXXX, and highlight that step.
ASRS:1767001.s: A pilot issued an MEL to a maintenance technician but failed to generate the required follow-up inspection form due to being out of practice and personal stress. The pilot recommended refresher training and procedural updates to prevent recurrence.

ASRS:1767009.n: Had Aircraft X assigned to me and Mechanic on my shift DATE third shift. Aircraft X had an inbound write up for potable water system inop. The t/s was started on first shift DATE and continued thru second shift. Parts was changed and panels remove but when I got aircraft assigned to me and my work partner there was no work turnover in the log book or no form 10194. My work partner and I was expected to continue work on the issue with on clear understanding with what work was actually done. The event occurred because of improper turnover.Document work that is done. I was assigned Aircraft X with NAME1. I was informed by my lead that there was an inbound discrepancy which was worked by 1st and 2nd shift and that parts were changed. I asked where are turnover was at, which is supposed to be documented on a company form, I was informed there was none and that he was given a verbal turnover only. I immediately informed my supervisor. We then went out to aircraft to perform RON service check and found multiple cargo panels removed which just confirms maintenance was being worked and not documented. The event occurred due to maintenance being done accomplished on Aircraft X with none of it documented. This happened across 2 shifts.Supervision and Leads/Crew Chiefs need to make sure all turnover is documented per company policy.
ASRS:1767009.s: Mechanics on the third shift found undocumented maintenance on Aircraft X's potable water system and cargo panels after two previous shifts failed to log work or provide Form 10194. The incident resulted from improper verbal turnover instead of required written documentation per company policy.

ASRS:1767016.n: Our operation was just notified on Date that our aircraft registration expired. I operated two training flights as PIC. The first was [date] and the second was [date]. I am guilty of just looking to ensure that the document was on the airplane, while completely disregarding my duty to ensure that it was valid. A contributing factor to this is that the aircraft registration is addressed to our company headquarters, which is a different address than our operations base hangar. Due to COVID related staffing at our headquarters, our FAA reminder postcards were never delivered to our hangar. Again, it is my responsibility as PIC to ensure that the correct paperwork is on the aircraft prior to each flight.We have instituted the following changes to ensure that this does not happen again: 1) Added the registration expiration to our maintenance tracking software, Flight Docs. This will flag our maintenance team when expiration is close to occurrence. This will also be printed on the preflight form that all pilots utilize. 2) Training will occur and language will be added to our manual and/or expanded normal procedures document emphasizing the action to ensure that a valid registration is onboard the aircraft. 3) A consultancy company has been hired to automatically renew our registration and deliver it directly to our hangar.
ASRS:1767016.s: The PIC operated two training flights in an aircraft with an expired registration, admitting they only checked for the document's presence rather than its validity. The oversight occurred because FAA renewal notices were not delivered to the hangar due to staffing issues, prompting the company to implement new tracking and renewal procedures.

ASRS:1767058.n: While doing pattern work, I was number two to land following a Citabria, I believe, which was doing a touch and go, and the spacing was close, but I was certain there was enough spacing for the Citabria to take off prior to my landing, but the tower issued a go around to me. When I reached down to retract the flaps I lost sight of the Citabria momentarily and when I reacquired it I was closing on it very fast, just left of my course. I immediately made a right climbing turn to avoid the Citabria.The tower gave me traffic that was in the right pattern, I had originally been using the left pattern, and I acquired that traffic and was instructed to follow it, and completed a touch and go. After the event, my passenger said he thought he had heard the controller instruct me to turn left on the go around. It's possible, but my passenger had just said something to me as the controller was issuing instructions and I missed that.It appeared the primary tower controller was a trainee, we could hear someone in the background instructing him to correct instructions to aircraft in the pattern and approaches. This whole event could have been avoided had the controller not instructed me to go around when there was enough spacing to avoid a conflict with the departing aircraft.
ASRS:1767058.s: A pilot conducting pattern work received an unnecessary go-around clearance from a trainee controller, causing a loss of sight of a departing Citabria and a rapid closure. The pilot executed an evasive right climbing turn to avoid a collision, attributing the incident to the controller's premature instruction.

ASRS:1767073.n: 'Our operation was just notified on [date] that our aircraft registration expired. I operated a training flight on [date]. I am guilty of just looking to ensure that the document was on the airplane, while completely disregarding my duty to ensure that it was valid. A contributing factor to this is that the aircraft registration is addressed to our company headquarters, which is a different address than our operations base hangar. Due to COVID related staffing at our headquarters, our FAA reminder postcards were never delivered to our hangar.
