Again, it is my responsibility as PIC to ensure that the correct paperwork is on the aircraft prior to each flight.We have instituted the following changes to ensure that this does not happen again: 1) Added the registration expiration to our maintenance tracking software, Flight Docs. This will flag our maintenance team when expiration is close to occurrence. This will also be printed on the preflight form that all pilots utilize. 2) Training will occur and language will be added to our manual and/or expanded normal procedures document emphasizing the action to ensure that a valid registration is onboard the aircraft. 3) A consultancy company has been hired to automatically renew our registration and deliver it directly to our hangar.'
ASRS:1767073.s: The pilot conducted a training flight in an aircraft with an expired registration, admitting to checking for the document's presence but failing to verify its validity. The oversight occurred because FAA renewal notices were not delivered to the operations base due to staffing issues at the company headquarters.

ASRS:1767077.n: During let-down on a VFR descent from 11,000 ft., I noticed the power would not retard below 22 inches of manifold pressure. I continued my let-down to ZZZ1 to 1000 ft. above the pattern altitude while troubleshooting the problem. I lowered the landing gear to increase drag in an attempt to get below flap extension speed. I had to apply approximately 2Gs to the aircraft to slow to flap speed. Once the flaps were extended, I determined that the aircraft would continue to accelerate, I raised the flaps.During troubleshooting, I noticed that I could still get maximum power if required. I let traffic in the ZZZ1 pattern know that I was an emergency, and that I was working the issue. A local pilot awaiting takeoff (who apparently was also an Airframe and Powerplant Mechanic, and an Inspection Authority) recommended leaning the engine to LOP (Lean of Peak) on final to control airspeed, and a diversion to ZZZ due to more runway available. This comment was helpful, as I was already considering a diversion due to greater runway length, and the availability of emergency crews. After one turn over the airport, I diverted to ZZZ.I contacted ZZZ Approach, formerly requested priority handling with them and [stated] my intentions. I was able to clear the terrain between ZZZ1 and ZZZ easily and set up for a long, flat, straight-in approach to Runway XX. The handoff to Tower was uneventful. I flew a flat, power-on approach and maintained approximately 120-130 KIAS. As I approached the runway, I gradually leaned the engine to the onset of roughness. I maintained a zero-flap approach. As the aircraft slowed, I lowered flaps to 10 degrees, and executed a normal landing. While in the flare, I reduced the mixture to idle cut-off and touched down. I maintained an aero-brake, and lowered flaps to 30 degrees to increase drag. I turned off at the taxiway turn-off, with approximately 3000 ft. remaining. Airport Fire and Rescue helped recover the aircraft to the FBO maintenance hangar.Post-flight maintenance revealed the control rod from the throttle housing to the waste gate controller had become disconnected, preventing the waste gate from fully opening, and provided boosted power with the throttle fully retarded.Kudos to the crew at ZZZ1 for offering help without knowing I am a former military pilot. Their timely comment confirmed for me an appropriate action, and helped me maintain control in a critical phase of flight.
ASRS:1767077.s: During a VFR descent from 11,000 ft, the pilot experienced a throttle malfunction preventing power retardation due to a disconnected waste gate control rod. The pilot diverted to ZZZ, executed a zero-flap approach with leaned mixture to control speed, and landed safely with 3,000 ft of runway remaining.

ASRS:1767082.n: On final there was a near midair collision. We turned final and base without being cleared to land. Our radios had shut off and the pilot in command had thought he had heard a clearance to land, but he had not. A Cirrus in bound on a straight in final had to go around to avoid the collision.
ASRS:1767082.s: The pilot in command and a Cirrus aircraft were involved in a near midair collision on final approach. The incident occurred because the crew's radios failed and they landed without clearance, forcing the Cirrus to go around to avoid collision.

ASRS:1767126.n: I flew the aircraft on the previous flight and everything was normal. On preflight, oil levels were normal. No issues were noted on run up. Everything seemed normal and I thought nothing of the flight. We took off from Runway XXL. We didn't level off until our cruise altitude of 7,000 ft. At that altitude the student ran the cruise check. We did offset our 65% cruise power setting for the 1% difference with an ISA (International Standard Atmosphere) of -12C. Shortly after the cruise checklist was complete we were handed off to ZZZ Center. At this point we were just passing ZZZ2. Then the EGT on the right engine began to roll back. It stopped around 1,000 degrees. I immediately checked the selectors, boost pumps, mags, turned on the alternate air and then went to the mixture to adjust it. I brought the mixtures to rich and the EGT went to 200 degrees. I then re-leaned the mixture and the engine momentarily went up to around 1,300 to 1,400 degrees. At that point the engine started running rough and then quit. We tried running the engine failure during flight non-memory items but that did not restart the engine. At that point I decided it was time to secure the engine to maximize our performance. I immediately requested priority handling with ATC before assigning my student the roll of PM (Pilot Monitoring). I identified and verified the right throttle, prop and mixture with him and our engine was then secured. At this point I coordinated with Center and was cleared back to ZZZ1 via a right or left hand turn. I turned to the left and we were then proceeding direct to ZZZ1. On the way back to ZZZ1, we conducted the non-memory items for the engine securing procedure. I then contacted the Dispatcher to inform him that we were coming back to ZZZ1 single engine and that we would like a tug to meet us on the runway. Due to strong winds out the northwest the flight back to ZZZ1 was long. This gave my student and me plenty of time to brief how our landing was going to work and coordinate what each of our responsibilities would be. On the flight back I did my best to maintain as much altitude as possible. With our performance we were able to maintain 6,000 ft. without issue. Around 20 miles from ZZZ1, Approach gave us a clearance to descend at pilot's discretion down to 3,000 ft. I maintained 6,000 ft. until we were approximately 10nm away from the airfield. At that point I began maneuvering to enter a four mile final for the visual Runway XXR. I also did the descent checklist at this time. Around 2,000 ft. on the base for the visual, I conducted the One Engine Inoperative landing check. I did not extend the gear until I was on a two mile final and landing was assured. From there I did my final call around 1,600 ft. and landed on Runway XXR around the 1,000 ft. markers. I let the aircraft roll out to the taxiway before coming to a stop. We then conducted the shutdown.
ASRS:1767126.s: The pilot and student experienced a right engine failure at 7,000 ft due to erratic EGT readings and rough running shortly after cruise. They secured the engine, returned to ZZZ1 single-engine, and landed safely on Runway XXR.

ASRS:1767131.n: On date I was informed by my manager that our aircraft registration had expired on [date]. I operated one training flight as PIC on [date]. I am guilty of just ensuring that the document was onboard the aircraft while not ensuring that it was valid. A contributing factor is that the aircraft registration is addressed to our company headquarters, which is a different address than our hangar. Due to COVID related staffing, our FAA reminders were never delivered to our hangar. It is still my responsibility to ensure that the correct documentation is on the aircraft prior to flight. We have instituted the following changes to ensure this does not happen again:1. Added the registration expiration to our maintenance tracking software. This will flag our maintenance team when expiration is near. It will also be printed on the preflight form used by the pilots.2. Training will occur and language will be added to our Operating Procedures and/or our expanded normal procedures document to ensure that a valid registration is on board.3. A consultant company has been hired to automatically renew our registration and deliver it directly to our hangar.
ASRS:1767131.s: The pilot-in-command operated a training flight in an aircraft with an expired registration because FAA renewal notices were not delivered to the hangar due to staffing issues. The operator implemented software tracking, updated procedures, and hired a consultant to ensure future registration validity and delivery.

ASRS:1767140.n: Test flight being carried out after prop overhaul. Propeller went to feather shortly after rotation. Aircraft was cleaned up and engine shut down. Tower notified of problem on downwind to runway XX and request for immediate return made. Cleared to land on runway XY, which we were on a close right base to. Landed without difficulty without realizing we were on taxiway which was the first pavement I lined up on as we turned a short final. No conflict with any traffic and was cleared to taxi by tower and ground to parking without incident.
ASRS:1767140.s: During a post-overhaul test flight, the propeller feathered shortly after rotation, prompting an immediate return. The crew landed safely on a taxiway instead of the cleared runway but encountered no traffic conflicts and taxied to parking without incident.

ASRS:1767143.n: On helicopter air to air, I announced while departing from field. Shortly after clearing the end of the runway I noticed a shadow cross the shadow of my aircraft. I was able to see [another] helicopter that had just crossed my path at a near 90 degree angle directly above me. I attempted contact again, and then on my monitored the frequency for the nearby airport without any contact. I am not sure of the vertical separation at the moment we were directly above & below each other. The attached link to go pro video does not accurately show how close we were, as the camera was blocked by the window frame as it is mounted approximately where NVG (Night Vision Goggle) would mount 3-4' above the pilot eye level.
ASRS:1767143.s: A departing helicopter pilot reported a near-midair collision with another helicopter crossing at a 90-degree angle directly overhead shortly after runway clearance. The pilot could not confirm vertical separation or establish radio contact, noting that onboard video footage was obstructed by the window frame.

ASRS:1767149.n: I'm not sure if, or how many errors I had, but I'm submitting this report for consideration. Everything described below happened within about 3 minutes and it wasn't until the dust settled about a half hour later I had time to reflect on things and wonder what just happened. I took [position name] Radar at or around XA:57z. I was working all TRACON airspace combined, no hand-off, no radar split and no CIC to help. I was all things TRACON. Sector was busy with, I don't know, 12, maybe 15 flights of aircraft talking to me. Everything fell to pieces 5 minutes after taking the position.Aircraft X [flight of 2 VFR] were returning from the Range Complex from the south, set up for about a 10 nm left base, coming fast, at 310 kts to beat Aircraft Y straight in for RWY XXR. I vectored Aircraft Y on a 270 Hdg down to 7000 (6500 mva) for sequencing to follow the Aircraft X [flight]. At or around XB:02Z, Aircraft Z in the southwest practice area, about 12 - 15 nm southwest of ZZZ called me but was blocked. He called again and stated he is 'Priority inbound, my engine just let go'. I told him to enter left traffic RWYXXR, I called Ground Control on the override, told them to roll the equipment for Aircraft Z emergency inbound had lost his engine. I tagged Aircraft Z as an emergency and then started issuing traffic to Aircraft Z to follow the Aircraft X flight, about 8nm straight in. I knew I needed to slow the problem down, and began by slowing my Aircraft A on north downwind to 180kts. I slowed Aircraft Y and all the other traffic in the queue to 180 kts and began vectoring people wide for sequencing. I looked about 15 nm east and realized Aircraft Y was at 6100 in my 6500 MVA, and descending! I told him to maintain 6500 (forgot to say low altitude alert). He acknowledged and descended to 5700. I told him to climb immediately to 9000 no delay through 8000. I needed to break him out to the south because it was going to be a three-way tie with him, Aircraft X and Aircraft Z. I had to get him above my MVA's to break him out to the south for re sequencing.Without benefit of reviewing the tapes to hear the audio, I'm very sure Aircraft Y was never cleared for a visual approach, but maybe I did and that was why he was so low. Again, I don't have tapes to listen to and there's no management in the building to help me answer that question. Did I miss him read-back a wrong altitude? At some point in this fiasco, I realized the Aircraft Z way too fast (280kts) and catching the Aircraft X flight and told tower to move the Aircraft X flight to the south runway, 'Aircraft Z does not have them in sight'.By now, Aircraft Y was at 6000 slowly climbing but still in the face of Aircraft Z, 5 nm opposite direction at 6000, talking to tower with the Aircraft X flight are on short final. Next thing I know Aircraft Z is basing at 5000 and the Aircraft X flight are in the flare. Aircraft Z had his hands full and mis judged his approach so he made S-Turns or a right 360 on final to get down and land. I got Aircraft Y out of 7000 and turned him Heading 230 for sequencing following another flight of Aircraft X flight on a dogleg to follow the Aircraft A on the north downwind and another commercial aircraft straight in. All the fighters and air carriers parked north side and wanted RWY XXR, but I knew it would close behind the Aircraft Y so I changed them all to the south runway. I got everyone in line, speed controlled, cleared and visual separation applied.I switched Aircraft Y to the tower earlier than I would normally when I saw the Aircraft Z starting to base to about a 3 mile final and put him on the tower for landing clearance. I don't think I ever got a response from him that he had Aircraft X flight in sight. I was very rattled, in damage control mode and trying to fix the air carrier too low on final where I didn't expect him to be.Now that I had time to think about what just happened. Here's what I don't know:1.) Did Aircraft Z have Aircraft X in sight and pilot applied visual separation? He flew around a bit on final and maybe even 360'd, was above the Aircraft X flight altitude at all times, was never behind them on final but did overfly the south final to maneuver north of it for XXR. 2.) Did I clear Aircraft Y for Visual approach? I don't think so because I was intending to have him follow Aircraft X flight and I didn't even have time to try and tell him about Aircraft X flight yet. Did he read-back an incorrect altitude when I told him 7000? If he did, I didn't catch it. Did he bust his altitude assignment? I believe he did because I wouldn't have issued such a low altitude in that 6500/7100/8000/9000 area on our final extending out from 20 nm. What was he doing so low in there? Well, for starters, I should have said 'LOW ALTITUDE ALERT' to Aircraft Y when he was at 6100' in my 6500 MVA. It was just unreal, I couldn't believe what I was seeing. What was he doing below 6500 there? I didn't clear him yet! I told him to climb, he acknowledged yet he descended further to 5700'! I was incredulous and told him to immediately climb through 8000 to maintain 9000. He finally understood that and did what I instructed. Once Aircraft Z dropped his situation in my lap, I immediately and with out delay coordinated with the tower, did an 'EM' Slew/Enter so they could see he was the emergency and modified the SPAD for the north runway. I had data tag over-lapage (multifunction O/E doesn't work at TRACON so our auto-offset feature didn't do anything to keep data blocks from overlapping) and I didn't realize Aircraft Z was SO fast on a 2nm downwind. With the Aircraft X flight on a 5 nm straight in that math wasn't gonna work. He was catching them FAST and I pointed out traffic, he said 'looking'. I know he was busy and in a bind and I needed him to see those Aircraft X flight. I tried to fix it, saw that Aircraft Z was in position, already basing, needing a landing clearance, not going to physically catch the Aircraft X flight so I dumped him to the tower so I could try and fix the Aircraft Y who was not doing anything I wanted, needed or expected him to do. Plus, I had 12 other pilots going places and calling me all this time too. Everything transpired in 3 minutes, from the time I understood Aircraft Z was in trouble to the time where he was on final and I could deal with the other traffic.There's nothing that can be done 'to prevent a re-occurrence of this event'. You can't anticipate emergencies. That said, I should have issued a low altitude alert, and I should have had the Aircraft Z call the Aircraft X in sight or break the Aircraft X flight off final, sterilize everything and let the Aircraft Z do his thing. Also, this very same Aircraft Z has pulled this stunt on me in the past. He called with an engine failure, bombing into the left downwind at 280-300 kts. Prior to this incident, I didn't have other traffic to conflict with him. This was a rapidly devolving situation I did my best to manage and in retrospect realize a couple lapses in my control actions. I was just working the problem in the moment, trying to make planes miss and not overly concerned over 'words'.
ASRS:1767149.s: A single TRACON controller managing 12–15 aircraft faced an emergency when Aircraft Z reported an engine failure while Aircraft Y descended below 6500 MVA. The controller managed the conflict by issuing speed restrictions, altitude corrections, and runway changes, acknowledging lapses in issuing a low altitude alert and verifying visual separation.

ASRS:1767155.n: Aircraft X was going direct to ZZZZZ [Intersection] landing, so he was in a slow descent I told him to increase the rate, he did. Aircraft Y was climbing on a 300 heading the aircraft were going to be separated and the RA alert made the Aircraft X climb into the Aircraft Y and then forced the Aircraft Y to descend.I should have had a Human [assisting me], but it's too difficult to speak through a mask and give control instructions.
ASRS:1767155.s: An air traffic controller instructed Aircraft X to increase descent rate while Aircraft Y climbed on heading 300. A resolution advisory caused Aircraft X to climb into Aircraft Y's path, forcing Aircraft Y to descend, which the controller attributed to difficulty communicating through a mask without assistance.

ASRS:1767173.n: ZZZ Center issued a clearance to climb and maintain 26,000 ft. At approximately 11,400 ft., we received a TCAS descending RA. The Pilot Flying without delay complied with the descending RA. The autopilot and auto throttle were disengaged, and a smooth adjustment to a pitch down attitude was completed to satisfy the RA command. The Pilot Flying followed this planned lateral flight path until approximately 10,500 ft. when the Clear of Conflict was heard. ZZZ Center was advised of the TCAS deviation.Some important points that I (Pilot Monitoring) and the First Officer (Pilot Flying) took away from this event includes knowing company policies and procedures. The Pilot Flying did not hesitate to comply with the TCAS RA. The teamwork between the roles of Pilot Flying and Pilot Monitoring worked. I can contribute this to our TCAS training. This real life TCAS RA with passengers onboard was just like the scenarios we receive in the simulators.[We also had] a concern regarding ZZZ Center. Our flight was never given any traffic advisories to be on the lookout for this aircraft. The TCAS equipment on the aircraft was our first signal that there was a traffic conflict. Only after ZZZ Center was notified of the TCAS RA, did ZZZ Center start issuing traffic advisories to another company flight behind us. This is my first time in XX years of flying Part 121 operations that I have come this close to another aircraft. When ATC asked if I could identify the aircraft, I had no trouble identifying it as a King Air. During this descending TCAS RA, the closest I saw the two aircraft apart was 500 ft.
ASRS:1767173.s: The crew received a TCAS descending RA at 11,400 ft while climbing to 26,000 ft after ZZZ Center issued a clearance. The Pilot Flying immediately complied, descending to 10,500 ft with a minimum separation of 500 ft from a King Air, noting ATC provided no prior traffic advisories.

ASRS:1767178.n: On short final into ZZZ Runway XXL, we received a GPWS 'Too Low Terrain' warning. We were on glideslope and on PAPI (VMC conditions). We executed a go-around and as we leveled off we received several error messages in the scratch pad [including] 'GPS L incorrect' and a 'Runway/Approach CRS ERROR'. The Captain was flying and could not get NAV data to display on his PFD (Primary Flight Display). He also was unable to tune the ILS frequency for the subsequent approach. We consulted the checklist, then transferred the controls to the First Officer whose displays and NAV data appeared to be reading correctly and hand flew an approach in VFR conditions to a landing without incident. There was a lot of confusion with multiple errors occurring in the cockpit. The GPWS that sounded while we were on the glideslope during short final seemed to be erroneous, but then again with all the errors with the NAV data on the Pilot Flying side, maybe his glideslope was incorrect. In the end, going around and troubleshooting put time on our side and allowed us to determine the best course of action.
ASRS:1767178.s: During short final to Runway XXL, the crew received an erroneous GPWS warning and multiple NAV errors on the Captain's PFD, preventing ILS tuning. They executed a go-around, transferred controls to the First Officer, and landed safely in VMC after troubleshooting the navigation system failures.

ASRS:1767196.n: Passenger seated in XX5 wore [a] mask during boarding however was not wearing [a] mask after being seated. When approached by the Flight Attendant the passenger said she had a medical exemption and did not have to wear the mask. Customer Service Supervisor was called and passenger said they would comply, but continued to lift the mask off her face stating she had difficulty breathing. As a possible solution the Flight Attendant offered the passenger an airline paper supplied mask as an alternative however the passenger's behavior became further defiant and belligerent. It is my understanding other passengers were also expressing concerns about [the] passenger not wearing [a] mask. I made the decision to have her removed from our flight. Customer service escorted both she and her companion off the aircraft. Customer Service Supervisor did a stupendous job. Extremely professional and helpful.
ASRS:1767196.s: A passenger on flight XX5 refused to wear a mask after boarding, citing a medical exemption and difficulty breathing, despite offers of an alternative mask. The Flight Attendant and Customer Service Supervisor subsequently removed the passenger and her companion from the aircraft due to her defiant behavior.

ASRS:1767198.n: It is becoming all-too-common to see the ground crew member fail to follow safety protocols. Today was the latest occurrence. The sprayer neglected to tell us he was starting his process even though we were both in the cockpit with the door open. This is the second time in two weeks I've seen this. I've only been in the area two other times when spraying was underway recently.Another issue with today's event was how the spraying was done. I haven't been trained on it, so there may have been nothing wrong, but the sprayer did little more than march rapidly down the aisle waving the spray machine back and forth like he was swatting at flies. He did not pause to spray into a single row or overhead bin.I would like to think this is something that could be better trained on several levels.
ASRS:1767198.s: A ground crew member sprayed the cabin aisle while the pilot was in the cockpit with the door open, failing to announce the start of the process. The reporter noted the sprayer waved the machine rapidly without pausing to treat specific areas, citing a lack of safety protocol adherence and training.

ASRS:1767200.n: After landing, while taxiing to park at ZZZ [airport], we forgot to contact ZZZ Ramp for entry lane assignment before entering the ramp. Threats leading to omission: Reserve pilots, reduction of flights leading to reduced proficiency/recency, limited experience at ZZZ as ZZZ1-based pilots, lack of thorough identification of requirements during arrival brief. During the arrival brief, we failed to mention an operations note to 'Contact ZZZ Ramp for entry point assignment.'Due to renovations at the terminal, we should have briefed the ramp entry/exit procedures in advance and highlighted the terminal construction and area as a threat to mitigate. This was the last leg of our trip. We were assigned Gate X at the end of Terminal XX. There was no traffic in/outbound as we taxied in, and as we approached lane Y on Taxiway A heading toward Gate X it was completely clear with what appeared a direct entry to the gate. This may have contributed to us thinking our Ground Control taxi clearance was sufficient. The unusually short taxi with no traffic erroneously led us to believe our ground taxi clearance took us all the way to the gate. After landing, and while taxiing to the gate, in ZZZ [airport], we forgot to contact ZZZ Ramp Control before entering the ramp. Threats that led to this omission were: being on reserve, and because of the reduction in flights, this was the first trip for both of us in many weeks, and we were both admittedly rusty in our procedures. Being ZZZ1 based, we don't fly into ZZZ often. During our arrival briefing we failed to mention the operations note that requires a call to Ramp Control. Since the renovation to the ZZZ Terminal, there have been recent changes to the procedures for exiting and entering the Ramp, and knowing this we should have briefed those new procedures in advance. This was the last leg of the trip. Our assigned Gate X, was at the very end of Terminal XX;, and appeared to be a direct access from Taxiway A, which may have contributed to us thinking that access was controlled by Ground Control, when in fact the access to the gate was through lane X, which was controlled by ZZZ ramp. After landing, we were given instructions by Ground Control, to, 'Taxi to the gate via 'taxi route' with no mention of lane X, or Ramp Control, which led to our complacency in omitting their call. Also, after landing, we both remarked at how unusually empty ZZZ was of traffic, we appeared to be the only aircraft moving on the field, which allowed for an unusually short taxi to the gate at the usually crowded ZZZ, this also led us to forgetting that there was a Ramp Control around the terminal.
ASRS:1767200.s: Pilots taxiing to Gate X at ZZZ Airport after landing failed to contact Ramp Control for lane assignment due to reduced proficiency, an incomplete arrival brief, and complacency from low traffic. They erroneously believed their Ground Control clearance covered the entire route to the gate.

ASRS:1767202.n: We arrived at the airport this morning and headed right to security and over to the X Concourse for departure. I totally forgot the COVID screening and headed to the gate and off to ZZZ1.It was not until we got to ZZZ1 that I realized the error.
ASRS:1767202.s: A cabin crew member boarded flight ZZZ1 at the X Concourse but realized they had forgotten the required COVID screening before reaching the gate. The narrative reports this procedural error but does not describe any specific outcome or corrective action taken.

ASRS:1767217.n: After flight I was informed that I had been exposed to COVID-19 the day prior to my 2 day trip. I called the flight operations manager and informed him of my exposure. I made sure that he knew to contact the Captain on my trip as I know that he was going to his relative's home after work and that older people are more likely to have complications. Additionally, I knew that he had a trip leaving the next day. I was called by the on call assistant chief pilot, and told that the Captain would be contacted. I failed to mention that I had dinner with another airline crew on my layover, as I had been concentrating on getting the Captain informed quickly. Had either the flight operations manager or the assistant flight manager on call asked me about other interactions I would have listed the close contact I had with 2 other employees and been able to have them not show up to work for subsequent trips potentially exposing more crew members. Additionally, I found out that the Captain was not informed about his exposure until after his return from his next trip. I was surprised that given my reported exposure he was permitted to operate his subsequent trip.
ASRS:1767217.s: A crew member reported COVID-19 exposure to flight operations but omitted contact with two other employees, focusing only on alerting the Captain. Consequently, the Captain operated a subsequent trip before being informed of the exposure, potentially risking further transmission.

ASRS:1767223.n: Passenger in [seat] X1 refused to wear a mask. Dispatch was notified. [Requested] aircraft [be met] upon arrival. Landed without further incident. I initially told Dispatch it was not a security threat level 1. I was in a busy part of the flight and did not have time to look it up. After landing, I reviewed the flight manual and realized it was a security threat level 1. Either way, all security threat level one procedures were followed.
ASRS:1767223.s: The pilot reported a passenger in seat X1 refused to wear a mask, prompting a request for ground meet upon arrival. Although the pilot initially misclassified the incident as not a security threat level 1, all required procedures were followed and the aircraft landed without further incident.

ASRS:1767231.n: We were just outside the MNARK waypoint descending via the TBARR1 into Denver when I requested an unrestricted descent in order to expedite down through some turbulence. ATC granted my request and cleared us to descend and maintain 14,000 FT. I took the aircraft out of the managed descent mode and used open descent to descend to 14,000 FT. ATC subsequently amended our clearance as follows, cross BDIVN at or above 14,000 FT then descend via the TBARR1. The next waypoint after BDIVN is KUSHH which has an altitude restriction of 14,000 FT. The Pilot Monitoring (PM) put 13,000 in the FCU as the bottom of the TBARR1 is 13,000 FT at LDORA which is the next waypoint after KUSHH. I acknowledged the change to the altitude in the FCU but failed to put the aircraft back into a managed descent. We were between BDIVN and KUSHH when Denver Center switched us over to approach. As the PM checked in with approach I was expecting the aircraft to level off at 14,000 FT in order to meet the restriction by KUSHH. Just as the aircraft approached 14,000 FT two things happened simultaneously. One, I realized the aircraft wasn't leveling off as I expected, and two, approach cleared us to descend to 10,000 FT and turn left to a heading of 040. I don't believe there was an altitude deviation but I was certainly very fortunate that approach gave us a lower altitude when they did. On TBARR1 arrival asked for expedited decent to 14,000 feet to get out of moderate turbulence. I put 14,000 feet in altitude window, captain started open descent. Next ATC transmission was a decent via following BDIVN intersection. I put 13,000 in altitude window. Approaching KUSHH intersection captain realized plane was not going to capture altitude to cross KUSHH at 14,000 feet. Managed descent was not selected. At same time got ATC frequency change and new instructions heading 020 descent to 10,000. I don't think we went below 14,000 feet, but would have if not given new ATC instructions while in an open descent Mode.
ASRS:1767231.s: The flight crew descended via TBARR1 into Denver in open descent mode after requesting an expedited descent for turbulence. They failed to re-engage managed descent for a 14,000-foot restriction at KUSHH, but avoided an altitude deviation when ATC issued a new clearance to descend to 10,000 feet.

ASRS:1767239.n: 34 departures. 21 on north side.....11 in horseshoe...1 757. 6 arrivals holding ( 4 for horseshoe). Aircraft came to maintenance. BP Full6 supertugs calling to come to gate as soon as it opened regardless of alley trafficAircraft X blew taxiway Kilo , good thing I was looking out window.With the amount of aircraft physically on my taxi ways my attention needed to be looking out the window making sure everyone was following my instructions , if my attention was not focused looking at window Aircraft X would have caused a nose to nose. Therefore when I had a second I looked at the pushback screen, this resulting in delays, I still had to have a list of flights that called that I need to hold and try to integrate the two lists in order that the aircraft called
ASRS:1767239.s: A ground controller managed 34 departures and 6 arrivals while monitoring heavy taxiway traffic. A 757 blew Taxiway Kilo, nearly causing a nose-to-nose collision, forcing the controller to prioritize visual monitoring over the pushback screen and resulting in delays.

ASRS:1767261.n: Upon being cleared for the visual approach to XXR ZZZ, Pilot Flying set FAF altitude and continued descent from 4000 ft. to 2400 ft. PM (Pilot Monitoring) contacted tower to inform them of their flight path: turning base [runway] XXR. The crew turned base inside of the FAF, and therefore continued descent to an intermediary altitude appropriate for the glide path intercept inside FAF. In the base turn, the aircraft aurally alerted to a group of antennas in the vicinity of our flight path. As we were already in the base, we continued in the base without interruption and continued the approach to land XXR. The cause was an EGPWS aural alert to man-made group of obstacles, antennas, in the vicinity of flight path. Crew suggest [increased] distance in the turn from proximity of antennas to prevent future aural alerts from EGPWS. Flying the visual backed up by the ILS XXR, we were cleared for the approach, turning right base for the XXR runway during VMC, crew was aware of the set of antennas in the vicinity, however the GWPS was trigger issuing a 'Caution Obstacle' alert. Pilot Flying increased rate of turn as a preventive course of action to stay south of the obstacle. The crew safely remained out of the path of the manmade obstacle and landed without any interruption. EGPWS ALERT of the antennas in the proximity of the field Increase lateral distance from obstacles to prevent alerts from anything around or in the EGPWS to avoid situations like this.
ASRS:1767261.s: The flight crew received an EGPWS "Caution Obstacle" alert for nearby antennas while turning base for a visual approach to runway XXR. The Pilot Flying increased the turn rate to maintain lateral distance from the obstacles, allowing the aircraft to land safely without interruption.

ASRS:1767272.n: I read the company e-mail concerning Runway 16 at AVL being closed. At the time I didn't realize I had a trip coming up to go there. During the flight over to AVL, my FO (First Officer) and I looked over the special airport qualification pages for AVL. Pages indicated that the closed Runway 16-34 was completely torn up, and just dirt. I forgot the e-mail I had read that stated that the runway was actually almost finished. It was hazy in the AVL area. I had not landed there in several years, so we decided to do the RNAV approach to Runway 17. I expected to see just one runway as shown on Jeppesen 19-3 chart. We got the airport in sight and the Tower cleared us to land. When fully configured and below 1,000 AGL, Runway 16 was much more prominent than Runway 17. We both thought 16 was 17. Both of [us] saw a small light flash on the runway that looked like an aircraft taxing onto the runway. I saw the flash again, and it looked like a very small 'X'. I reported that to the Tower, and they instructed us to go around, which we did. After talking to the Tower and being vectored back around we saw our error, and successfully landed on Runway 17. I blame myself for not putting the information together and noticing that there was a discrepancy between what the e-mail stated and the Jeppesen charts. It would be nice if Jeppesen could keep their airport qualification charts updated. We were going to Asheville North Carolina which was my first time going there. I asked the Captain to request the RNAV approach going into Asheville since there were mountains and I'm not familiar with the airport, we have reviewed the special airport on the Jepp chart which was showing one runway and the runway [that] was shown was much torn up and under construction. When we were on final, I noticed there was an X on the runway which I thought was an airplane. I did not see another runway next to it even though there was. But the runway that was next to it, was very small, narrow, short and nothing like the runway [that] was showing on the [Jepp] chart. I realize that's not an airplane on the runway but it was an X flashing. I asked the Captain to let Tower know what's going on. Tower said go around, and after completing the go around procedure Tower has informed us that the main runway is closed and we are supposed to land on the adjacent runway. The adjacent runway is nothing like what was showing on the special airport chart. The picture that was showing in the special report chart is very different than what is in real life. People need to be aware that the predominant runway is not the runway that is used.
ASRS:1767272.s: The Captain and First Officer misidentified Runway 16 as Runway 17 at Asheville due to outdated Jeppesen charts and haze, mistaking a flashing 'X' for an aircraft. They executed a go-around after Tower instruction and successfully landed on the correct adjacent runway.

ASRS:1767276.n: In Cruise Flight at FL380 approaching ZZZZZ north boundary of ZZZZ airspace we were denied right deviations for active military airspace. Left deviations at that point were no longer an option and appeared worse. We were on the western edge of a line of weather moving East we were deviating just slightly left of our course to go through what appeared to be the thinnest area of weather on our radar. I had made a PA and had all passengers and Flight Attendants seated. We experienced a brief 10 to 15 seconds of Moderate Turbulence which cause our Altitude to drop 200 ft. to about 37,800 ft. and the a gain of about 300 ft. to about 38,100 ft. and then settled back to level at FL380. We also experienced some airspeed loss and then gain briefly as well as some left bank. It felt much like wake turbulence briefly. Just then MIA center told us to maintain FL380 and contact ZZZZ, before leaving the frequency I stated we had experienced some moderate turbulence which had caused some altitude loss, a couple hundred feet, and that we were now level at FL380 and we were told 'roger' contact Center which we did. The remainder of the flight was uneventful and smooth to destination. [The cause of the event was that] a deviation 100's of miles earlier to the left would have been a better choice and I believe a couple of aircraft behind us after hearing my report to MIA Center deviated into the Military Airspace. I do not know if the aircraft behind me declared an Emergency to do so or not, as we were changing frequency to next center during the radio discussions. That may have been a better choice but I did not expect the turbulence to be that bad, but was very glad I sat the Flight attendants down prior, as well as making a very clear PA to the passengers that we were going to experience some Turbulence since we had to fly in the area of some weather and insisted that they be seated with their seatbelts securely fastened. An earlier plan for weather deviations 100's of mile away if necessary would have helped knowing any right deviations would be denied. Level at 380 approaching XXXXX, there was some weather close to the intersection. Requested right deviation and Center informed that Warning Areas were active so unable right deviation. We encountered some moderate turbulence in the clouds for a few seconds. The airplane descended 200 ft. before returning to level. Miami informed to maintain 380 and to contact next center over ZZZZ which we did. Flight continued uneventfully.The cause of deviations was not being able to deviate due to Center's instructions.I suggest deviating ahead of time if known that no deviations allowed.
ASRS:1767276.s: The flight crew encountered moderate turbulence at FL380 while unable to deviate right due to active military airspace, causing a 200-foot altitude loss. The pilot attributed the event to delayed deviation planning and noted that earlier left deviations would have been safer.

ASRS:1767306.n: During boarding, two jumpseaters came up to the cockpit to identify themselves and ask permission to ride. The first one was originally assigned the jumpseat, but was told by the gate agent to take [seat] X1, and his coworker was assigned X2. Prior to departure, we became aware of a cargo loading issue that required both my and the FO's attention, and we both diverted most of our focus to taking care of that and getting the manifest to match where the cargo was moved. During this time, the gate agent sent the passenger numbers via auto-closeout. They indicated that there was an additional crew member listed (totaling X crew), and Y passengers in Zone X (where row X is located). I was aware that we needed to remove the additional crew member from the crew total and move him to Zone X, where [he] was actually seated, but it was my understanding that the Zone X total did not include the second jumpseater who was also assigned row X, as a result, we added two passengers to the Zone X total, making it [a count of] Z.After this occurred, ramp re-sent our cargo numbers, and somehow in that process our passenger numbers were reset to their original, too. After this occurred, we again removed the additional crew member from the crew total and changed Zone X back to Z instead of X passengers. At this point, I asked the Flight Attendant to count the number of passengers in Zone X, just to make sure it correlated with the change we made in the ACARS. She confirmed that there were Z passengers seated in Zone X. We sent for the manifest with that load and departed for a normal flight. During our next flight, we were faced with an almost identical situation with two jumpseaters. In discussion with this gate agent, he made it clear to us that when they send the passenger count via auto-closeout, the second jumpseater is already included in the passenger count, meaning we only need to remove the additional crew member from the crew total and put them in their respective zone if they are also assigned a seat in the back. Based on this information, I then realized that on our previous flight the passenger total already included one of the jumpseaters, and by adding 2 to Zone X, we ended up sending the manifest with an incorrect passenger total, in the sense that we added in one more than there actually was. As a result, our calculated versus actual weight was off by the weight of one adult passenger. We experienced confirmation bias in me asking the Flight Attendant to count Zone X, due to the fact that we heard what we expected to hear, but likely a totally unrelated passenger had moved into Zone X without their noticing, which resulted in her telling us we had Z in Zone X.This event was caused largely by not understanding some of the smaller details of the auto-closeout process. I do not recall personally having a situation before where we have had two jumpseaters on a not-full aircraft. It was my understanding that a jumpseater assigned a cabin seat needed to be manually placed there and wouldn't be included in the auto-closeout sent by the gate agent, the exception being if they are included in the auto-closeout crew total as an additional crew member in the actual jumpseat, but need to be moved to the correct zone if assigned a cabin seat prior to departure. That logic was incorrect, as confirmed when the next flight's gate agent mentioned that the first jumpseater is always listed as an additional crew member in the actual for auto-closeout, and any subsequent jumpseater is scanned on as any passenger would be, which would include them in the auto-closeout total. Also contributing to this was the distraction with the ramp agents and making sure that our cargo was loaded correctly. That task saturation combined with nearing departure time led to distraction and a bit of rushing that kept me from slowing down and thinking carefully about the jumpseater seating situation. Additionally, our flight attendants informed us that on this particular partner, paper sheets were no longer available, and so conducting a full passenger count didn't necessarily come to mind. Having asked them to do one likely would have us discovering that our ACARS manifest total did not match their passenger count.In the future, especially with COVID seating restrictions that complicate accommodating jumpseaters, I will be extremely vigilant in these situations to confirm with the gate agent that if there are multiple jumpseaters, that they are accounted for in the auto-closeout already. Doing so will prevent these double counting errors and ensure greater accuracy. If there is ever any question, I'll not be shy to ask the flight attendants to conduct a passenger count to ensure the greatest and most up to date information. Finally, to prevent rushing associated with task saturation, I'll be very diligent about taking things deliberately slowly and only accomplishing one task at a time, to prevent errors like this from occurring. From a technical standpoint, it could also be helpful to include the number of jumpseaters on board in the remarks section of the auto-closeout. 'Additional crew member Listed' seems to have the connotation of only one being on board, and could potentially be misinterpreted.
ASRS:1767306.s: The flight crew incorrectly calculated the passenger manifest during boarding due to misunderstanding how auto-closeout counts multiple jumpseaters. This error, compounded by cargo distractions and confirmation bias, resulted in a weight discrepancy equal to one adult passenger.

ASRS:1767354.n: Went in to see Person Y re: possible exposure to the COVID-19 virus. No matter when the Company found out they, 1) made 1 attempt to contact me and 2) did nothing, but ask me 'form' questions.I was told to self-monitor and quarantine for 14 days from date of exposure. Really! I've worked 9 of 13 days. (Had 2 days off after being exposed which at that time could have been a spreader.)-Company only made 1 attempt to contact me of possible exposure.-Repeatedly told me 'my overall risk is very, very low.'The Company is dealing with one's health. I'd say they need to show a little more urgency, and watch wording i.e., self-quarantine for 14 days, when you've worked 9 of the 13 with 1 quarantine day left when being notified was a joke. Don't try to play Doctor.
ASRS:1767354.s: A crew member reported potential COVID-19 exposure to Person Y and was instructed to self-quarantine for 14 days despite having worked nine days post-exposure. The reporter criticized the Company for making only one contact attempt, minimizing the risk, and failing to show urgency regarding health protocols.

ASRS:1767368.n: Aircrew got into the seat to launch the aircraft. Normal pre-flight operations, but once crew got link with the aircraft, the chiefs loaded new DLI keys onto the plane without telling any of the aircrew about the new procedures. This caused over an hour of trouble shooting in order to establish link with the aircraft. The GCS maintenance guys reloaded the DLI keys into the GCS, but the crew was still unable to establish link with the aircraft again. Aircrew had seen some abnormal readings from the GCS about the aircraft being at [Altitude] when the crew had no link with the aircraft, same with the RPM (108.7) and Uplink sig 1 (112.4%). The Maintenance crews were able to finally get the correct DLI keys loaded into the aircraft. Aircrew completed all checklists up to the C-band link test. At that point the RX2 when checked would send the aircraft lost link. Aircrew had maintenance swap to a new GDT, which fixed the problem and the C-band link check completed fine.Crew completed the rest of the launch procedures without any problems. During the taxi out to Runway XX, aircrew started getting 'LOS UPLINK Secondary - LOST' warning. There were no indications of anything being wrong with the link. Crew kept an eye on the systems to make sure there wasn't any problems with any of the links. At the time there was nothing showing that there was anything wrong.Aircrew was cleared to line up and wait on Runway XX. Once the crew lined up and waited the aircrew got the same warning as before. The warning did clear, so once the aircrew got clearance to take up the crew did. Right after the 50 kt. call, the warning came back up. Pilot decided to continue the take off, but shortly after that, the primary uplink was lost. Sensor called out lost link. Pilot aborted, sensor responded with abort, abort, abort. Shortly after sensor reminded the pilot to match settings just in case the aircraft did get airborne. During this time the crew still had no control of the aircraft. Aircraft departed the prepared surface. Aircraft came to a stop after Taxiway X with engine off.
ASRS:1767368.s: Aircrew and maintenance encountered pre-flight link issues due to unannounced DLI key changes and a faulty GDT, which were resolved before taxi. During takeoff, a lost uplink warning triggered an abort after the primary link failed, causing the aircraft to depart the runway surface and stop on Taxiway X.

ASRS:1767369.n: Following landing on Runway 17 I was given taxi instructions to remain on the tower frequency and to taxi north via Taxiway A and hold short of Taxiway C. I continued north on Taxiway A and was then told to hold short of Taxiway D. Nearing Taxiway E Tower asked me to stop and I asked the location of Taxiway D, as I had not seen the sign for Taxiway D. I told the tower I was approaching Taxiway E.The tower stated I had passed Taxiways C and D and asked if I could make a 180 on the taxiway to make room for traffic exiting A4. Upon making the 180 I saw signs for Taxiways D and C visible south on Taxiway A and could see that the opposite direction sign for both Taxiways D and C were blank. Tower apparently realized this and asked me if the signs were blocked and I confirmed this. No incursion took place. There is significant construction at this airport and Tower was not informed that the northbound signs for these taxiway were blank and there was no NOTAM (Notice To Airmen) to this effect.
ASRS:1767369.s: The pilot reported that after landing on Runway 17, they overshot Taxiways C and D because northbound signs were blank due to construction. Tower instructed a 180-degree turn to clear traffic, and no incursion occurred despite the lack of a NOTAM regarding the obscured signage.

ASRS:1767373.n: I had not flown since March of this year, due to all the COVID virus going on nationwide. A friend asked me to reposition a newly acquired aircraft from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2. Weather was currently and forecast to be VFR the entire route, but I filed it IFR to get myself back to speed on instruments, which I thought I did a good job of this trip. My first stop was ZZZ for fuel. Had gotten dark by then, about XA:30pm local time. [My] clearance departing was to fly the 'ZZZZZ X to ZZZZZ [Intersection], then on course'...as I heard it and understood. My next intersection, which I had filed to from the airport was ZZZZZ1 Intersection. So that is where I was attempting to navigate to after I passed ZZZZZ. So ATC calls me on radio and says I was supposed to fly on to ZZZZZ2 Intersection and then do the 15 mile arc around to ZZZZZ1. (This was not what I understood in the departure clearance.) They vectored me on towards ZZZZZ1, and I continued.I should have asked for vectors before departing the airport, instead of the SID. The GPS in the airplane was not quick/easy to alter any data, but I was doing OK with it enroute.
ASRS:1767373.s: The pilot, repositioning an aircraft from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 at night, misinterpreted a departure clearance to fly direct to ZZZZZ1 instead of via ZZZZZ2 and a 15-mile arc. ATC corrected the error with vectors, which the pilot attributed to failing to request vectors before departing and difficulty altering GPS data.

ASRS:1767378.n: I was conducting a flight training event with my student pilot. We just returned to the airport to practice performance takeoff and landings. We had just made a full stop - taxi back. We called holding short that we were ready for touch and goes. We were told to hold short for landing traffic. Several planes land and depart. Both my student and I hear what we believe to be our abbreviated tail number being cleared for takeoff. We read back cleared for takeoff instructions, finish final items on the checklist, and take the runway. On our takeoff roll we hear Tower ask who is on the runway and I respond with our tail number. Tower then advises to either exit the runway or begin our roll. We were already on the roll, so we continued the takeoff. After our lap in the pattern we terminate the training flight and contact the ATC number. I believe I heard our tail number and believed it was a takeoff clearance. However, due to a high volume of traffic the morning of the event due to a lengthy TFR that lasted most of the day, there was a lot of training and jet traffic. I could have heard a similar call sign and my student could have stepped on the intended recipient of the ATC instruction. I know when there is a high volume of traffic waiting to arrive and depart it could be best to use my full tail number to lessen confusion, and take extra measures to ensure all radio communications are properly received and copied. Aircraft X called up requesting pattern work during a high traffic volume session and was given hold short instructions, due to the fact that there was an IFR arrival jet on about a 3 or 4 mile final. Aircraft X subsequently read back his hold short instructions. I talk to 3 different aircraft before I cleared Aircraft Y for a touch and go. Apparently Aircraft X read back 'Aircraft X cleared touch and go' and then subsequently got onto the runway without me catching it. Aircraft Y clarifies their touch and go clearance and I canceled the touch and go clearance and gave them a left 360. During this time inside the cab my CIC/GC/FD was trying to clarify information about a TFR that was supposed to be going into effect shortly and we had received no prior information on. This resulted in several phones ringing during this already busy time. After scanning the runway I saw an aircraft who appeared to be holding on the runway with my jet traffic now within 2 miles of the runway, since I had multiple aircraft holding short of the runway I tried to quickly identify the aircraft, so I could taxi them off the runway in a timely manner. However Aircraft X didn't identify himself by name until about the 3rd time I reached out to them. With minimum time to react I told the aircraft to taxi clear of the runway or depart immediately. Aircraft X started their departure roll and as soon as airborne I told them to offset the runway so I had sufficient spacing with my IFR aircraft on final. Immediately following my Jet traffic landing the OM entered the cab and started trying to have the CIC help him find our local weather form, so our new trainee could fill it out. We started the day short staffed with no prior knowledge that someone would be coming in to cover for a couple hours, so the rotation wasn't going to happen as expected. When there are less people in the cab we have enough space to work without our masks and due to the fact that there were extra nonessential people in the cab I had to replace my mask, while I firmly believe mask should be required, they do interfere with the side tone which affected my ability to catch Aircraft X's incorrect readback. No one in the facility had received any information on the TFR that was supposed to be going into effect. This resulted in several miscommunications and confusion.
ASRS:1767378.s: A student pilot and instructor entered the runway believing they had a takeoff clearance during high traffic, while the controller issued the clearance to a different aircraft due to similar call signs and radio interference. The controller ordered the aircraft to depart immediately to avoid a conflict with an arriving jet, attributing the error to communication confusion and staffing issues.

ASRS:1767399.n: I was in the PIC (Pilot In Command) (right) seat conducting training for a CFI student in the left seat. We were performing simulated hydraulics failures in the traffic pattern at ZZZ airport. We were using the hydraulics isolate switch on the right seat collective to shut off the hydraulics on downwind and performing simulated run on landings at hover height over the runway. While climbing away from the runway I told the left seat pilot I was ready for the hydraulics to be turned back on. I felt him flip the switch on my collective back up and heard the normal warning horn come on briefly. Normal control forces returned, however, the HYDR light remained on. We turned crosswind and decided to recycle the switch again to see if the light would turn off. It did not. Instead of turning downwind at ZZZ we turned back towards our home base of ZZZ1. We discussed if there was anything we were missing and how we could determine if it was just the light or if it was an actual hydraulics failure and we were on the backup accumulators which only offered a limited amount of time before they would deplete. The other pilot and I determined that there was no way to determine if we still had the main hydraulics system functioning normally so we has to assume they were off-line. The emergency procedure is to level the aircraft and fly between 40-60 kts. , then use the collective HYDR cut off switch and shut down the system before the accumulators start to deplete before performing a run on landing. I [advised ATC] with ZZZ1 and told them I would need Runway XX/XY for a run-on landing. The run on landing was performed normally. Once on the ground I reengaged the hydraulics system and manipulated the controls long enough to determine that we were not working off the limited supply of the back up accumulators. We hover taxied over the taxiways back to our ramp. After landing our Maintenance staff found the switch for the hydraulics warning light needed to be replaced. After replacement of the switch the system worked properly. I contacted ZZZ1 Tower and Airport Rescue and Fire asking if they required any reports from us and both indicated that the phone call was sufficient.
ASRS:1767399.s: The PIC and a student pilot experienced a persistent HYDR warning light during simulated hydraulic failures in a helicopter at ZZZ airport. They diverted to ZZZ1 for a precautionary run-on landing, which maintenance later attributed to a faulty warning light switch.

ASRS:1767403.n: I was cruising at 8,000 ft. I was on an IFR flight plan talking to ZZZ Approach. Conditions were VFR, good visibility, no clouds, a little low lying fog in the valleys. All of a sudden I got an immediate and strong vibration. Initially I checked the engine instruments and everything appeared normal. I turned on the fuel pump and pushed the mixture full rich. I also pulled the throttleback to 'ease' the vibration, no significant change. I changed the propeller speed and that changed the vibration, but did not make it go away. I was able to maintain airspeed and altitude and alerted ZZZ Approach that I had [requested priority handling] and was diverting ZZZ1. I was not within gliding distance, but would be in about 3 miles (1 minute). I told ZZZ of my fuel (35gal) and souls on board (1). Once I had the airport in sight I told ZZZ of my intentions to fly over the field at 8,000 ft. and then start circling down to land. I began descending and pulled the power back further which further increased the vibration. I noticed the nose gear transit light was lit, and that the gear system had low pressure. I moved the gear switch to the down position and nothing happened. I moved the gear selector back to the up position and nothing happened. I checked the circuit breakers and noticed the landing gear pump had tripped. I reset it and extended the gear normally, three green. At this point I was about 2,600 ft. MSL on downwind at about 100 kts. I started putting the flaps out to add some drag and get lower. Any power changes made the vibration worse. On short final I pulled the power back and the vibration got really bad. Over the numbers I could not move the control stick it was shaking so badly. I turned off the mags and landed while the engine stopped. After the engine stopped the vibration went away and I could see part of the propeller blade was missing.I taxied off the runway just using the momentum and I had and cleared the hold short line. The fire and police were waiting at the intersection, and were a big relief to see. After I gave them my driver license and told them what happened, we pulled the plane using the tow bar onto the ramp. Upon inspection of the fracture surface, there was evidence of corrosion 1/8 in. back from the leading edge indicating the crack had existed for some time. I had recently dressed the prop during a conditional inspection, but did not see the crack. About 6 in. of one of the two blades had departed in flight. The prop had been overhauled about 10 years prior by a reputable shop and had 960 hours time in service.
ASRS:1767403.s: A pilot experienced severe vibration during cruise at 8,000 ft caused by a propeller blade fracture due to corrosion. After resetting a tripped landing gear circuit breaker, the pilot executed an emergency landing with the engine stopped, revealing a 6-inch blade section had departed in flight.

ASRS:1767415.n: Annual inspection was performed, item on annual checklist was to perform inspection of fuel gas-collator filter screen- inspection was complied with and no issues noted. I had personally flown the aircraft several times prior taking it for new owner delivery. After descending down from 7,500 ft. to 3,500 ft. I noticed the engine was running rough. RPM was low for cruise power setting and unable to get more than 2000 RPM. [I] decided to land aircraft immediately at ZZZ.Maintenance on field discovered that one fuel nozzle was plugged. [They] cleaned fuel nozzle and replaced fuel supply line to the injector. Ops checked engine and it was all satisfactory. I insisted that we look into right fuel tank for contamination- no debris found. Later Maintenance performed another engine run and discovered that engine is running rough again. Continued with troubleshooting and discovered that screen element installed in fuel gas-collator was not the correct screen. I advised them to install new screen. They suspected unapproved filter screen installed. I did last annual on airplane and screen check. There was no way for me to know that the screen was not aircraft approved or type approved.
ASRS:1767415.s: The pilot experienced rough engine operation and low RPM during descent from 7,500 to 3,500 feet, forcing an immediate landing. Maintenance later determined the cause was an unapproved fuel gas-collator screen element installed during the annual inspection, which was subsequently replaced.

ASRS:1767434.n: While at the gate pre flighting, I was informed that we were carrying an aircraft battery to ZZZ1 and was given two copies of the Notice to Captain (NOTAC) to sign. At that point, I had already reviewed our Release and signed it. I gave the Operations Agent a copy of the NOTAC and kept one myself. While at cruise altitude, I received an ACARS message from Dispatch informing me that the HAZMAT was not annotated in the remarks section of the Release in accordance with Bulletin. The Dispatcher and I made a pen and ink change to the Release and the Dispatcher informed he would report the event.
ASRS:1767434.s: The pilot discovered during cruise that a hazardous aircraft battery shipment to ZZZ1 was missing from the Release remarks. The pilot and Dispatcher corrected the document with a pen and ink change, and the Dispatcher agreed to report the event.

ASRS:1767444.n: ATC on CPDLC (Controller Pilot Datalink Communications) gave us a climb and maintain FL 360 without an ATC controller assigning us a clearance via radio. I don't know if it's legal in our ops spec for a B737. We called ATC via radio instead to verify assigned altitude. I don't remember seeing or reading if B737's can legally accept this type clearance. Why is ATC giving us CPDLC altitude clearances? We're not ETOPS over Washington DC! Now they're giving us reroutes via CPDLC. I don't know if we can accept these as well. I have talked to many pilots and the Assistant Chief Pilot and no one has an answer to my situation.
ASRS:1767444.s: A B737 crew received a climb to FL 360 and reroutes via CPDLC without radio confirmation, raising concerns about the legality of accepting such clearances under their operations specifications. The crew contacted ATC by radio to verify the altitude, but no definitive answer regarding the validity of these CPDLC instructions was found.

ASRS:1767455.n: Towed aircraft to remote Gate X. It's dark and wet out from rain/raining. I was lined up correctly on the 'J-Line' for pulling in plane. When pulling in to space, wings made contact. The wing walker had lit wands, but I do not recall seeing him give me an 'X' to stop. If he had given me an X, early on, I could have stopped and re-evaluated the conditions further to explore my options, and incident would have been avoided. Now, it's night time, and raining. Remote lines are not well lit, not even reflective. Aircraft was towed to remote Gate X. Gate Y and Gate X are too close together in proximity. Gate Y shouldn't even be there, or Gate X should be moved farther down away from Gate Y, as there is lots of space on the other side of Gate X. Gate Y had the wrong kind of aircraft parked there. There wasn't supposed to be an [X type aircraft] at Gate Y. With both aircraft being [X type], this was bound to happen, as the wing tips are going to touch (found out after the fact). Was towing this aircraft really necessary? We had 2 empty gates, the gate it was originally parked at (Gate Z), plus gate ZA. We only had 1 other aircraft to arrive for the night. In trying to save money on the rental of a gate, we now have an aircraft damage that now costs more. As far as manpower, people are flying again, flights are reinstated, and we furlough people. With business picking up, there should have been fewer furloughs. Each airline should have its own parking space in the middle, with excess, if any, as first come first served. Some stations have a designated tow team. Our station is smaller, but we could still manage to have a tow team if the manpower permitted, and when not towing or repositioning, they help out in other arrivals/departures.
ASRS:1767455.s: A pilot towing an aircraft to remote Gate X at night in rain reported wing contact due to insufficient spacing between Gates X and Y and poor lighting. The reporter attributed the damage to cost-saving decisions that forced the tow and inadequate gate configuration, noting that available gates were ignored.

ASRS:1767488.n: This report covers two events generated from the same aircraft condition. At FL370, I, as pilot flying received an Engine 1 EPR (emgine pressure ratio) Mode fault. The FO (First Officer) ran the ECAM procedure and we selected N1 modes on and ran the autothrust manually. We almost had to ask for a descent because the speed was bleeding off. I managed to correct the speed, and noticed the thrust levers were quite split. I needed to transfer aircraft control to the FO so that I could call Dispatch and Maintenance. I explained the split throttle situation to the FO and gave him the aircraft and radios. Shortly afterwards, he said we needed to descend. I saw the speed deteriorating and immediately said to start down, we were going below green dot and into the hook. I took back the radio, and we descended. Our fuel situation was such that at the lower altitude we couldn't continue on to ZZZ1, so we coordinated to divert to ZZZ2. Everything was non eventful until we started the approach. I had the FO flying because he was handling the split thrust levers well and I thought it would be best for him to continue. He asked for a longer final then they were vectoring us for and ATC gave us a long final. When cleared for the Visual, the FO decided to descend from 8000 feet to 7000 feet. I should have told him to maintain 8000 feet. I wanted him comfortable on the approach and let him descend early. ATC called us with a low altitude alert, stating the MDA was 7500 and we climbed back to that altitude and intercepted the glide slope and landed without incident.The cause of the low altitude alert was that I had already told the FO how to make the descent with the throttle situation and didn't want him to feel like I was flying while I was Pilot Monitoring, and we were visual so I knew we were safe as far as terrain and obstacles, but we were definitely dragged in. Normally when FO's ask to descend early on visuals I mention class B airspace or terrain, but this time I wanted him to be comfortable just working the split thrust levers. I've thought about this for about a day now, and what I've come up with is try to keep things as normal as possible even in an abnormal situation. The extended final was fine. It actually made it easier to accomplish what he was trying to accomplish and made the descent totally unnecessary. I also want to mention that the mechanic who greeted us asked why we hadn't applied the MEL, which would have helped us with our power settings. We don't reference the MEL in flight, but either the QRH should address the thrust situation or it should mention to refer to the MEL because it would have been helpful. During cruise at FL360, in the vicinity of the ZZZ VORTAC, flight experienced a Master Caution and a following ECAM warning message of ENG 1 EPR MODE FAULT. The CA (Captain) who was the Pilot Flying (PF) stated 'My Aircraft' and I, the FO who was the Pilot Monitoring (PM) immediately began the procedures to address the ENG 1 EPR MODE FAULT caution. After referencing the Quick Reaction Card (QRC) we determined this was not a Quick Action or ECAM exception, and after concurrence between the PF and the PM began the ECAM Actions for ENG 1 EPR MODE FAULT. After completion of the ECAM actions, and the aircraft was stabilized we both noted the trust levers were split in their position to maintain corresponding N1 and N2 engine settings. The CA (PF) then transferred the aircraft and ATC communications to me and I became the PF. The CA began an aircraft wifi internet phone call to company Dispatch and Maintenance and began to discuss follow-on options. I then informed ATC Center that the flight would be diverting due to 'engine issues' but the divert destination was not yet determined and we did not require any priority handling at that time. The decision to divert was made and ZZZ1 was determined the best place to divert. Once the CA completed coordination with Dispatch and Maintenance, he assumed the ATC Communications and assumed the PM duties and I remained the PF. During this time we noticed the power setting, as to not exceed any N1 engine limitations, were not sufficient to maintain the desired airspeed at FL360, and I notified the CA (PM) we needed an immediate descent out of FL360. The CA (PM) attempted to communicate with Center for the immediate decent, but was not able to establish communication due to frequency saturation from other radio calls. I (PF), in order to maintain airspeed, immediately disconnected the autopilot and began a shallow descent out of FL360. The CA (PM) made a call and notified Center of our descent out of FL360 and we were requiring a lower altitude. Center immediately responded to call and then cleared us to FL340, I estimate our altitude to be 35,850 feet when Center responded to call. The flight continued, uneventfully, to land at XXR a ZZZ with a visual approach.
ASRS:1767488.s: The crew managed an Engine 1 EPR Mode fault at FL370, causing split thrust levers and a diversion to ZZZ2. During the visual approach, the First Officer descended below the 7500-foot MDA, triggering a low altitude alert before the aircraft climbed back to intercept the glide slope and land safely.

ASRS:1767490.n: Our flight clearance to ZZZ ended with ZZZZZ [Intersection] ZZZZZX [Arrival] which is the arrival for ZZZ landing direction. I confirmed all crossing altitudes and speeds were in the FMC. We had ATIS automatic updates and received information just prior to the start of the descent confirming ZZZ landing direction. Prior to descent, we briefed the various expected taxi routes from the possible runways, flap setting, landing assessment, and autobrakes. We held off on briefing the ILS pending the runway assignment. At some point we were cleared for the ZZZZZY Arrival but then given various headings, speeds and altitudes for spacing before clearing us direct to ZZZZZ1 [Intersection]. At that point, I believed the ZZZZZY Arrival was the name of the arrival we had in the FMC and I still expected to land direction. As we crossed ZZZZZ1, ATC told us to depart ZZZZZ2 [Intersection] heading 300. ZZZZZ2 is not on the STAR we had in the FMC. That is when we realized we did not have the ZZZZZY Arrival in the FMC. The routing prior to ZZZZZ1 is the same on both STARs. The Captain selected the STAR in the FMC and we flew the route. ATC continued to directed speed and altitude. We were never off route. I'm not certain but I don't think we were ever off altitude because ATC was assigning us incremental altitudes the entire descent. Confirmation bias was one causal factor for me. I had a flight clearance, current ATIS, and waypoints in the FMC that coincided with the arrival clearance. After various vectors, ATC cleared us to a point that was six waypoints into the arrival, a point with the same name as the new arrival, and it didn't occur to me that the arrival had changed. My currency and recency was another causal factor. I completed IOE, but didn't consolidate before starting a six month leave of absence. The Captain was exceptionally helpful and specifically stated in the departure brief that me not speaking up for any reason was his biggest concern. I wanted to brief the approach during the initial descent to stay as far ahead as possible. He suggested we hold off since we didn't know the runway yet. I wanted to ask approach for an expected runway, but I assumed that he didn't want to do that because he flew into ZZZ enough to know when they usually give you the runway. That was a moment to speak up. Requesting the expected runway at that point would have clued us in to the change of runways and change of STARs.I will confirm the STAR with the other pilot the same way I confirm an approach, altitude or landing runway, e.g., I heard cleared for the ZZZZZY or descent via the ZZZZZY.
ASRS:1767490.s: The First Officer and Captain flew a descent where the crew initially loaded the wrong arrival into the FMC due to confirmation bias and the First Officer's lack of recency after a leave. The Captain corrected the route after ATC issued vectors to a waypoint not on the loaded STAR, though the aircraft remained on assigned altitudes and headings throughout.

ASRS:1767491.n: This event actually happened twice, but I kept the dangerous goods form for second event and investigated cargo myself. On ZZZ-ZZZ1 flight, I was handed a dangerous goods form. It stated dangerous goods of 'Non-Flammable Gas OX' in [cargo] A1. I am an engineering major, so I immediately questioned that oxygen is non-flammable and looked below for more information. It stated that cargo was UN1072 Class Div 2.2-5.1 compressed oxygen. Now it really had my attention. It had multiple designations and I am pretty sure compressed oxygen is flammable. I could not find anything discussing this in FOM, preflight, Dangerous Goods [section] which is where it should be, but my FO (First Officer) found it under GEN Ops, Dangerous Goods. This is where it got real confusing. It apparently says that Class 2.1 Flammable Gas is okay for carriage and for Class 2.2 non-flammable gasses with subsidiary risk of Class 5.1 will not be accepted. This appeared to be what we have, so I called Cargo which immediately denied all knowledge of the issue, but gave me a number for the guy who runs dangerous goods for Operations Control. He explained to me that there was an exception (which I found in that section of FOM, but really doesn't make sense). Only company may ship compressed oxygen in a special container which supposedly makes this all okay. He explained that it must be in a special metal container (I'm guessing that's what a DOT 31FP compliant container is, but he did not say so). It must be stamped with company name and have two hazardous goods stickers, one yellow Division 5.1 sticker and one green 2.2 Nonflammable Gas sticker (even though its oxygen). His answer was that, although it was flammable, it was not in its packaging theoretically. Okay, so that explains the FOM exception that is poorly written. However, I have no idea if this extremely questionable cargo is properly packaged by the dangerous goods form and was reluctant to accept this answer. Since we were late in the boarding process, I sent FO down to inspect cargo to make sure it was packaged as explained to me by Operations Control. Turns out they handed the paperwork to me very late in boarding but had loaded said cargo much earlier. They had to remove most of the bags for FO to verify cargo was safe and thus we took about a 20-30 min delay. I accepted it as proper and flew on to ZZZ1. Now you would think this is rather rare, but sure enough on this flight the very next day, I get the same dangerous goods form very early in the boarding process. What are the odds? Since I was now educated, I elected to go down and look myself. Since early in boarding process and less bags stacked on top, I was able to quickly located and verify for the flight to ZZZ2. We departed on time and with said cargo.
