The aircraft owner and airport manager coordinated to make arrangements to remove the aircraft from the ditch.
ASRS:1767950.s: The pilot experienced a bounced landing and runway excursion during final approach in gusty winds, causing the aircraft to roll off the runway into a drainage ditch. The incident resulted in damage to the left wingtip, propeller, and landing gear, with no injuries or airport property damage reported.

ASRS:1767961.n: I was training my student in uncontrolled airfield operations and emergency landings. We were departing Runway 25 when I heard Aircraft X call that they were in the upwind for Runway 25. As the plane was about to rotate I asked where the Aircraft X was and they confirmed in the upwind. I cleared the whole upwind as we climbed and I could not find the plane. I remembered that my plane has TCAS and switched to the map to find the plane. I saw that he was 400 ft. away and slightly above me and at my 4 o'clock and flying right towards me and overtaking my aircraft. I then heard the Aircraft X call that he was entering left crosswind for 25. I immediately radioed 'Aircraft X, we are on a collision course, change course to fly over midfield immediately'. There are towers and hills on Runway 25's departure so I was limited in my options to take evasive action. Someone who I assumed was a flight instructor called 'roger Aircraft X crossing midfield'. I [saw] the plane at my 5 o'clock turn away from my aircraft towards midfield as we climbed and attempted to get out of the way.
ASRS:1767961.s: A flight instructor and student departing Runway 25 detected Aircraft X on a collision course via TCAS while climbing. The instructor directed Aircraft X to fly over midfield to avoid a crash, as terrain limited evasive options, and the other aircraft subsequently turned away.

ASRS:1767971.n: Prior to flight, I queried my flight school about the status of the aircraft following an ECU (engine control unit) B failure on the left engine I had experienced during a previous flight. They had a flight instructor meet with me before the flight and he described an operating procedure that they allegedly received from the aircraft manufacturer. This procedure included avoiding touch-and-go landings and keeping the engines below 1200 rpm on the ground. As I had not planned for any touch-and-go landings, I was not worried about adhering to that requirement. However, I found it difficult to adhere to the advice I received about keeping the engines below 1200 rpm while on the ground. The airplane itself idles at 900 rpm and that gives me very little throttle to work with in order to get the airplane to move. However, I was able to successfully taxi the airplane out of its home airport at ZZZ while adhering to this requirement. The flight to ZZZ1 went smoothly and I encountered no problems. However, I found it necessary to bring the airplane above 1200 RPM to taxi to the runway while attempting to leave ZZZ1. Due in part to the relatively high density altitude of 7000 feet combined with the upsloping taxiway out of ZZZ1, I had to bring the engines up to approximately 1700 RPM to taxi to the runway. I ran the before takeoff checklist before takeoff, which included an ECU health test on both engines. The aircraft indicated no problems with ECU health prior to takeoff.With an aircraft inbound with intentions to land in the opposite direction from the runway I intended to use for takeoff, I began my takeoff roll after coordinating with the incoming aircraft via CTAF. At approximately 60 knots and 1/2 way down the runway, I noticed a dual ECU failure on the right engine. I elected to continue the takeoff since the ability to stop in the remaining distance was questionable, and the severe dropoff at the end of the runway increased the hazard to me should I be unable to stop. The engine was still producing power, but I noted it was maxed at 80% load on the right engine and the prop was overspeeding at approximately 2200 RPM. I climbed to approximately 1000 feet AGL before beginning my troubleshoot procedure. I reduced power to approximately 65% load to prevent the overspeeding of the propeller and pulled out the Dual ECU Failure emergency checklist. I climbed to an altitude that would ensure safe single-engine diversion to ZZZ2 airport and followed the procedure, which called for reducing the power to zero on the problematic engine and bringing it back up to full power. Upon following this procedure, both of the ECU Failure warnings on the right engine disappeared and I monitored the engine instruments to verify proper operation. The problem seemingly cleared itself and I proceeded with my flight to the aircraft's home base in ZZZ. I encountered no more issues for the rest of the flight.At aircraft check-in, I wrote up the aircraft with an abbreviated description of my incident and left my phone number with the flight school in case they had any questions for me regarding my incident. I checked on the progress of the aircraft's maintenance about a week later and discovered that no one had translated my writeup of the aircraft to the electronic squawk list visible online. I asked what was being done to fix the problem and my flight school told me they could not replicate the problem and considered the aircraft safe. I became agitated and declared that I believe that by not putting my write-up in the squawk list and continuing to rent the airplane to potentially unsuspecting pilots that they are in effect renting an unsafe airplane. In what I feel is an act of retaliation for my challenge to their concern for safe operation of their aircraft, the flight school then pulled my qualifications on the airplane and refused to rent it to me (and only me, as far as I am aware) until I had completed another checkout with one of their instructors. As of date the aircraft is still being rented, and no mention of my incident has been written down and made available for other pilots.I feel that by renting an aircraft with the requirement to operate the aircraft in a manner inconsistent with the approved flight manual that they are subjecting their renters to unnecessary and avoidable risk. I do not feel as though company in ZZZ has the same concern for safety that I do and I have ceased my business there. I only worry that another pilot may encounter the same problem that I had with a different outcome.
ASRS:1767971.s: The pilot experienced a dual ECU failure on the right engine during takeoff at ZZZ1, likely exacerbated by high density altitude and a restrictive ground RPM limit. Although the issue cleared after following emergency procedures, the flight school failed to log the incident, leading the pilot to cease operations there due to safety concerns.

ASRS:1767981.n: We had approximately XXX passengers in coach. Many of the passengers were traveling in large groups/families. All came on with masks, but during boarding, masks started to come off and many were worn under the nose. It was a bit chaotic during boarding because about 1/2 of the passengers remained standing in the aisle, looked around to change seats, etc. PAs were made and we followed the new COVID-19 guidelines. However, during the flight, almost all of the many children would not wear their masks. Many of the adults wore their masks under their nose or not at all. We spent the entire flight reminding them to wear the masks. The parents did not enforce this with the children. Passengers around the families complained about the lack of social distancing because of the standing and no masks. I had to re-seat passengers who felt unsafe.As a crew member, I felt we followed what was expected of us, however, there were so many passengers who did not follow the COVID-19 prevention guidelines. I do feel that we as flight attendants and passengers traveling in the coach cabin were at higher risk of being exposed to COVID-19 if anyone on the flight was infected. Many of [the] passengers were in non-compliance in all phases of the flight. The purser came back to speak with the groups that were not in compliance, but it did not change the behavior of the passengers. Additionally, we were over the Ocean, any threat of landing immediately to remove the non-compliant passengers could not be accomplished.
ASRS:1767981.s: Flight attendants reported widespread non-compliance with COVID-19 mask and social distancing guidelines by passengers, including children and adults, during boarding and flight over the ocean. Despite crew reminders and re-seating efforts, the purser could not enforce compliance, and the crew felt at higher risk of exposure as immediate diversion to remove non-compliant passengers was impossible.

ASRS:1767992.n: Aircraft X checked on inbound at 13,000 feet descending to 9,000 feet. I told him to expect vectors for the ILS as that was what was being advertised and issued a heading of 130 and descended him to 3000 ft. He stated he did not want to go southeast bound because of weather south of the field. I was only showing small areas of light precipitation building 15 miles south of the field. After his request I told him an approach to the opposite runway circle to land will probably be okay but I will need time to get it approved as I was busy and a few other aircraft were deviating and one was having some radio issues. He then says he'll take a vector to the southeast for the ILS Approach. Once he is about 10 miles southwest of the field he reports the airport in sight. I clear him for the Visual Approach and call the tower to tell them of the change. I switched him to tower. I noticed him turning and figured he was either turning directly towards the field or deviating for weather since he was complaining about it before. He suddenly made a sharp left turn heading due north and descended to 1,000 feet. The low altitude alert goes off and I called the tower to issue it. They informed me he had lined up for the wrong airport. Tower handed him back off to me and I climbed him the 3,000 feet, re-vectored him for the ILS Approach and he landed safely. The pilot seemed rushed or impatient. I should have verified the azimuth and distance to the field even though he called the field in sight himself. The private airport should be displayed on the main map instead of a random roadway emergency map.
ASRS:1767992.s: An air traffic controller vectored Aircraft X for an ILS approach, but the pilot, appearing rushed, mistakenly lined up for a nearby private airport and descended to 1,000 feet. The controller issued a low altitude alert, re-vectored the aircraft, and the pilot landed safely after the error was corrected.

ASRS:1767995.n: Aircraft X handed off on a 110 heading. I assumed he was climbing high and climbed him to 140, pilot corrected me and said he was landing at ZZZ. My heading for ZZZ approaches for sector is 140 for a downwind leg so I automatically issued the pilot a 140 heading. This heading took him into (on my map- as I pulled the map up in front of my supervisor) 5,700 foot MVA. I instantly turned the aircraft to lower terrain. The frequency congestion and having to say to things twice had me frustrated.
ASRS:1767995.s: An air traffic controller issued Aircraft X a 140-degree heading for a downwind leg, mistakenly assuming a climb instead of a landing at ZZZ. This error directed the aircraft toward 5,700-foot minimum vectoring altitude terrain, prompting an immediate course correction to avoid the hazard.

ASRS:1767999.n: I was riding in the back of the aircraft on the flight from ZZZ to DEN. On arrival, the descent path took the aircraft straight through the middle of the enormous smoke column from the large wildfire in Colorado. The cabin immediately filled with smoke dense enough to make my eyes water and my throat burn. At the same time, there was nothing but dark orange light in the windows. The light, while not a Safety concern, was certainly eerie. Several passengers were visibly concerned and some pressed their call buttons to ask the Flight Attendant about the situation. We were in the column for several minutes. I was a little surprised when we landed in DEN to look back and realize that there were no other clouds in the sky. The smoke column looked, for all intents and purposes, like a thunderstorm. In my opinion, based on my experience in wildland fire fighting aviation, it would have been reasonable and prudent to ask for a deviation around the smoke column just as any of us would have for a thunderstorm. I've never been certain whether there is actually an aircraft Safety concern regarding flying through dense wood smoke but based on what I saw in the back of the aircraft yesterday there's definitely a passenger comfort concern. It might be worth addressing this in some kind of publication to the pilots.
ASRS:1767999.s: A passenger on a flight from ZZZ to DEN reported the aircraft descended directly through a dense wildfire smoke column, causing eye irritation, throat burning, and passenger concern. The reporter suggested pilots should request deviations around such smoke as they would for thunderstorms to address passenger comfort.

ASRS:1768000.n: I observed the C Flight Attendant in the jetway in close proximity to other Company Employees without her mask on. I informed her that Company policy required use of a mask. Instead of putting on her mask, she initiated a phone call on her mobile phone and proceeded to walk onto the aircraft and down the length of the cabin aisle to the rear galley. It should be noted that while she walked down the aisle talking on her phone and with her mask off, there were approximately 12 through passengers on board the aircraft.
ASRS:1768000.s: A flight attendant entered the aircraft without a mask while talking on a mobile phone, violating company policy. She walked down the cabin aisle past approximately 12 passengers before reaching the rear galley.

ASRS:1768014.n: Aircraft X [had] a pre-departure issue [that] contributed to a late and rushed departure and a distraction that affected the crew. Next the Runway XXR departure had a new heading clearance and a new altitude assignment in rapid succession that contributed to the distraction of PM not making the 1,000 foot call while trying to set new heading.Prior to departure there was an issue that required the flight crew to discuss with Dispatch, the FOM and FA crew regarding X deadheading ZZZZ based FAs that had been exposed to COVID-19. With 25 minutes prior to departure I found out that deadheading FAs on my flight had been exposed to a COVID positive crew member for an extensive period of time and would be sitting in Area X with other revenue passengers. They had been cleared to travel by being asymptomatic with no temperature. The outcome was my decision to not allow them to travel on my flight with some pushback and pressure to have them fly. The crew was upset with the way this was handled. Once resolved we quickly finished prep and briefed to get flight pushed.First Officer was flying the departure off of XXR at Intersection 1. Takeoff was normal with the typical busy departure of an initial XX0 heading then back to YY0 heading with an initial level off of 2,500 feet. Just as FO was heading YY0 and approaching 2,500 feet altitude we received a climb to 6,000 feet and a heading of 0Z0 degrees which was more than XA0 degrees to the right. I acknowledged clearance and reset MCP to 6,000 feet with VVM sop. I then started to slowly spin the heading knob to heading of 0Z0 so as not to induce a left turn because it was more than XA0 degrees from our current heading. While maintaining traffic watch and setting the new heading the FO went through 6,000 feet and I saw the 300 feet amber warning and an altitude of 6,380 as the FO was already correcting. This all occurred within a 30-45 second time frame. The remainder of departure was uneventful.Once at altitude we debriefed as a crew and outlined contributing factors:1. Pre-departure issue with COVID-19 deadheading crew members and airline's poor handling and pressure was a distracting and still on top of mind.2. PM while setting MCP with ATC instructions was distracted and missed the sop 1,000 feet call (5,000 feet approaching 6,000 feet)3. IRO started to put times on Master flight plan below 10,000 and was also not monitoring the PF and ATC clearance.
ASRS:1768014.s: The flight crew of Aircraft X faced pre-departure distractions regarding COVID-exposed deadheading cabin crew, leading to a rushed departure from Runway XXR. During climb, rapid ATC heading and altitude changes caused the Pilot Monitoring to miss the 1,000-foot call, resulting in a minor altitude deviation to 6,380 feet.

ASRS:1768018.n: DSTG is reflecting 426 lbs of freight which was to be loaded as Item 3, Pit 3. When the flight arrived in ZZZ1, the freight was not onboard the aircraft.
ASRS:1768018.s: The flight crew reported that 426 lbs of freight designated as Item 3 for Pit 3 was missing from the aircraft upon arrival at ZZZ1. The load sheet incorrectly reflected this freight as loaded, but it was not actually onboard.

ASRS:1768032.n: Upon starting number two engine, the FO miss-configured the pneumatics panel and left [the] left pack in auto. Could be due to both packs in high instead of auto while at the gate and boarding due to COVID-19. When number two N2 didn't rise to a normal RPM the FO mistakenly closed the cross feed valve instead of the left pack valve. The N2 RPM began to decrease. We realized what happened and did the memory item, the QRC, then the QRH. No engine limitations were exceeded. The subsequent start was normal.
ASRS:1768032.s: The First Officer misconfigured the pneumatics panel and closed the cross feed valve instead of the left pack valve during the number two engine start, causing N2 RPM to decrease. The crew executed the Quick Reference Checklist and Quick Reference Handbook procedures, resulting in a normal subsequent start with no engine limitations exceeded.

ASRS:1768042.n: During descent to ZZZ for visual approach, FO PF (First Officer Pilot Flying), CA PM (Captain Pilot Monitoring). Crew called the airfield in sight and was frequency changed to tower. Once on tower frequency, we heard Tower call a Seneca directing them to clear the approach path of runway XX. The next call was to a departing aircraft calling out our aircraft for separation which they did not see us. TWR then called our aircraft saying traffic 12 o'clock 3600 ft. north northeast bound. We responded with leveling and we have them on TCAS. Noting on TCAS the aircraft climbing toward us and it's very close proximity and rapid closure rate, we leveled our aircraft. The approaching TCAS target continued climbing from less than 1,000 ft. below us at our 12 o'clock into our flight path rapidly. TCAS quickly displayed a climb for the RA OF 3,000 fpm. The PF added thrust to TO (Takeoff) power and climbed with the RA at 3,000 fpm. The PM called tower notifying them we were responding to an RA. The TCAS target continued climbing passing 400 ft. directly under the aircraft from the 12 o'clock position to the 6 o'clock position. After the RA was complete, the crew began the descent again coordinating with tower for a right 360 degree turn in order to reestablish the approach. The crew landed on runway XX without further incident. No heavy aircraft loading during climb and no passenger complaints on landing. No PA's were made to passengers [in] reference [to] this event.Frequency changed from approach to tower at 10 miles for the visual without any traffic notifications. Contacting tower we were given a traffic advisory with less than a 1,000 ft. separation descending while traffic climbed with a rate of closure of at least 400 knots.Before being given a frequency change by approach control crews should be given traffic advisories in the area in order to build situational awareness. While descending into ZZZ out of approximately 3500 ft. MSL, and on about a 10 mile left base for XX, we received an advisory and then an RA to climb. We had been talking to approach and had just reported the field in sight. We were cleared for the visual and advised to switch to tower frequency. The FO (First Officer) was the PF (Pilot Flying). I switched to tower and heard the tower advising another aircraft to stay clear of the approach area. I checked in and was cleared to land. The tower then advised a Seneca that he needed to clear the approach area due to our approach and was advised to turn left. We then received a traffic advisory from the tower that was simultaneous with TCAS traffic alert, followed shortly by a RA to climb. I was looking outside and did not see the conflicting aircraft. The FO advised it passed underneath approximately 400 ft. below us. The entire event took less than 15 seconds as best I can recall. At that point we advised the tower we had complied with an RA and that we were high and needed a right 360 to re-establish on the approach. The tower responded that where we were was class E airspace and that the opposing Aircraft was not under radar control, and words to the affect that we were not in his airspace. He cleared us for the maneuver and again cleared us to land. Once on the ground we advised the tower via ground frequency that we would be filing a report for a near miss.Changed from approach control to tower after reporting field in sight without being given any traffic advisories before the frequency change. Also departing conflict aircraft departing along approach corridor.Approach controller should coordinate with tower to ensure approach path is clear prior to allowing frequency change.
ASRS:1768042.s: During a visual approach to ZZZ, the crew received a TCAS climb Resolution Advisory after Tower failed to provide traffic advisories before frequency change. A departing aircraft climbed rapidly through the flight path, passing 400 feet below, forcing the crew to execute the RA and perform a 360-degree turn to re-establish the approach.

ASRS:1768056.n: I received the inbound aircraft with an open AML write up for the aft cabin FA handset PA function inoperative. The interphone function was operative. I briefed the affected FAs on alternate communications as per the MEL. Maintenance personnel arrived at the aircraft just prior to departure and deferred the aft cabin handset as inoperative per the MEL. I received the AML, reviewed and signed it. While receiving the AML, myself, the FAs and the agents were dealing with a boarded passenger not properly wearing a face covering. All issues were resolved just in time to make departure which was otherwise uneventful. Shortly after getting airborne I realized that I had gotten distracted prior to departure and I had neglected to receive an amended release for the MEL item.[I was] Distracted by operational, maintenance and passenger issues. Be more diligent. There was an MEL write up for rear cabin phone unable to do a PA. It was deferred, but we forgot to get an amended release with the MEL on it before we took off.Cause - Flying a red eye. Late night departure.
ASRS:1768056.s: The pilot departed with a deferred aft cabin PA handset but failed to obtain an amended release due to distraction from maintenance, passenger, and operational issues. The cause was attributed to fatigue from a late-night red-eye flight.

ASRS:1768077.n: Due to Sigmet 7 and Sigmet Juliet 2 we were aware of the eruption of X Volcano in the area and on our route. At FL320 we communicated with ATC via CPDLC about observations. They asked if we observed VA (Volcanic Activity), we responded, 'No VA seen. Dark sky no moon. Lights down-EFVS shows clouds below.' We entered a layer of IMC and identified it as volcanic ash. Left and right turnoff lights were on, showing a very different layer: dark shadows, haze, shadows and contrast. Not normal diffusion from clouds. We monitored engine instruments/airpseed and immediately contacted Center on voice/VHF, reported the VA and requested and received immediate climb to FLXXX. At FLXYY there was no smell, no dust in the cockpit. No Saint Elmo's fire. No abnormal indications from engines or airspeed. The onset was sudden. At FLXXX clear skies returned and the layer lasted below us.QRH and FOM and training all underscored the importance of fast action, and reporting to ATC to alert other flights.
ASRS:1768077.s: The flight crew encountered sudden volcanic ash at FL320 while monitoring Sigmet alerts. They immediately reported the hazard to ATC and climbed to FLXXX, where conditions cleared with no engine abnormalities or cockpit contamination observed.

ASRS:1768082.n: Aircraft X released by previous shift Dispatcher ZZZZ-ZZZ as a re-release flight plan as is normal. After I took over and flight had been in air for several hours over mid-Ocean, we received a no-notice NOTAM advising that ZZZ Center was going to be closing from XA:30z-XC:00z for COVID cleaning. Aircraft X planned right through that airspace during that time frame (release prepared well before NOTAM was ever issued or any notice was received). Spoke with both ZZZ Center watch desk who stated that absolutely no traffic would be allowed through, no matter when they departed and if they didn't have enough fuel to go-around, they would have to land. Attempted multiple different routings around ZZZ [Center] airspace but not enough to circumnavigate. Consequently, flight had to divert to ZZZ1 for fuel.This was caused by ZZZ Center failing to provide notice of a closure in a timely manner as other centers have done when they have needed to close. Also at issue is why it requires shutting down the entire facility while someone sprays disinfectant. Absolutely no reason why Controller stations can't be shut down a few at a time to enable continued, if limited operation rather than a total shutdown.FAA needs to establish contingency plans for each center to remain open for at least a minimal level of service during COVID cleanings. As an essential safety function, it is unacceptable for them to just decide to go ATC zero when planes are already in the air.
ASRS:1768082.s: The dispatcher and flight crew of Aircraft X diverted to ZZZ1 for fuel after a late NOTAM announced a total closure of ZZZ Center for COVID cleaning. The reporter attributes the diversion to the center's failure to provide timely notice and its decision to shut down all operations rather than maintaining minimal service.

ASRS:1768161.n: We were on Departure out of ZZZ on the ZZZ 4 from Runway XXR W intersection. The flying FO executed TO and initial left turn and then the subsequent right turn to 220 and started the level off at 2,500. ATC then issued climb to 6,000. Followed shortly by an additional right turn. The Captain changed the heading bug at about the time he would normally have called for 5 for 6 for level off. We were at high rate of climb and the flying FO started the level off late and ballooned through 6,000 feet to approx 6,400-6,500 feet and quickly corrected back to 6000. I was the pilot flying on Aircraft X, ZZZ-ZZZZ. We were cleared on the ZZZ4 Departure, maintain 2,500 feet. I was hand flying the departure. We were cleared to a new heading of 050 and altitude of 6,000 feet. I turned to the new heading as I continued to climb to our cleared altitude of 6,000 feet. While in the turn, I realized I had passed 6,000 feet and the altitude box turned yellow. I immediately stopped climbing and descended back to 6,000 feet. The highest altitude was 6,380 feet. ATC commented to us to maintain 6,000 feet. There were no other issues regarding the altitude deviation.Other issues:At about 30 minutes from departure, we had an issue regarding deadheading flight attendants that were exposed to a COVID-19 positive flight attendant on their crew. We had an extensive discussion with the company representatives from Flight Operations, Dispatch, Medlink, and Inflight Services. This situation was very distracting to the pre-flight planning and the subsequent departure.I believe it was an influence in my altitude deviation.I deviated from the altitude clearance of 6,000 feet. I allowed the aircraft to reach an altitude of 6,380 feet.
ASRS:1768161.s: The Pilot Flying on Aircraft X hand-flew the ZZZ4 departure and ballooned to 6,380 feet while climbing to a cleared 6,000 feet. The pilot attributed the altitude deviation to distraction caused by a pre-flight discussion regarding crew exposure to COVID-19.

ASRS:1768194.n: I'm not sure the best way to address this, so I figured I would write a report to document this event. On departure from ZZZ, the flap handle became momentarily stuck in the Flaps 20 detent. It required excessive, and unusual amounts of force to select the flaps from the takeoff setting of 20, to flaps 8 during the climb sequence. After landing I documented the maintenance irregularity per FOM Airworthiness procedures. The write up in the maintenance log I submitted was 'While selecting flaps from 20 to 8 on departure, flap handle sticks in the 20 position, requires excessive force to move to flaps 8.' I then left the aircraft in the care of the next crew. I explained to the Captain the Maintenance discrepancy. After getting home, and plugging my iPad in to charge, I happened to see the flight, and out of curiosity decided to review the Maintenance Log again to see what they did to address the discrepancy. In my professional opinion, an incorrect corrective action was applied. The Maintenance corrective action states. 'The CRJ-200 flap selector has a built in gate between flaps 8 and flaps 20 that requires the operator to depress the lever when passing the gate. This is normal operation. Ok for continued service.' This is not true however. There is a gate that prevents selecting flaps past 20, without depressing the flap handle during flap extension, and a gate at flaps 8 to prevent retraction past flaps 8 in the event of a go around and during normal climb flap retraction. There is not a need to depress the flap handle to move it from 20 to 8 during flap retraction however, as the corrective action states. According to the CRJ PRM (Pilot Reference Manual) for the CRJ-200, it states on page 9-18 'Two flap gates are incorporated within the flap lever quadrant. The forward gate at the 8-degree setting minimizes the possibly of accidental flap selection to 0 degrees during a go-around procedure. The rearward gate at the 20 degree setting, minimizes the risk of Vfe (Flaps 30) being exceeded.' I'm not sure how to address this further, but I do not believe this discrepancy was appropriately dealt with by our maintenance. Furthermore, I do not believe the mechanic that submitted this corrective action has a full and appropriate understanding of the CRJ flap handle mechanics and operation, and it might be appropriate to consider passing this information to Maintenance for a bulletin or some sort of 'heads up.' The CRJ-200 is sensitive to flap fail events, and this is a critical component to the flap system, it's important for it to work properly and without issue. We don't want the flap handle getting stuck between detents, or preventing a crew from selecting flaps 8 appropriately in the event of a go-around.Improper procedure applied by maintenance. Failure of maintenance personnel to fully understand the flap handle flight control system and operational mechanics. Most likely added pressure to get the next flight out on time.I would suggest first and foremost that this aircraft is pulled out of service, properly inspected, and fixed if necessary. The maintenance write up does not even say that the system was properly ops checked. It was very simply ignored by the maintenance personnel attending to the write up, and not properly inspected or checked. I believe that a maintenance bulletin describing the correct operation of the CRJ-200 flap handle and the flap gates would potentially help further the understanding of our maintenance personnel to be able to properly address this write up.
ASRS:1768194.s: During departure from ZZZ in a CRJ-200, the pilot reported the flap handle stuck between detents 20 and 8, requiring excessive force to retract. The pilot concluded maintenance incorrectly dismissed the issue as normal operation without proper inspection, citing a lack of understanding of the flap gate mechanics.

ASRS:1768195.n: I was PM for this leg back to ZZZ1. We were cleared for takeoff on Runway XX, lined up on the runway, and I gave the controls to the FO. He set the thrust levers to CLIMB and called 'set thrust.' I checked the stack and verified the N1 indications were in the carats and stated 'thrust set.' I failed to push the thrust levers into the TOGA detent and neither of us noticed. The remainder of the takeoff was uneventful. When performing the after takeoff flow I realized that the thrust levers were already in the climb detent.This was my first trip on the type aircraft since being checked out earlier this month. I have exclusively flown the different version of aircraft type for the last X months and have not become accustomed to setting the thrust in Aircraft X compared to the previous type aircraft. I was a type Y aircraft FO before upgrading into this type aircraft so my time in all three variants is very limited. I had only done three legs in this type aircraft as PM before today, the rest of the legs being as PF to practice landings. My habit of pushing the thrust levers past the climb detent and into the TOGA detent has not been set yet, as for the majority of my legs I was only setting them to CLIMB, then the PM pushing them up to TOGA before I put my hand back.I need to fly this type aircraft more often to become/stay proficient. It also would have been better to do OE in this type of aircraft sooner to start those habits earlier and not get into such a groove in only the other type aircraft. I guarantee I will never make the same mistake again as it was quite a shock when I realized what I had/had not done.
ASRS:1768195.s: The Pilot Monitoring failed to advance thrust levers to the TOGA detent during takeoff on Runway XX, leaving them in the climb detent. The error occurred due to the pilot's limited recent experience on this specific aircraft variant and established habits from flying a different type.

ASRS:1768203.n: On the arrival into Atlanta we experience a severe wake turbulence event. Aircraft banked 45 degrees each side. I clicked the autopilot off and counteracted the rolling motion with full opposite aileron. First Officer communicated to ATC we needed to level off at 6000 ft due to wake turbulence. ATC then communicated that a 747 had just been through there landing on the parallel. We could see the 747 ahead and [to our] right landing, as well as a company CRJ 200 12 o'clock. In proper separation between us and the heavy considering current wind conditions, additional separation or off-setting the arrival course could have helped. 'Caution wake turbulence' would have prepared us.
ASRS:1768203.s: The crew encountered severe wake turbulence from a landing 747 during arrival into Atlanta, causing 45-degree banks requiring manual control. The pilot attributed the event to insufficient separation and a lack of wake turbulence warnings from ATC.

ASRS:1768207.n: During the climb we briefly received a Master Caution and the annunciation, AP (Autopilot) PITCH MISTRIM. Several seconds later the airplane abruptly pitched down about 5 degrees. The pilot monitoring (PIC) then retrieved the emergency checklist and we began running the procedure. Before disengaging the autopilot, the airplane again abruptly pitched down about 3-5 degrees. After the autopilot was disengaged, I hand flew the airplane briefly and noticed the pitch portion of the flight controls were partially stuck. I then asked the Captain to see if he could feel the same thing. We exchanged controls, and he confirmed that the controls were sticky about the pitch axis. We then exchanged control of the airplane back, and I resumed flying the airplane. The Captain then requested immediate vector to the nearest airport. ATC then gave us a vector to ZZZ and a descent altitude. We then engaged the yaw-damp, but left the autopilot off. During the descent, we had at least four more events where the flight controls appeared to be stuck. Each time I was able to over-power the control. I also noticed that once I freed the controls, they appeared to be freed for 20-30 seconds. During the descent, I was monitoring the outside temperature to detect when we got to warmer air, as I was concerned that all the rain that we had at ZZZ may have frozen and caused the controls to momentarily freeze. After we passed the freezing level, I did not notice any more problems with the pitch control. After landing at ZZZ, we de-planed the passengers at [the] FBO. At that time, we observed water draining out of the bottom of the airplane. We estimated that about a quart of water drained out of the airplane. We then re-positioned the airplane to ZZZ1. After parking, we again observed water coming out of the airplane.
ASRS:1768207.s: During climb, the crew experienced autopilot pitch mistrim and abrupt nose-down movements caused by sticky pitch controls, likely due to frozen water. After hand-flying through multiple control stickiness events until passing the freezing level, they diverted to ZZZ, where approximately one quart of water drained from the aircraft.

ASRS:1768208.n: ILS approach into ZZZ. I briefed the approach with course and frequency and confirmed the points in the FMS. Vectors to final were activated and I missed the course was not set on the inbound and I think when I briefed the frequency I was reading the frequency from NAV 2. We turned inbound and not seeing the errors I told the PNF that he had control, but this time we were well above the GS. We notified ATC that we were going to go missed and were given new instructions. After the missed, I reset the inbound course and reset the frequency. I then told the PNF that I had control and the next approach was done to a safe landing.I haven't flown in several months and the other pilot was his second flight in this type aircraft. I believe was a contributing factor on this approach. While being vectored to the ILS for Runway XX, the crew noticed that the localizer failed to auto-tune when the approach was armed. When it was determined that the course was not going to be captured the pilot transferred the auto pilot to the pilot monitoring side where the localizer did tune correctly. However, by this time the aircraft had flown through the course. The autopilot attempted to capture the course, but completed one or two 'S' turns. The crew agreed that the approach was not stabilized and we indicated to ATC that we intended to go-around and try the approach again. We were given vectors and an altitude and were cleared for the approach again. The following approach to landing was completed without issue. Crew should have been more vigilant to ensure that the correct NAV frequency was tuned and the decision to transfer the coupled side autopilot could have been made earlier.
ASRS:1768208.s: The crew, consisting of a pilot returning after months and a second-time type pilot, missed the ILS approach due to incorrect NAV frequency tuning and delayed autopilot transfer. They executed a go-around, corrected the setup, and completed a safe landing on the second attempt.

ASRS:1768219.n: I started work of a 3 day trip. 1st day 13 hour duty day so almost 15 hours with mask on!! I tried to take several masks (maybe 15). She said I could only take so much and I replied it gets wet so often I need to change it, especially if airline requires me to talk to people as much as we do. She finally gave me more. If I am required to wear something that I know is harming my health at least let me do less harm by changing it constantly. Then I was denied access to the bus because of social distancing. Airline must pick and choose which guidelines it would like to follow because every seat is taken and there is no social distancing on an airplane, but I can't even get to work to get to the packed airplane cause I need to social distance. This trip had 2 legs with severe turbulence. I am the one that has to sit in a passenger seat. I don't get the harness to keep my body from slamming all over the place. Yes, people were crying and screaming, that is how bad it was. But unfortunately our pilots took off without asking if we were okay. Wow, but the next flight into ZZZ1, she screamed over the PA to sit immediately!!! First officer made sure we were safe and apologized forever on how bad she felt with the last minute notice. I again was thrown to my seat and no harness. It is difficult to pass information on to each other that the passengers probably shouldn't hear, but there is no choice if I need to know. The FA in the back has to yell to me, not only because of a mask, but because I am so far away. Again, safety and security is tossed aside. After the 13 hour duty day my head was throbbing. I again get severe headaches the longer I am masked. These days are just too long wearing a mask and now they put out an article to the public about the safety of wearing a mask on a plane. I can do the same and say mask wearing does nothing. Both articles would be correct, because they aren't peer reviewed science. Science doesn't lie, people do.
ASRS:1768219.s: A flight attendant reported severe turbulence on two legs without a safety harness, causing injury risk, while also facing mask supply restrictions and denied bus access due to inconsistent social distancing enforcement. The crew noted communication difficulties and health issues from prolonged mask wear during a 13-hour duty day.

ASRS:1768223.n: On our third and final flight after an exceedingly long day with an early sign in, out of a remote co-terminal, (3 legs, with a 3 hour sit out of ZZZ1 having to leave my house at XA:00am to catch the shuttle) and dealing with mechanical issues, stressful delays, and upset passengers along the way, I became distracted when a dead heading crew member wanted to move his seat to a completely empty row in the unusually empty last flight, in order to increase social distancing.He moved to the exit row seat XX4, and was talking to me during boarding about changing seats, seniority, furloughs, and the general state of things. The boarding was very short and the lead flight attendant said to prepare, I had thought she meant the cabin, and she had actually meant the doors.She did the all call and I answered the phone but, being caught off guard, I failed to arm the doors, because I had still been talking to the deadheading crew member who would be working the return flight. Then I proceeded to head up to 2L and R, (which is my demo position;) to do the safety demo. During the demo the Captain called back to ask us to check the 2 and 3, L and R doors.I verified the 2 L and R doors were armed and went to check my doors (the 3 L and R doors;) and realized they were disarmed. I immediately corrected the situation by arming the doors, and called the cockpit to verify. The cockpit confirmed, and we resumed the safety demo.In the future I will NOT allow myself to become distracted from my door procedures by any and all outside influences. I have never failed to arm a door before, and realize now how easy it is to slip up on a long day when we let our guard down, and allow outside factors to affect us. I will practice constant vigilance in the future.Also, I will visually verify and crosschecked myself during the all call, to make certain that the doors are armed, and if I would have done that this time, instead of being distracted, I would have noticed that the doors were Not in fact armed, and been able to correct the issue immediately rather than after the fact.
ASRS:1768223.s: A flight attendant on the final leg of a multi-segment flight failed to arm the 3L and 3R doors during boarding due to distraction from a deadheading crew member. The error was discovered during the safety demonstration, and the doors were immediately armed and verified with the cockpit before departure.

ASRS:1768229.n: The #1 Engine [Oil Filter] bypass light illuminated. As per crew and QRH (Quick Reference Handbook), engine required to be shut down as a precaution. [Aircraft] diverted to ZZZ for repair.
ASRS:1768229.s: The crew diverted the aircraft to ZZZ after the #1 engine oil filter bypass light illuminated. Following the Quick Reference Handbook, they shut down the engine as a precautionary measure.

ASRS:1768230.n: I believed [I] closed cap and tab locked the right engine oil fill cap but [it] wasn't locked. Then right engine [started] losing oil and pressure.[I recommend] to confirm cap closed and locked before closing service panel or panel can't close unless cap is locked.
ASRS:1768230.s: The pilot reported failing to lock the right engine oil fill cap, causing the engine to lose oil and pressure. The pilot recommends confirming the cap is locked before closing the service panel, as the panel should not close unless the cap is secured.

ASRS:1768231.n: DATE. First day back from days Off, started at TIME and was turned over 2 out of service aircraft, and a ferry flight. Turnover for ferry flight was everything in order will require the inspection sign off and MFD, it was to be a 3 leg ferry due to biobore in the tanks. Each leg requiring a new MFD (Maintenance Ferry Document). First leg was scheduled for a XA:30 departure. During this time I was updating logs, fielding phone calls, and reviewing ferry checklist. Started to review ferry documents and noted that there were a few overtime items that were not documented in the logbook on logs N and 5N1. I then documented the missing items under log page N2. Overdue items were transcribed. Under this transaction you will find open log pages, open work control packages, and overtime items. Aircraft was then issued MFD. Checklist completed.2nd leg of ferry was ZZZ-ZZZ1. Ferry arrange was prepared and sent when aircraft arrived ZZZ. I discussed the inbound discrepancies with ZZZ, a dual tire replacement due to one tire being underinflated. We noted, log page N as stating one or more items have been identified as overtime or becoming overtime. I again reviewed maintenance release and noted no change in items. Paperwork was completed, inbound discrepancies addressed and MFD issued.3rd leg of ferry was ZZZ1-ZZZ2. During review of paperwork in preparation for ferry, it was noted 2 additional items under maintenance release as being expired. It was during this time I discovered that these 2 items must have expired in flight and were not in a log item or on the MFD. Part of the Ferry checklist is to ensure time-controlled workload items that will expire by the end of the flight are documented.Task Card X and -0024 GVI (General Visual Inspection) Strut 1 and 2 Insp appear to have expired in flight. At this point I spoke with my co-worker and we generated another log with the 2 out of time items. I was asked if it showed due in maintenance release. My reply was that I have been viewing out of time items under maintenance release which will show task that are currently out of time vs forecasted task. My oversight led to expiring of time-controlled workload items in flight. Policies, procedures and processes are area that I feel I am thorough in. For me this is a lesson learned and something that I will not forget in future ferry flights.
ASRS:1768231.s: A mechanic conducting a three-leg ferry flight discovered that two time-controlled maintenance tasks expired in flight due to an oversight in reviewing the maintenance release. The mechanic documented the expired items in a new log and acknowledged the error as a lesson learned regarding ferry checklist procedures.

ASRS:1768255.n: I was doing my rounds of the aircraft here in ZZZ. As I drove by our pre-flighted Aircraft X, I could hear an APU running and stairs were up to the aircraft. As I walked up to the aircraft and entered, I noticed the aircraft was sealed from the pre-flight, I broke the seal and confirmed via EICAS indication that the APU was running. The pre-flight crew typically completes the pre-flight between XA-XA:30L. The aircraft was pre-flighted and sealed and left with the APU running for 2.75 hours with no one to monitor for fire events and EGT (Exhaust Gas Temperature) temps, this is a severe hazard and had there been a fire event there would have been no one to activate the fire bottle or follow proper procedures. [Recommend] following proper procedures and if no one is left in the cockpit to monitor the APU, please shut it down. [I] was told that maintenance filed a report saying they found the APU running on Aircraft X after we performed a pre-flight on [date]. To the best of my recollection I completed a full shutdown checklist which includes turning off the battery switch.
ASRS:1768255.s: A cabin crew member discovered Aircraft X's APU running for 2.75 hours after the pre-flight crew sealed and left the aircraft unmonitored. The reporter identified this as a severe fire hazard due to the lack of personnel to monitor EGT or activate fire suppression, despite claiming to have completed the shutdown checklist.

ASRS:1768266.n: Filed flight plan about 20 minutes before calling to see if flight plan was in the system. I informed Ground Control that I would pick it up in the air but was just checking to see if it had arrived. Ground did not have flight plan so I started up and taxied to runway figuring it would be out by the time we were at the hold line. Called at the runway hold line and still no flight plan - Ground suggested I just take off and have the Departure Controller enter one for me. Just to be safe I quickly filed another one on my phone, did my checks and when I called for takeoff they told me it had just come through. I had filed NAVHO intersection then BLD VOR on the first flight plan, then just direct BLD VOR on the second - rest of route to ZZZ the same for both plans.On VFR climb I skipped NAVJO because I thought it was the second flight plan that had popped up on the system. Phoenix Approach was in a long conversation with a VFR plane so couldn't contact until I was at 14,500 feet - climbing to 16,500. They told me I was almost out of their airspace and to call ABQ Center. Level at 16,500 I called ABQ and they cleared us to ZZZ as filed. Here's where there was a problem. Just to be safe I asked if I should be going direct NAVHO then BLD and the controller said 'affirmative' as I was climbing to FL280. I knew I wasn't at NAVHO yet so entered it in as 'NAVJO' (incorrect). I noticed that the needle pointed over 30 degrees to the right as I engaged NAV - figuring something was wrong I disengaged NAV and turned back to something close to direct BLD and asked if I could just go direct BLD which I was given. NAVHO was pretty much on a direct line from FLG to BLD so I was doing okay before entering 'NAVJO' which is way up to the North.Looking at the track log I never was more than 17 degrees off and that was for as long as it took to reverse the turn, but this was embarrassing. Don't want to do this kind of thing when departing a NY Metro area airport. Contributing factors: Flight plan late arriving at FLG. My desire to do a quick turn and keep the boss happy - this was a fuel stop. Misspelling 'NAVHO' because I was rushing - trying to keep the controller happy. Two flight plans in the system, each with a different initial fix. I neglected to enter NAVJO because it would be departing VFR and it was pretty close to the airport. Ways to prevent this from recurring: File my flight plans earlier just in case - even if I'm not sure we will use it. I thought we may be able to make it all the way to ZZZ so didn't file the plan for departing from FLG (fuel stop). Don't be so quick to engage NAV - make sure it looks correct first. Don't rush when entering waypoints - if I had entered with the correct spelling there would not have been more than a few degree turn to the left involved. Enter all the fixes when departing VFR - don't assume you won't get one of them.
ASRS:1768266.s: The pilot departed FLG VFR with a delayed flight plan and, while rushing to satisfy the controller, misspelled waypoint NAVHO as NAVJO in the FMS. This error caused a 30-degree deviation, requiring the pilot to disengage navigation and request a direct clearance to BLD VOR.

ASRS:1768267.n: Upon arrival in NEW airspace. ATC cleared [us] for approach via SAFES IAF to RNAV runway 36L. Clearance was then modified and was told to stay at 3,000 ft. until further advised for departing traffic. Aircraft flew past initial approach descent point. FMS dropped vertical navigation guidance at that point. A manual descent was initiated just prior to that. I hurriedly reloaded the FMS to re-establish vertical guidance. While reloading, I received a low altitude alert from ATC with my call sign. I appeared to be in the vertical path of the approach just inside TOYBO at 2,400 ft. I had the runway insight and asked for and was cleared for visual approach.I am unsure if descent rate or altitude tripped the low altitude warning issued by ATC as I appeared to be in parameters while trying to re-establish the approach in the aircraft FMS.Flight continued to runway on glide path with nothing unusual other than the low altitude warning from ATC near TOYBO intersection.
ASRS:1768267.s: The pilot flying an arrival into NEW airspace received a low altitude alert from ATC near TOYBO at 2,400 ft. after manually descending and reloading the FMS following a modified clearance. The flight continued safely to a visual approach on runway 36L after the alert.

ASRS:1768270.n: At the end of a night training flight with my certificated student, we were instructed to taxi from our runway exit point to parking via a parallel taxiway. As we taxied along the parallel taxiway, I noticed a regional jet pass our aircraft while decelerating on the runway next to us. I saw the regional jet begin to exit the runway on a high-speed taxiway that intersected the parallel taxiway ahead of us. I told my student, who had the controls, to keep an eye on the exiting regional jet. Without stopping, the regional jet crossed the parallel taxiway in front of us and I instructed my student to stop the airplane while I began reaching to take control of our aircraft, though it ended up not being necessary. My student applied maximum braking, stopping our airplane approximately 25 ft. from the regional jet wingtip as it rapidly crossed our path. Without our prompt and aggressive action, a collision would have occurred.I suspect improper coordination between the Local and Ground controllers or an inappropriate approval by the Ground controller to the Local controller allowed the Local controller to clear the regional jet on Tower frequency, we were on Ground frequency, to exit and taxi to parking without stopping. Additionally, the Ground controller did not provide instruction nor information regarding the exiting regional jet to us, [with] no time for us to query either. Regardless, the regional jet crew should have been visually clearing as they exited the runway and crossed the intersection into the ramp. Though dark, our aircraft lighting was on and operating normally, bright LED navigation lights, beacon, and taxi light. Our aircraft is small, but it was visible.Fortunately, we were able to prevent one of the links in the safety chain from breaking to avoid an accident. I will continue to be vigilant throughout every phase of flight.
ASRS:1768270.s: During a night training taxi, a student pilot stopped their aircraft 25 feet from a regional jet that crossed their path without stopping. The reporter attributes the near-collision to suspected controller coordination failures and the regional jet crew's failure to visually clear the intersection.

ASRS:1768272.n: While flying at an altitude of 3,000 feet, ATC assigned new altitude of 2,500 feet. I mistakenly entered 2,000 feet in my autopilot. Once leveling out at 2,000 feet ATC informed me of my error and reassigned existing altitude (2,000 feet) as my new altitude.I believe this occurred due to a heightened work load environment I was experiencing at the time, rapid fire instructions being given by Controller within his busy airspace, and my reduced flight proficiency due to fewer hours flown over the prior several months. I plan on making a concerted effort to fly at a minimum of once per week to maintain suitable level of proficiency.
ASRS:1768272.s: The pilot mistakenly entered 2,000 feet instead of the assigned 2,500 feet while descending from 3,000 feet. The reporter attributed this error to high workload, rapid ATC instructions, and reduced flight proficiency due to low recent flight hours.

ASRS:1768283.n: I was the PNF on this leg. The Captain was in the cockpit and started the right engine while I loaded equipment on board. I closed the main cabin door and briefed the passengers. This was their second leg with us so the briefing was abbreviated since a full briefing was given on the prior leg. I was in a COVID mask and it was warm outside (82 degrees). After the load I entered the cockpit and strapped in. I received a briefing on the clearance and we started the left engine. I was a bit rushed and I didn't review the departure procedure plate as thoroughly as I should have. We departed [Runway] XXR and I didn't hear or the captain didn't call for me to select NAV on the MCP. Therefore, we were late to make the required right turn to 025 degrees. The Tower asked us to begin the turn. I was rushed, hot and distracted by the COVID mask a bit. I should have prompted the NAV selection if the Captain didn't call for it. This was not a DP where there is a complicated course. It is RNAV but basically a heading to a vector. The heading change was subtle and I reviewed the DP in a hurry.
ASRS:1768283.s: The PNF reported that while departing Runway XXR, the crew failed to select NAV on the MCP, delaying the required right turn to 025 degrees. The PNF attributed this error to being rushed, hot, and distracted by a COVID mask, which led to an inadequate review of the departure procedure.

ASRS:1768313.n: During the flight portion of a flight review/IPC, we experienced a taxiway excursion due to a total loss of brake pressure.After landing and taxing back to runway XX, in ZZZ, the brakes lost pressure while entering the runway. We decided not to takeoff. I checked my brakes and they did not work either.Exiting on taxiway, the aircraft seemed under control and we were discussing shutting down the engine once we made it to the ramp area.The aircraft started veering to the left. I joined on the pedals, full right rudder and full brake, no change, still veering. I told pilot to shut it down. He pulled the mixture to cutoff. The aircraft then went off the side of the taxiway, the propeller struck two taxiway lights and the right main ran over one light before the plane came to a stop. The engine seemed slow to shut down while at mixture cutoff. Pilot said that the boost pump was on and that was most likely the reason for the delayed shutdown. The engine was shut down, however, the propeller continued to windmill.Two of the propeller blades were damaged and there was a scratch on the side of the wheel fairing. No other damage to the aircraft. Neither of us were injured.
ASRS:1768313.s: During a flight review, the pilot and instructor experienced a taxiway excursion after total brake pressure loss caused the aircraft to veer left and strike taxiway lights. The engine shutdown was delayed due to the boost pump being on, resulting in damaged propeller blades and a wheel fairing scratch, but no injuries occurred.

ASRS:1768327.n: The issue we had was that we departed on a revenue flight without reviewing all required forms. I was acting as First Officer and non flying pilot in a three pilot crew. This was my first time working in the First Officer position in X months which was in initial training.We were initially setup for a departure on Runway XXR. On the taxi out we were given a last minute runway change to Runway XYR. Performance Data for this runway was not provided on the release. This required me to 'manually' acquire the data from the MCDU. This was the first time online or in training for me of obtaining data in this fashion. It required me to input the current conditions at the airport. When the takeoff data printed out it was in a format that I was accustomed to. I imputed the computed speeds and verified the thrust settings were proper, we weighed less than the maximum allowed assumed weight, the current winds were within tolerances, and that the temperatures were correct. The Captain and Relief Pilot then reviewed the data and all agreed we were legal to takeoff. I mistakenly assumed that we had already received the load closeout and because of this the data I obtained superseded that and the load closeout data was contained with the new takeoff data.Several hours into the flight the Relief Pilot advised myself and the Captain that the load close out in fact printed out a few minutes after rotation. After reviewing the closeout I determined the takeoff was well within the performance data I imputed. However, we are required to review the load closeout prior to takeoff.
ASRS:1768327.s: The First Officer, acting as non-flying pilot in a three-pilot crew, departed without reviewing the load closeout due to a last-minute runway change requiring manual MCDU data entry. Although the takeoff was within performance limits, the required load closeout document was not reviewed prior to rotation.

ASRS:1768350.n: I was in cruise phase on the flight, from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Around Yuma there was an object in the air which me and my passenger couldn't identify but seemed like a balloon with a human size gray color metal part at the same altitude. We passed very close by, it was scary and since it was a relatively small object I couldn't see it from very far, so I didn't have much time to react. It wasn't moving in horizontal (not 100% sure about horizontal) or vertical space. Also didn't appear on Stratux or GPS. I was on flight following, so I immediately communicated with the ATC and shared details. 2 days after this incident, we were on the way back to ZZZ, exactly same happened around the same area, reported again to ATC the same way. The only difference this time was, it was [a] little smaller. Few days ago, since I'm currently in IFR training I shared my experience with my CFII except giving the location but the destination, he immediately asked if this happened around Yuma and I was surprised with his question. He is not sure what the object is either, but obviously I am not the only one seeing these. So wanted to create this report since I think it's a high potential danger especially if that would be an IFR flight.
ASRS:1768350.s: A pilot and passenger encountered an unidentified, stationary object resembling a balloon with a metal part near Yuma during cruise on two separate flights. The object did not appear on Stratux or GPS, prompting immediate ATC reports and concerns about potential hazards to IFR operations.

ASRS:1768383.n: Our operation was just notified on Date 3 that our aircraft registration expired on Date 1. I operated one training flight as SIC. The flight was on Date 2. I am guilty of just looking to ensure that the document was on the airplane, while completely disregarding my duty to ensure that it was valid. A contributing factor to this is that the aircraft registration is addressed to our company headquarters, which is a different address than our operations base hangar. Due to COVID related staffing at our headquarters, our FAA reminder postcards were never delivered to our hangar. Again, it is my responsibility as a flying crew member to ensure that the correct paperwork is on the aircraft prior to each flight. We have instituted the following changes to ensure that this does not happen again: 1) Added the registration expiration to our maintenance tracking software. This will flag our maintenance team when expiration is close to occurrence. This will also be printed on the preflight form that all pilots utilize. 2) Training will occur and language will be added to our General Operations Manual (GOM) and/or expanded normal procedures document emphasizing the action to ensure that a valid registration is onboard the aircraft. 3) A consultancy company has been hired in ZZZ1 to automatically renew our registration and deliver it directly to our hangar.
ASRS:1768383.s: The SIC operated a training flight on an aircraft with an expired registration, admitting they failed to verify document validity. The oversight occurred because FAA renewal notices were not delivered to the hangar due to staffing issues and the registration being addressed to headquarters.

ASRS:1768384.n: My student and I [were on a] 6 mile visual straight-in approach to ZZZ airport at 2,300 ft. MSL. My student made numerous radio calls reporting our position every 2 miles. We understood there was another aircraft making radio calls in the pattern. The last call reported by Aircraft Y was a left base turn with visual and Sentry ForeFlight contact by us. I asked Aircraft Y if they had us in sight, no response. My student made a final call and we began to enter the runway environment. I could see the notification on my iPad stating there was a target just behind us, same altitude and extremely close. My student landed and while rolling on runway Aircraft Y made a go-around call while flying extremely close and around, slightly above, our aircraft. I replied, 'Appreciate it' and they replied with a confirming double radio click. The other aircraft continued to climb runway heading and we both stayed in the pattern for a few more landings with no other issues until we departed the area to the south.
ASRS:1768384.s: A student pilot and instructor on a visual approach to ZZZ airport experienced a close call when Aircraft Y flew extremely close and slightly above them during landing. The incident occurred despite prior radio contact and an iPad alert, prompting Aircraft Y to execute a go-around while the student continued the landing.

ASRS:1768389.n: I was working Local 2 and Ground Control combined during slow traffic and the airport was in a North flow deice configuration. The aircraft were landing XXL with med-good braking action reports from pilots. Aircraft X was given a clearance to land with a med-good braking action report. Aircraft X rolled quickly pass to high speeds so I figured he was trying to roll to the end quickly. I instructed Aircraft X to turn left at the end. At that point he was approaching the end at a good rate of speed. I sent the next aircraft around as I watched Aircraft X go slightly passed the end of the runway, make a hard left turn back onto taxiway M from M10 taxiway. Aircraft X verified that he was off of runway XXL so L let the next aircraft continue and land without any issues. Aircraft X asked to have airport vehicle to check his aircraft in case he had hit any taxiway lights. The airport closed runway XXL. I later observed Aircraft X taxi back to the gate on his own power.Other aircraft seemed to be able to make the high speed taxiways without any issue. Maybe if the pilot came in with a slower approach speed it could have helped him not to roll long and slide. Completed all briefings prior to approach. We were expecting a VFR approach but briefed like full IFR approach and were prepared for the weather to change. We were preparing for a normal approach and landing to Runway XXL. ATIS Bravo showed three miles and overcast 4100 feet. ATIS BRAVO also advised RCC CODE 5-5-5 for Runways XXR, XXL, XYL. Planned a flap 15 landing. We used conservative number of CODE 4 RCC giving us Autobrakes 2, 1530 stopping margin. In essence 3000 feet, touchdown zone being the most restrictive of the 12,000 foot runway. On final approach, Tower stated Braking Action Good to RJ in front of us.We landing uneventfully. I believe we landed within 3,000 TDZE, however, I do remember floating a little with 10 knots ice additive. We did not have any markings visible outside center line do to white snow. Decelerated to 60 knots, F/O called 60 knots. I stowed the thrust reversers and pressed brakes to disconnect autobrakes. Nothing seemed unusual at that point. Deceleration rate seemed normal up to that point. Tower stated: 'Roll to end, aircraft behind you two-mile final.'I depressed brakes to further decelerate and realized there was zero braking available. I stated 'No brakes' to F/O a couple of times. F/O immediately told Tower and aircraft behind us went around. I extended full reverse thrust again to try and get aircraft stopped. We drifted about 45 degrees toward intended exit. We never left hard surface of runway/taxiway. I briefed F/O to contact Ground immediately and notify 'NILL BRAKING LAST THIRD OF RUNWAY XXL.'I also had F/O ask for inspection of runway/taxiway lights to make sure aircraft had no damage before we taxied any further. He also notified Company Ops what had just occurred. I briefed what had happened to Passengers on PA. ZZZ Ground Ops notified there were no runway/taxiway lights damaged. We taxied aircraft to gate without any further issues. Maintenance was waiting for us at gate and we described what had occurred. They inspected aircraft and found an actual blue taxiway light laying on top of wheel carriage on right main. There was no aircraft damage noted by the Maintenance inspection. I put a note in logbook and we deadheaded to ZZZ1.I take briefings very seriously. This was not the type of flight that either Pilot was out of loop or just not having a bad day. We were configured at the marker and on speed the whole time on approach. I may have floated a little do to 10 knot increase of VREF. The ATIS reports from ZZZ were RCC 5-5-5. The two previous aircraft reports BRAG. The only difference was, the two previous aircraft exited 2nd high speed. We rolled past the second high speed for passenger comfort. We never expected NIL braking under light snow covered runway in front of us. The airport needs to actually test the runway, if they're going to advertise 5-GOOD. It was one of the worst feelings a Pilot can have realizing he/she has lost effective control of an aircraft. Had I not redeployed the thrust reversers, I believe we would have encountered aircraft damage and maybe even injuries even though aircraft would have been exiting hard surface at a slow speed. I am actually shocked the runway had not been prepared for arrivals with so much equipment and men available at that airport. Very disappointed.
ASRS:1768389.s: A pilot reported that Aircraft X experienced zero braking on the last third of Runway XXL despite ATIS reporting good conditions, causing the aircraft to overshoot the runway end. Maintenance later found a taxiway light on the right main gear, but no aircraft damage occurred.

ASRS:1768391.n: Aircraft X overflight at 9,000 and Aircraft Y departed a satellite airport with 9,000 as his final altitude. I was working numerous aircraft doing IFR practice approaches in our airspace with weather that aircraft were starting to deviate around. I noticed these two aircraft were on converging courses about 5 miles separation between the two. I gave both aircraft heading altitudes and called traffic to try and keep separation. They got within about 2 to 2.5 miles lateral before altitude separation was established. It has been a difficult day as it's the first day being back on our bid schedule. Only having one day off after numerous months of time off between work sessions to recuperate. More positions open and not being able to maintain social distance, which is now requiring to wear a mask the entire time working. I am required to wear glasses all the time and wearing the mask is causing fogging of my glasses as my mask moves when I talk. Which is causing a distraction.[I recommend being] more vigilant of altitudes. Eliminate or limit distractions or things distracting me. Maybe ask for a split of positions since some distractions like a mask can't be eliminated at this time allowing for more time to overcome the distraction.
ASRS:1768391.s: An air traffic controller managing Aircraft X and Y during an overflight and departure reported a near-midair conflict where lateral separation reduced to 2.5 miles before altitude separation was established. The controller attributed the incident to personal distractions caused by fogged glasses from wearing a required mask while working a difficult shift.

ASRS:1768392.n: Climbing out, approximately XX00Z, the left engine had loss of thrust associated with compressor stall / surges. Flight attendants rang the call button and indicated they heard loud banging and wanted to verify we heard the same. We shallowed our climb then leveled off at FL 280 and [advised ATC]. Subsequent flight attendant chime indicated they saw flames had extended aft of the #1 engine. We had already begun to tackle the surge / stall QRC followed by QRH checklist when they called advised of flames. We recognized and agreed that ZZZ was our best option due to proximity (80 miles roughly ) off our nose with optimum field capabilities. We coordinated with flight attendants and talked with a non-rev commuting Company Captain who had been sitting on left side of cabin and had seen the flames. During this process, we coordinated with ATC for direct and began a descent to ZZZ [and] fired off a quick message to Dispatch indicating engine malfunction and plan to divert. We coordinated with crew of the precautionary landing and advised passengers of our intentions. In the descent we completed the appropriate checklists, acquired the [weight and balance] data for landing in addition to brake cooling then were vectored for a visual approach to [Runway] XXL. We landed uneventfully and taxied clear of the runway and we were met by Fire and Rescue. We shut down the #1 engine and awaited CFR to evaluate. CFR gave us the all clear and we taxied to gate and began to coordinate with all appropriate personnel. Normal climbout passing FL 282. Initially heard banging outside of aircraft followed by a reduction in climb, decreasing airspeed and aircraft vibration. Immediately followed by a call from the A F/A (flight attendant) reporting flame emanating from #1 engine. Engine problem was confirmed in the cockpit by high temp (800 EGT) and diminished N1. My F/O (First Officer) immediately notified ATC that we have an engine issue and need to maintain FL 280. I told him to [request priority] at that time. I reduced the thrust lever to observe changes in engine indications. The vibrations ceased and temperature reduction. We both believed we had a compressor stall. We were holding FL 280 on one engine, albeit with excessive thrust on #2 engine. F/O asked for lower and we were cleared to FL 240. We had two jumpseaters onboard, so I got an experienced set of eyes on the engine. He confirmed all that we knew and that the engine no longer had flames coming from the tailpipe. Assessing the non-normal together, I called for the QRC (quick reference checklist) Engine Limit or Surge or Stall Checklist. The QRH (quick reference handbook) confirmed our assessment. We completed down to Step X (QRH) at that point. An engine shutdown was not required, but thrust lever remained at idle for remainder of flight. ZZZ was 80 miles from our present position and we agreed was the nearest suitable airport. ATC cleared us direct. While I was PF (pilot flying), F/O communicated with F/A's and passengers. I sent a message to Dispatch about our diversion. We ran the Diversion Checklist. F/O ran weight and balance data for a 'One Engine Inoperative' approach and landing data. We planned for and flew a 'One Engine Inoperative Landing'. An uneventful landing in ZZZ culminated with a check of the engine/damage by Emergency Personnel. We taxied under our own power to the gate.
ASRS:1768392.s: During climbout, the flight crew experienced a left engine compressor stall with flames, high EGT, and reduced N1. They leveled at FL 280, diverted to ZZZ, and landed safely on one engine after confirming no further flames.

ASRS:1768393.n: Aircraft was stopped at intersection X waiting to taxi to [Runway] XR. Last ground instruction was to use Taxiway E, but then was changed to follow company off right by different Controller. FO and I both missed transition to Taxiway F instruction. Controller said 'No big deal;' but it was clearly a pilot error in not understanding and reading back correctly the instructions. Day five of flying led to slight fatigue, coupled with change of ATC instructions leading to failure. We were approaching ramp number [X] from the gate for departure. Contacted Ground for taxi clearance. They instructed us to proceed onto Taxiway Echo westbound to Runway YR, the rest of the transmission was difficult to understand. We, instead, turned westbound on Taxiway Foxtrot. While I was trying to interpret what the second part of the transmission while I was starting the number one engine, a second Controller informed us of our error. Lots of time compression and task loading along with part of the Ground Controller's transmission being difficult to understand. The airport was busy, lots of aircraft simultaneously taxiing in and out with numerous 'stepped on' transmissions. An additional 'additive condition' was the Ground Controller's transmission. I believe a contributing factor was mask wearing in the Controller facility. If this is true, they need to standardize what type of masks they wear and work harder to enunciate their syllables.
ASRS:1768393.s: The flight crew missed a taxi instruction change due to fatigue, high task loading, and a Ground Controller's difficult transmission, causing them to turn onto the wrong taxiway. A second Controller corrected the error, which the pilot attributed to communication issues potentially exacerbated by the controller's mask.

ASRS:1768435.n: I was scheduled for the re-qualification X course. I requested a warm up sim and was denied by Person X going through my chief pilot office. Person X claims that warm up sims are a waste of time and don't improve an already high pass rate. Person X said training is designed to catch any lack of proficiency prior to the CQLOE [Continuing Qualification Line Operational Evaluation], so a warm up sim isn't necessary as normal training will catch any lack of proficiency.I did the traditional re-qualification X course in month after being off the type X aircraft for X years. I only flew about 90 hours on the type X aircraft prior to the reduction of flying. I haven't flown since the middle of month. I thought requesting a warm up sim was reasonable considering my lack of recency/proficiency on the type X aircraft, and a new very short re-qualification course.The new re-qualification X course has several areas that aren't covered prior to the LOE [Line Operational Evaluation]. In the curriculum, it shows the initial 3 sims all start engines running on the runway. There is no practicing flows, FMS work on the ground, starting engines, or normal ground ops getting to the runway which are some of the most high risk areas. There is no time built into the curriculum to work on procedures for people that have [not] flown for 8-9 months and didn't have much recency.I feel the company is focused on pushing through as many people through as quickly as possible when the company let them lose currency. I don't feel that the new re-qualification X course is appropriate or safe for all pilots that can be trained under it.
