After review of the time stamp (ADSB out), it is to my knowledge that both aircrafts had departed from opposite runways.
ASRS:1768824.s: A pilot and student departing runway 5 encountered a head-on conflict shortly after takeoff with an aircraft departing the opposite runway. The other pilot veered right to avoid a collision, and ADS-B data confirmed both aircraft had departed simultaneously from opposite runways.

ASRS:1768830.n: I was working Approach, it was south flow. I cleared Aircraft X, a heavy B7XX RNAV approach then switched him to tower. Then, tower called me said that Aircraft X was going around and they issued him 185 heading climbing to 5000 ft. Then, Aircraft X came on my frequency, I radar identified him, told him to climb to 7000 ft., because there was a 6300 ft. MIA block to the east. Once he was level at 7000 ft., he was about 14 miles southwest, I issued him a 030 heading, then a 350 heading vector for RNAV approach. There was a 11000 ft. MIA block east of the 6300 ft. MIA block, but the distance from Aircraft X's position when he made the turn to the boundary of the 11000 ft. MIA block was about 5.6 miles. I thought that was enough space for him to make the turn. However, Aircraft X took an unexpected very wide U turn and clipped the corner of the 11000 ft. MIA block, he clipped the corner of 11000 ft. MIA for about 3 seconds while turning to the north, the MSAW alert was triggered, I issued him a low altitude alert. The aircraft then exited the 11000 ft. MIA back into the 6300 ft. MIA safely.
ASRS:1768830.s: An Approach controller vectored a heavy B7XX executing a go-around around 6300 ft and 11000 ft MIA blocks. The aircraft clipped the 11000 ft MIA corner for three seconds due to an unexpectedly wide turn, triggering an MSAW alert before exiting safely.

ASRS:1768832.n: When I arrived at work for my XB00-XJ00 shift there was a CIC on the Supervisor desk. The area was still combined at the mid sector (XX) except for sector XY which sits 4 inches from sector XX. Sector XY was open and staffed by a Supervisor not wearing a face covering over any part of his face other than his neck. This Supervisor has been repeatedly told to do so, but most of the time doesn't do so. The adjacent airspace was ATC zero for a positive COVID case that had been reported the previous afternoon. This Supervisor often opens this sector between XA00 and XC00 am to avoid going to stand up and also avoid any sort of volume or complexity in the airspace. I understand normally it's not an issue besides that it's an awkward configuration that confuses everyone in and around the area, but today it was much more than that. Today marked ZZZ's X confirmed positive COVID case in X days' time and X [number] in X weeks. This supervisor not wearing a mask and opening the sector to get time was not only dangerous but just plain rude as the controllers sitting next to him were forced to work the other sectors while properly adhering to mask wearing guidance. I wish this was the end of this report however the day progressed to be even worse. During the morning the contingency plan was abandoned and we were told we could go through the sterilized airspace however far 'we felt comfortable.' In fact we were told it would be OK to give IFR clearances off the ground in the sterilized airspace as well. I don't think this is a safe idea. One person's comfort level could be more than a different person's. We don't know how far frequency coverage goes into the sterilized airspace and this could result in NORDO aircraft in conflict in the airspace with no way to resolve the confliction. To add further to this, later in the day a D-side trainee was brought to the area to give an over the shoulder for the resumption of training. 4 people were plugged in to one sector while the same Supervisor still wore his mask around his neck. This put 3 more controllers at risk unnecessarily during the middle of a facility outbreak. This D-side trainee is now fully certified again on all the area D-sides after working a total of 1 week in the past 7 months which presents even more risk both to proficiency and also to proper social distancing measures. After this certification was complete he was used throughout the day and told to 'pick a D-side' at the instruction of the Supervisor further combating any social distancing guidelines that have been set in place by state health officials, NATCA, and facility management.If this is how ZZZ center is going to continue to operate this is only the tip of the iceberg with how much crossing paths there is since the return of normal schedules and staffing. Supervisors do not need sector currency.
ASRS:1768832.s: An air traffic controller reported that a Supervisor at ZZZ Center failed to wear a mask while staffing a sector adjacent to a COVID-14 quarantine zone and allowed a trainee to work in close proximity. The reporter stated these actions violated safety guidelines, increased infection risk during a facility outbreak, and compromised social distancing measures.

ASRS:1768848.n: After pushing back from the gate the aircraft was deiced using Type 1 fluid to remove excessive ice buildup. The aircraft had been RON for nearly 10 hours and spent most of its time exposed to FZRA (freezing rain) and -FZRA. The deice crew completed spraying/decontaminating the aircraft and called 'aircraft deicing complete'. At this point, I still could not even see out of the co-pilots number 3 window due to excessive ice buildup. This made the Captain and I suspicious (identified a threat) and asked the ground crew to spray the window and to be sure that they observed a clean airplane. They resprayed and said the aircraft was clean. To be sure, I performed a 'wing check' prior to engine start and noticed the wings were completely saturated with at least a quarter inch of ice. We called them back and asked for a complete re-do explaining how difficult it may be to remove the ice. They completed a second total deice and stated the aircraft was clean. We elected to perform another 'wing check' and noticed that nothing had changed. In fact, on one side of the aircraft we were unable to view the wing from any of the passenger windows due to ice buildup. At this point neither one of us felt confident in the aircraft's condition and the Captain elected to return to the gate to perform both a walk around as well as conference with all ground personnel. His communication was effective. As a note, during the walk around noticed icicles hanging from the leading edges and the upper wing surface was completely saturated with ice. We pushed a 3rd time, deiced by a different crew member, performed a 'wing check' and were satisfied the wings and control surfaces were clear. Departed nearly 4 hours late. An unsuspecting crew could have very easily departed with an aircraft completely covered in ice.
ASRS:1768848.s: The flight crew identified excessive ice on the wings and windows after two failed deicing attempts by ground crews following a long RON in freezing rain. The Captain returned to the gate for a walk-around and a third deice by a different crew, resulting in a four-hour delay but ensuring a safe departure.

ASRS:1768858.n: The Flight Attendant (FA) in charge advised that passenger in XX10 would not wear mask and was becoming belligerent changing seats at will while disregarding FA instructions to wear his mask and return to his seat. Dispatch [was] notified. We decided to have personnel meet aircraft in ZZZ and advised that this passenger should be denied boarding on next leg to ZZZ1.
ASRS:1768858.s: A Flight Attendant reported a passenger in seat XX10 refused to wear a mask, became belligerent, and changed seats despite instructions. Dispatch was notified, and the crew arranged for personnel to meet the aircraft at ZZZ to deny the passenger boarding on the next leg to ZZZ1.

ASRS:1768874.n: IOE (initial operating) student was attempting a flaps 22 landing. During the approach, gusty winds from outer bands of an approaching hurricane contributed to an unstable approach and generating two glide slope EGPWS annunciations. We initiated a missed approach and were put in sequence to reattempt the approach. The vectors from the second approach brought us in above the glideslope. We engaged the vs (vertical speed) mode initially at 1,200 feet per minute (per GOM) and then 1,000 feet per minute as we closed in on the glide slope and stabilized approach criteria. The student had NAV armed, not APP, which as PM (pilot monitoring) I should have caught. My attention was briefly diverted to reassessing our fuel, which was 200 pounds over final divert at the final approach fix. At 1,000, instruments cross checked, the GS (glideslope) was exact (though not captured). At this point, we had been in visual conditions for several minutes. The runway did not have visual guidance (PAPI nor VASI), I looked out the window to verify the runway was clear, of which I annunciated. At approximately 700 feet AGL, we fell below the glide slope, generating additional glide slope EGPWS annunciations. Due to the winds, fuel nature, incoming weather, and diversion airport expecting similar conditions, I used my command authority to take control of the airplane, reestablish ourselves on the glide path, and land without further incident.
ASRS:1768874.s: An IOE student and instructor attempted a flaps 22 landing in gusty hurricane winds, triggering EGPWS annunciations due to an unstable approach and the student having NAV armed instead of APP. The instructor took control at 700 feet AGL to reestablish the glide path and land safely.

ASRS:1768878.n: Left engine failure climbing through 18,000. Crew disengaged autopilot, leveled off and notified ATC and started diversion. PM (pilot monitoring) executed the engine failure and shut down checklists, and PF (pilot flying) took over the radios while PM was doing the checklists and programming FMS for arrival. ATC vectored us for a 15 mile visual approach for [Runway] XXL. Approach and landing were performed as normal as possible and without further incident. Crew felt heavy vibrations in airframe, ailerons, elevator and rudder and received 'L Engine Vibration' CAS. Felt it was a catastrophic engine failure so elected to perform engine shut down checklist. We also received 'L Engine Flameout' and 'L FADEC FAIL' CAS Messages. In flight: 'L & R AUX Bus Fail' CAS Messages (normal ops single engine) During descent, crew saw LH Engine N1 indications between 10-15% N1. But no ITT (interstage turbine temperature) indication (not sure if that is normal ops after engine failure) We elected not to start APU airborne or on the ground and upon parking on ramp did a full aircraft shutdown. No visual indication of external engine or cowling damage. No evidence of oil leaks from cowling. Climbing through approximately 18,000 feet the left engine failed. 'L Eng Flameout' and 'L Eng Fail' CAS posted. 'L Engine Vibration' posted and it was causing the entire airplane, including all flight controls, to vibrate severely. The pilot flying disengaged the autopilot and began hand flying. I notified ATC and asked for vectors and a new, lower altitude to be assigned. After a short discussion we agreed diverting would be the safest course of action. I asked for vectors. Executed the engine failure in flight and engine securing checklists from the QRH. ATC vectored us for the visual approach to [Runway] XXL. The subsequent approach and landing was completed without further incident. ATC called the emergency vehicles to be ready at our landing runway. Unknown reason why the engine failed. Unsure how to prevent this. A catastrophic engine failure is outside of our control.
ASRS:1768878.s: During climb through 18,000 feet, the crew experienced a catastrophic left engine failure causing severe airframe vibrations and multiple CAS messages. They executed shutdown checklists, diverted, and landed safely on a visual approach to Runway XXL with no external damage observed.

ASRS:1768901.n: ATC had given us a series of headings to avoid an active MOA. After the headings, they gave us direct CULAB then DIESL for the DRLLR5 arrival into IAH. I was writing the clearance while the captain put the change in the FMS. I copied the correct clearance (direct CULAB, DEISL then the DRILR5) and the captain input direct CULAB then DIESL for the MSCOT4, our originally assigned arrival. A proper cross check was not applied and the change was CONFIRMED. The MSCOT4 and DRLLR5 are very similar coming from that direction and both start at DIESL so upon looking at the first page of the FMS all seemed correct to me. It was not until later in the arrival were we/nor ATC aware we were on the wrong arrival into IAH until around the SUUNR intersection on the MSCOT4. Proper cross checking was not implemented on the arrival change. We did confirm the route change to CULAB then DIESL. A more thorough cross check of the arrival change would have caught the issue. Neither of us caught it and continued the flight to IAH on the MSCOT4, even fully briefing it. ATC said 'no worries' and left us on the MSCOT4 all the way into IAH.
ASRS:1768901.s: The crew and ATC were involved during the arrival into IAH when the captain incorrectly entered the MSCOT4 arrival instead of the cleared DRLLR5 due to a lack of proper cross-checking. The error went unnoticed until the SUUNR intersection, but ATC allowed the flight to continue on the wrong arrival without issue.

ASRS:1768947.n: During a VFR climb to 4,500 feet, I encountered what I believe to be a powered parachute at about 4,000 feet. I made a slight right turn to avoid the hazard and continued the trip without incident. The parachutist was in Class E airspace in VMC conditions and appears to have been complying with regulations. But it seems dangerous to have such slow-moving traffic in such busy airspace without ADS-B.
ASRS:1768947.s: A pilot climbing VFR to 4,500 feet encountered a powered parachute at 4,000 feet in Class E airspace and turned right to avoid it. The reporter noted the slow-moving traffic lacked ADS-B, creating a hazard despite the parachutist appearing to comply with regulations.

ASRS:1768964.n: I was acting as an instructor to a CPL who was new to flying the Aircraft X Type. He had spent all of his time up to this point flying the Aircraft Y Type, so I was helping him familiarize himself with the different aircraft. We were doing pattern work while several other aircraft were in the pattern. Upon getting abeam the numbers and beginning our descent, there was an aircraft on long final (roughly 2-2.5 miles) that we did not hear on the radio. We continued with our base, and final. The CPL whom I was instructing did not speak very strong english, and was having some trouble with the radio calls in the pattern, and occasionally neglecting to make them. In this instance, he neglected to call his base, and also neglected to call final. I noticed this only after him turning final without saying anything, and immediately announced our one mile final. This set up a situation where a near miss occurred between us and the other aircraft who was on long final. The aircraft that was on a long final did not call an extended downwind, or a base. They called final and neglected to give any mileage to indicate they had flown a much larger pattern than usual for a light general aviation plane. The other aircraft noticed us only because I called our final, and immediately broke off his final leg to avoid collision. I spoke with their pilot after this incident and he said we were slightly above them and cut them off. I believe this incident was caused by a number of factors mentioned above, and could have been avoided with better radio work on the part of my aircraft and the other one on final. I had a high workload at the moment, which caused my attention to lapse when the CPL turned base without making the call. However, the pilot on the other aircraft also did not specify that he was purposely flying a large pattern with an extended downwind/base/final. His failure and mine to accurately give position reports caused the incident. I also believe that often pilots become complacent and fly a pattern which is far too large at this airport. There are several times in a week where I have to extend my pattern to a point where I would not be able to make the runway in the event of an engine failure. Routinely, general aviation aircraft at the airport fly a 2+ mile final, which should be considered a 'long' final. Like in the incident mentioned, this can cause confusion when someone joins flying a smaller, more appropriate pattern.
ASRS:1768964.s: An instructor and a CPL student in Aircraft X Type experienced a near miss with another aircraft on long final during pattern work. The incident resulted from both pilots failing to make required radio position reports and the other aircraft flying an unusually large pattern without notification.

ASRS:1769038.n: On our enroute descent 30 miles west of ZZZ, ZZZ Center had to cancel our IFR flight plan due the ZZZ1 Center COVID related airspace closures. There was a miscommunication when we checked in with ZZZ Approach Control with us being VFR with the airport in sight. We picked up an IFR clearance with a Visual approach to the airport. We continued our arrival and landed uneventfully.The cause was that ZZZ1 airspace closed and there was a communication gap between ZZZ Center and ZZZ Approach.No suggestions, as our required cancellation of our IFR enroute with ZZZ Center and our subsequent picking up of our IFR with a visual approach from ZZZ Approach is what was required due to the ZZZ1 Airspace closures.
ASRS:1769038.s: During enroute descent west of ZZZ, the crew cancelled their IFR flight plan with ZZZ Center due to ZZZ1 airspace closures and miscommunicated with ZZZ Approach while VFR. The crew subsequently obtained an IFR clearance for a visual approach and landed uneventfully, attributing the issue to a communication gap between the two facilities.

ASRS:1769046.n: Unanticipated GPWS warning on approach requiring crew action. We were flying the freighter (tail), second leg ZZZ-ZZZ1 (1.5 hr delayed at start of day), 5-6 hours into the flight duty period (~XA:00 pm local time). Night IMC w/moderate to heavy rain showers in vicinity. I was Pilot Flying PF (Captain).Clearance was ZZZ...ZZZ1. On the ground at ZZZ we planned and briefed the departure and RNAV (RNP) Rwy XX from the ZZZZZ1 transition. De-iced, taxied, departed, climbed to cruise at FL280.Enroute to ZZZZZ1 at cruise, Center warned of areas of moderate to extreme precipitation from ZZZZZ1 fix to the airport and advised of better weather to the Northeast. After discussing a change to the arrival, we both agreed to request radar vectors to the approach segment from ZZZZZ (IAF). Center agreed to vector us around and down to put us on the published portion of the arrival with the stated intention of joining us to the approach path at ZZZZZ2. FO (First Officer) made the changes in the FMS and we briefed and then ran the Decent Checklist Change Triangles.Radar vectors included a descent and vectors resulting in established on published segment near ZZZZZ2 at 5000 and given approach clearance from center (I had directed PM to reset FMS Cruise Alt to 8,000 feet when we were on vectors). Once established near ZZZZZ2 at 5,000 cleared us for the approach. I engaged LNAV/VNAV and set airport elevation, but was high on the vertical path. I continued to slow to final configuration (gear down, Flaps 40) by ZZZZZ1, stable, but still 1,400 feet above the path in VNAV SPD (vertical navigation speed). After the turn at ZZZZZ1 I set 1,600 feet in the MCP ALT window (FAP 1,600 MSL) and at approximately 2,300 MSL, engaged Vertical Speed down in order to regain the VNAV Path before the FAP. As I approached the path, I reset MCP altitude to airfield elevation and engaged VNAV while pitch mode was in ALT ACQ (altitude acquire), resulting in an unrecognized mode change to V/S (2,100 ft/min) and projected vertical path well before the airport. It was at this point, we received a GPWS 'Caution Terrain' followed shortly by GPWS Warning 'Terrain Fly UP.' I immediately executed an escape maneuver/go-around, climbing and flying the go-around flight path to ZZZ2 and mistakenly climbed to 5,000 MSL (missed approach alt 3,000 MSL), entering the hold as published. I requested and was given a descent to 3,000 MSL in holding.We then built and briefed the RNAV (RNP) Rwy XX from ZZZ2, ran the Descent Change Triangles, received our approach clearance, and executed the approach to landing uneventfully. The FO and I thoroughly debriefed the events of the flight. I then called the Duty Pilot and DISPATCH to report the incident. I should have requested radar vectors ZZZZZ1 for the best opportunity to acquire the VNAV path. I allowed the Controller to compress and to keep me high on my approach, and reducing my situational awareness. I configured very early, but it still wasn't enough to regain the VNAV path. In the future, I will not allow the ATC Controller to dictate the terms of my energy management and will give myself the Flight Handbook recommended 3 miles per 1,000 descent planning as a minimum starting point.Because we compressed our arrival and ended up high above the VNAV path I attempted to use the Vertical Speed method on LNAV/VNAV Approach rules to regain VNAV path prior to the FAP. Had I cross-checked my FMA after selecting VNAV, I would have noticed the V/S mode and perhaps executed an uneventful go-around. In the future, I will make sure to always verify my FMA mode on the PFD after making a selection on the MCP.Lastly, after fully configuring and still not descending to the path, I might have been able to acquire VNAV path prior to the FAP using Speed Intervention. There was chance we were light enough (low Ref Speed) to accelerate the idle pitch descent to regain the path, ensuring the pitch FMA remained in VNAV and avoiding the unrecognized and inadvertent V/S mode descent that caused the GPWS Warning. Recommend expanding the understanding of VNAV speed during initial and continuing qualification training in the B737. Escape Maneuver occurred at approximately (time) local time on (date). Flight conditions at the time were night, IMC, rain, light turbulence.Leg 2 of a planned 4 leg day. Leg 1 was delayed 1 hours due to cargo loading. The flight was uneventful. Deiced in ZZZ after aircraft pushback. Filed route was ZZZ...ZZZ1. We planned and briefed the RNAV Rwy XX from ZZZZZ. Cruise was at FL280. PF (pilot flying) MFD was in WX Radar mode due to significant weather in the area. PM (pilot monitoring) was in TERR (terrain) mode with VSD (vertical speed) displayed. Cruise was at dusk. Shortly after starting the descent, ATC notified us that he saw an area of Moderate to Extreme precipitation ahead of us. ATC said it looked clearer to the north and asked if we would like vectors to the north for an approach via ZZZZZ1. We responded yes and he started vectoring us north. PF flew while PM loaded the arrival from ZZZZZ1 (via IAF ZZZZZ1). PM briefed the new approach and called for change triangles, which we accomplished. ATC had us do intermediate level-offs at 8,000 feet, then 7,000 feet. PF asked PM to reset the cruise altitude to provide an accurate flight path. In anticipation of being high on flight path, PF configured early to flaps 40. PM was actively monitoring the VSD and flight path, and requested lower when able from ATC. ATC said he would give us lower in a few miles. He then gave us a short vector prior to ZZZZZ2 with a descent to 6,500 feet. At approx 0.5 miles before ZZZZZ2 at 6,500 feet, ATC cleared us 'to cross ZZZZZ2 at or above 5,000 feet, cleared RNAV Rwy XX at ZZZ1'. When cleared for the approach over ZZZZZ2, PF dialed in field elevation in the MCP and descended towards the flight path. Flight conditions were night, IMC, rain, light turbulence. Approximately 1 mile prior to ZZZZZ3, we were still high on flight path so PF verbalized and set Vertical Speed down and reset MCP to 1,600 feet. PM saw the downward vector on the VSD and monitored it for approaching the flight path. Almost immediately thereafter, we received a 'Caution, Terrain' and the depicted island terrain went yellow on PM's MFD. This was quickly followed by a 'Terrain, Pull up' and the depicted terrain on the MFD went red. PF called for go-around and executed the escape maneuver. After aircraft was climbing, PF asked PM to reset MCP for missed approach altitude of 3,000 feet. PF initially had difficulty verifying the missed approach altitude on the EFB due to turbulence, transition to nighttime, and prioritizing monitoring the aircraft state while performing aircraft cleanup. PF put and verbalized 5,000 feet in the MCP window, thinking 5,000 feet was better in case 3,000 feet was incorrect. PMs intent was to devote more brain cells to performing the aircraft cleanup items and monitoring the safe aircraft state as we climbed. Aircraft was cleaned up, leveled at 5,000 feet and continued to holding at ZZZ2. We then queried ATC for a descent to 3,000 feet, setup the RNAV Rwy XX from ZZZ2. Approach was briefed by Captain, flown, and landed uneventfully. Once the aircraft reached parking and shutdown at ZZZ1, Captain and FO debriefed the events. Captain called and briefed Duty Officer, who approved continuing to the remaining 2 destinations. Captain also called and spoke with Dispatch. The remaining flights to were flown with minimal changes. Post flight, the Captain called Quality Assurance to see what they could tell us, so that we could learn further from this experience.Stay on the magenta line, and if vectored off, get back on it as early as possible. Even though the controller had plans to vector us back onto the RNP approach, a better outcome likely would have resulted if we started at the IAP. This way we would have been able to descend on a normal flight path, with adequate time and pacing, vs. having to stay higher due to the controllers higher vectoring altitudes. Request the IAP next time.At nighttime in IMC, I need to have a faster response timecalling for the escape maneuver/go-around. I should clarify this maneuver more, particularly the triggers. I should have been the first to call for it since the Captain was the PF. Instead of trying to salvage a bad or difficult approach, make the decision to go-around earlier. Memorize the missed approach altitude prior to each approach, or ensure my EFB chart is not zoomed-in so far that I cannot see it without a quick glance.Clarify various 'what-if scenarios' on RNP approaches, Escape Maneuvers, Go-Arounds. If I haven't flown as much recently, spend extra time clarifying. Communicate with Center that 6,500 feet at ZZZZZ2 creates a very difficult approach to accomplish. Recommend to them that vectoring to the IAF is likely a better option.
ASRS:1769046.s: The Captain and First Officer flying a freighter at night in IMC received a GPWS terrain warning during an RNAV approach after an unrecognized mode change caused an excessive descent rate. The crew executed a go-around, initially climbing to 5,000 feet instead of the required 3,000 feet, before holding and landing uneventfully on a second attempt.

ASRS:1769060.n: On departure at about 300 ft. the left T-handle light illuminated. I immediately ran my memory items, checklist, set a timer, and continued my climb. I completed my climb checklist. At about 15 seconds, the light was still illuminated so I began preparing for an air return. At 20 seconds, it was still illuminated, this was at about 4500 ft. I informed departure that I needed an immediate return for a possible engine fire, [requested priority handling]. I was cleared for the Visual Approach, and switched to tower, and was cleared to land. I completed the rest of my checklists for landing, including single engine, because the left engine was still pulled to idle and ITT (Interstage Turbine Temperature) was stable. Landed without incident. As I pulled off the runway, the T-handle light extinguished.At about 300 ft. on my climb the t-handle was illuminated. Maintenance believes that the sensors/wiring had a malfunction. They were cleaned and returned to service. I ran my checklists. I stayed ahead of the plane by choosing to do them ahead of time, anticipating that the light might not go out. I communicated with ATC immediately, and decided the safest choice was to not be in the air should things continue to escalate.I don't really have control over this event happening again, however, you can always learn something to do differently or better. Now that I have an idea of what this type of event looks like, I would have also have done a precautionary engine shut down and had them send me on a downwind instead of a 180 into the runway I just departed.
ASRS:1769060.s: The pilot experienced a false left T-handle fire warning at 300 ft during departure, prompting an immediate return and landing. Maintenance attributed the event to sensor or wiring malfunction, which was cleaned, though the pilot noted a downwind approach might have been preferable to the 180-degree turn executed.

ASRS:1769064.n: A gentleman walked on the aircraft without a mask, I nicely asked him if he had a mask and if not, I would supply one for him. He said he did have a mask, but just needed to find it. He made his way to his seat in X6 and was putting his seatbelt on. I told him since he was in the bulkhead he'd have to stow his bags above him in the overhead bin. He is now moving around, bending down close to the gentleman beside him, who clearly looked uncomfortable. I then handed him a mask and told him he needed to put it on. He said once again, he has one. My B-FA then comes up and I inform him of the situation. B FA says to the gentleman he needs to put his mask on and the man loudly and rudely says, 'Oh would you just shut your mouth!!' Now, I inform our Captain on what is happening in the back and he said, 'He can't talk to you guys like that, get him off.' So I tell the gate agent, she gets her manager and the security coordinator and the man is escorted off.
ASRS:1769064.s: A passenger boarded without a mask, refused to wear one, and verbally abused a flight attendant. The Captain ordered the passenger removed, and security escorted him off the aircraft after he was rude to the crew.

ASRS:1769070.n: Passenger seated on X4 continued to disregard our request for him to keep his facial covering on at all times. We asked him several times (FA's # A, B & C) but continued to disregard our request. I even gave him a face mask but still, no compliance. Passenger seated nearby in X6 was very disturbed by it.
ASRS:1769070.s: Cabin crew requested a passenger in seat X4 to wear a face mask, but he refused despite multiple requests and being provided a mask. A nearby passenger in seat X6 was disturbed by the non-compliance.

ASRS:1769072.n: Passenger X that was escorted off previous flight for acting erratically and refusing to wear his mask was then given a boarding pass to fly on the flight I was working. Agent never informed Captain or crew of this passenger's history. The only way we found out was by Captain asking agent when she came to close the flight about the information of this certain passenger! I had to ask this passenger numerous times to follow the mask policy. Communication on the agents behalf would be a good start and for the company to actually follow through with the mask policy! I am risking my health and safety every time I come to work, it would be nice if my company would actually start to act like they care. Working on an aircraft has become a dangerous place to be. I'm begging the company to pull their head out of the sand and start taking my overall health and safety seriously!
ASRS:1769072.s: A cabin crew member reported that a passenger previously removed for erratic behavior and mask refusal boarded their flight without the ground agent informing the Captain or crew. The crew member had to repeatedly enforce the mask policy, citing a lack of communication and company support as a safety risk.

ASRS:1769082.n: I was moving a lift to do a door lube. When done with the R2 door I moved the lift while looking to the rear, I did not realize that the lift was in drive not reverse. While looking over my shoulder I felt the tug go forward I hit the brakes. I did not feel it strike the aircraft. I then moved the lift to the L2 door and completed the lube on the L2 door and then moved the lift back to the parking area. I did not know that I had contacted the aircraft until notified by the Senior Manager. The lighting was poor and I had never done a door lube on this type of aircraft. I also had just came back from almost three weeks off from being quarantined for COVID-19. I was not used to night and was very tired.When selecting the lift to Reverse it inadvertently ended up in Drive. Some of our lifts have drive forward on the gear selector and some have drive in the back of the gear selector. Shifters are not lit and some go forward to go forward and some go forward to go aft.I really have no idea [for suggestions] other than making sure all lifts have the gear selectors the same way. Gear selector levers should be lit at night so they can be observed.
ASRS:1769082.s: A ground mechanic inadvertently drove a lift forward into an aircraft while performing door lube at night due to poor lighting, fatigue, and inconsistent gear selector configurations. The contact was not felt by the operator until notified by a manager, prompting recommendations for standardized and illuminated shifters.

ASRS:1769092.n: Upon landing the student was going too fast to make a 90 degree turn on to the taxiway. The instructor did not have enough time to correct the rudder input. If the instructor had pushed on the rudder to correct the aircraft would have tipped. So the instructor kept the aircraft going straight once it was aimed off the runway. We went into the dirt and on to a taxiway. The aircraft did not hit any lights or signs. The aircraft did not appear to sustain any damage. The engine appeared to be fine. Taxi the aircraft everything seemed to be normal.
ASRS:1769092.s: A student pilot and instructor landed an aircraft too fast to execute a 90-degree turn, causing them to veer off the runway into dirt before reaching a taxiway. The instructor avoided tipping the aircraft by maintaining a straight path, resulting in no damage to the airframe or engine.

ASRS:1769100.n: Due to the COVID-19 slow down our department has flown our aircraft every X weeks to keep the plane and crew flight ready for our corporation. On this particular flight I the Captain, and the Second in Command were briefing the approach into ZZZ airport. While briefing we were headed direct to ZZZZZ intersection for the ZZZZZ6 arrival. The plane had not flown for two weeks and due to a cancelled trip I had not flown for 56 days. The Second in Command had flown a trip 2 weeks prior to this flight. On receiving the ATIS the approach advertised was different than what was usual and anticipated. So we as a crew briefed the approach thoroughly (it was noted it had some updated information). During this briefing I noticed we were below 10,000 feet, around 8,000 feet and traveling at 270 knots indicated airspeed. Upon this observation I slowed the aircraft to below 250 knots. The Controller never mentioned anything and there was no traffic noted on the TCAS or visually. The procedure I should have done differently/better was to transfer control or to have the Second in Command brief the approach.
ASRS:1769100.s: The Captain and Second in Command briefed an approach into ZZZ airport while flying direct to ZZZZZ intersection below 10,000 feet at 270 knots. The Captain reduced speed to comply with regulations and noted that transferring control to the Second in Command for the briefing would have been a better procedure.

ASRS:1769115.n: Good VFR weather and Forecast for destination, enroute, and return. Morning flight to destination was uneventful. Afternoon return flight at 6,500 feet, and 80 NM to destination an overcast layer developed. Obtained weather reports which indicated ceilings of 2,500 feet tapering to 900 feet at destination (forecast for improvement). Overcast conditions about 2,000 feet thick. Since it would be getting dark by the time I got to the destination, I elected to stay on top. Temperature at 6,500 feet was 45F (although I was flying North and knew it would decrease), surface temperatures around freezing. Obtained IFR clearance and completed ILS approach. Entered tops at 4,500 feet MSL and broke out at 2,800 feet MSL (1,400 foot ceiling). As soon as I entered the clouds the temperature dropped to freezing. Picked up about 1/8 inch of ice on the horizontal stabilizer, with less on the main wing. Windshield was warm enough and didn't have any ice.Best option would have been to land and stay overnight--while this is always a hassle, COVID pandemic has made this even less appealing. Flying underneath a deteriorating ceiling, I believe would have been a bad option, especially at night. The weather and temperatures of the upper Midwest limit the use of an airplane without deicing equipment for six months of the year. Anything other than local flights, always plan an option for a rental car, or overnight stays, and utilize those options.
ASRS:1769115.s: A pilot flying a return leg at 6,500 feet entered an overcast layer at 4,500 feet MSL and encountered freezing temperatures, accumulating 1/8 inch of ice on the horizontal stabilizer. The pilot completed an ILS approach but noted that flying without deicing equipment in these conditions is hazardous and recommended planning for overnight stays instead.

ASRS:1769120.n: Runway XXR was NOTAMed closed for 2 hours due to a crane on the departure end of the runway. Runway XXL was in use. Aircraft inbound from the west was given a right downwind entry for Runway XXL. The aircraft was sequenced to follow multiple aircraft ahead. On short final, I noticed that he appeared to be lined up for the closed runway (Runway XXR). I instructed the pilot to go-around and re-enter right traffic Runway XXL and emphasized to the pilot that Runway XXR is closed. When I cleared him to land Runway XXL, he again appeared to be lined up for XXR. I verified if he was lined up for the correct runway and on very short final, he appeared to maneuver for the correct runway.Background: all controllers at ZZZ have been on 6 day work week for the last few months due to a shortage in staffing. Our facility has also been experiencing roughly a 20% increase in traffic volume compared to last year. In September, our traffic count index has reached the numbers for us to qualify for a level 8 upgrade. If we sustain our traffic numbers for the next couple of months, level 8 at ZZZ will become a reality once it gets approved by the National Validation Team.We are all fatigued from the increase in traffic and the amount of overtime we have all been working. This is no doubt affecting our performance on position. Morale is down and controllers are becoming more and more impatient with pilots as a result of being over-worked. I worry that this will impact safety by increasing the possibility of human error.I felt noticeably fatigued towards the end of my work week. If I had not been as fatigued, I may have been able to recognize the aircraft lined up for the incorrect runway sooner. Thankfully, I recognized it at the last second, but it was very close.Yesterday, I was working CIC combined with GC. Traffic was busy. A Controller who was finishing an overlap in the back of the cab was on the phone with someone and relayed information to me. I was in the middle of working a lot of traffic on ground and what I thought I heard was to have the pilot of an Aircraft X with an XXXXX tail number call the airport manager when he lands. It turned out that the airport manager wanted us to call him when the aircraft landed. Had we had more staffing and CIC was de-combined, this information would have been properly relayed to me. I would have been able to figure out that we had to call the airport manager and not have the pilot call. Again, my lapse in judgement may have also been due to fatigue from prolonged 6 day work weeks.For the safe of safety, the agency needs to take our staffing situation seriously. In the midst of the pandemic, our tower hours have changed to XC:00am to XO:00pm. Even though we have a staffing issue, due to the compressed tour hours, there is a good amount of overlap between controllers so we can keep LC split into 2 positions. In a little over a week, we will be going back to our normal hours which are XA:00am until XQ:00pm. This means the staffing will be spread out and during peak work hours, we may be forced to combine the LC position. As busy as it has been, it is very unsafe to work the volume of traffic we have been working with a combined LC position. This will result in 2 hour holdovers for many of us on top of the 6 day work weeks we have already been working.We have been begging for better staffing for years. There has been word that the higher ups in our region are finally taking the situation seriously. I hope this is true and we get more staffing numbers to alleviate this serious issue.
ASRS:1769120.s: An air traffic controller at ZZZ Tower, fatigued by staffing shortages and overtime, instructed an inbound aircraft to go around after it appeared aligned with a closed runway. The pilot eventually corrected to the active runway, though the controller attributed the near-miss and a separate communication error to fatigue and combined positions.

ASRS:1769131.n: The VFR Aircraft, Aircraft X, was cleared on the [published VFR route] to maintain 5,500 feet. He was southbound and converging over the VOR with Aircraft Y who was IFR and descended to 5,000 feet and told about the 5,500 feet traffic that was at the time 4 miles north of the VOR. Everything was fine and it was a normal everyday situation. I was cleaning up some loose ends giving headings to other aircraft and traffic advisories, many traffic advisories. I had an aircraft report getting an RA but its resolution told him to stay where they were because there were just so many VFR's. Then I hear the Traffic Alert start which isn't uncommon for aircraft 500 feet apart in this airspace and as I look up the Aircraft Y tells me he's responding to an RA and his voice is clearly strained.I incorrectly said what I was thinking which was 'Aircraft X what are you doing! Climb immediately to 5,500' as I'm watching him descend through 5,200 feet right on top of Aircraft Y. He responds that he 'thought they were on a collision course'. To which I informed him that his actions caused the collision course. He also turned right which would have been fine if that's all he had done and stayed at 5,500 feet, but the descent made it a near or for sure mid-air if Aircraft Y hadn't taken evasive action. I issued a Brasher Warning to the pilot of Aircraft X because he 100% cause a perfectly separated situation to become a very ugly situation. Both aircraft were in the Class Bravo airspace and the VFR aircraft had no right or reason to descend at all.Over the top of LA is just a busy place where aircraft are routinely separated by 500 feet, that's just life. If they move the VFR areas where Special Flight Rules is to somewhere else then we would definitely have more altitudes to use to separate people by greater than 500 feet. but, until that happens it's just going to be what it's going to be. While on a Class B clearance through the Class Bravo airspace on published VFR Route southbound at 5,500 feet, I received a traffic notification from Approach for traffic at 11 o'clock, opposite direction, at 5,000 MSL a conflict for traffic that was approaching nearly head-on. I continued to visually scan for the traffic in front of me, and when I finally spotted the oncoming traffic it was at my 11 o'clock to 11:30 position in my windscreen, at eye level. I was unable to discern any relative motion of the target relative to my windscreen. The only change I could see in the target was that it was getting larger in my field of view, and that it appeared to be some type of small jet aircraft. I immediately initiated a turn to my right in order to avoid the oncoming traffic. The turn that I initiated was done very quickly, and was probably on the order of a 30 to 35 degree angle of bank. As a result of this turn, I lost approximately 250 feet of altitude from my cruising altitude of 5,500 feet. My change in heading was approximately 45 degrees, and once my turn was completed I was able to discern relative motion of the target with respect to my windscreen and left side window. The traffic was now moving to my left, and the separation between the two of us was increasing.The opposite directly traffic passed well behind me. At that point the TRACON Controller called me and admonished me for deviating from my assigned heading and altitude. I responded to the controller with an apology, and explained that the opposite direction traffic appeared to be on a collision course with me, and it required me to take evasive action. The controller provided me with a toll-free number to call after I landed. After landing I called the toll-free number and spoke to an individual at SOCAL who asked me to describe the occurrence from my perspective. I described the occurrence in an identical manner to what I have written here. The individual was very courteous and listened carefully to my explanation, and thanked me for calling. The call ended with no indication to me that any further action would be forthcoming.It is extremely difficult to estimate lateral and vertical separation of traffic, especially when a target has no apparent relative motion and is approaching head-on. Any vertical separation that does exist between two aircraft in this situation will not be perceptible until the aircraft are very close together, when there is very little time to take evasive action if it is required. In this particular case, the opposite direction traffic was probably traveling at least twice as fast as my aircraft, resulting in an effective rate of closure of at least 400 MPH. A vertical separation of 500 feet is very small, and when possible sources of altitude error are included, it is possible that the actual vertical separation between our two aircraft was less than 500 feet. Approximately ten minutes after this occurrence, I was in the vicinity of another airport and was in contact with another sector of the TRACON. This Controller provided me with a traffic advisory regarding jet traffic inbound from the west at 5,000 feet, and gave me instructions to climb and maintain 6,000 feet for separation purposes. I initiated the climb and leveled off at 6,000 feet, and observed the jet traffic passed well below me. After the jet traffic had crossed my flight path, the Controller cleared me back down to 5,500 feet. I have included a description of this action on the part of Approach as an example of prudent traffic management.In summary, I should have been more diligent in maintaining my assigned altitude of 5,500 feet during my turn to avoid the oncoming traffic. However, it was my belief that there was insufficient separation between the flight paths of our two aircraft, and seeing no relative motion of a target that was at eye-level in my windscreen, as pilot-in-command of the aircraft I took evasive action in the interest of collision avoidance.
ASRS:1769131.s: A VFR pilot descending to avoid perceived head-on traffic with an IFR jet in Class B airspace caused a near mid-air collision, prompting an ATC Brasher Warning. The pilot attributed the descent to a lack of visible relative motion and insufficient 500-foot vertical separation, while the controller stated the VFR pilot created the conflict by deviating from assigned altitude.

ASRS:1769137.n: FL370 enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1, we encountered an Air Traffic Controller that was clearly over saturated because of multiple frequencies or too many aircraft. Traffic in these 2 areas are returning to normal. We need more Controllers and frequencies to avoid safety of flight issues.
ASRS:1769137.s: A pilot reported encountering an over-saturated Air Traffic Controller at FL370 enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1 due to multiple frequencies and high traffic. The pilot attributed potential safety of flight issues to this workload and requested more controllers and frequencies.

ASRS:1769213.n: I was conducting a training flight with my student practicing engine failure during flight. I intentionally shut down the right engine and attempted an air start with the unfeathering accumulator. The engine would not start and the propeller was still feathered. [Without success], we tried an air start using the starter. The engine heavily vibrated for 20 seconds so we shut down and followed the procedure again, but the engine heavily vibrated again for another 30 seconds. We tried to adjust the power, but we had strong vibrations from the engine. After three unsuccessful attempts to air start the engine per emergency checklist, I decided to shut down and secure the engine, and come back to and land. I [requested priority handling], joined left traffic and performed a one engine inoperative landing. We landed safely and were towed back to the ramp and parked the plane.
ASRS:1769213.s: A pilot and student conducting engine failure training experienced repeated heavy vibrations during unsuccessful air start attempts on the right engine. The pilot secured the engine, requested priority handling, and performed a safe one-engine-inoperative landing.

ASRS:1769217.n: Nothing bad actually happened. All the taxi charts in PUW are currently not accurate. Just as more of a heads up. Taxied to the ramp Via A3, A, D. Lucky weather was good so finding the correct taxiways were easy. But there is little to no guidance that with A4 and closed and the construction maligning getting to the ramp via A1 impassable the only way to access ramp is via A3. Documentation kinda explains the ramp construction, but nothing about to how to get to the ramp with the taxiways closed.Add a taxi diagram with the new A3 and D taxiway and warn crew about if they land [Runway] 5 and exit on A1 their will be no way to the ramp. If a crew lands [Runway] 5 they will need to back taxi to A3 and WSI there. If landing [Runway] 23, A3 is the only way off with A4 closed.
ASRS:1769217.s: A pilot reported that inaccurate taxi charts at PUW failed to indicate that A3 and D are the only routes to the ramp due to construction closing A1 and A4. Although good weather allowed safe navigation, the pilot warned that crews landing on Runway 5 or 23 must use A3 to avoid being blocked from the ramp.

ASRS:1769313.n: During the takeoff roll, under 50 KIAS, the left engine failed to produce power. The left engine manifold pressure only reached between 20-25 inches and the RPM reached 2000-2200. This caused the airplane to yaw to the left. The takeoff was aborted and we returned to the gate. End of incident. Left engine failed to produce power for takeoff.
ASRS:1769313.s: During the takeoff roll under 50 KIAS, the left engine failed to produce power, with manifold pressure reaching only 20-25 inches and RPM at 2000-2200. This caused a left yaw, resulting in an aborted takeoff and return to the gate.

ASRS:1769317.n: The reason I am writing this is for safety. I would like to shine a light on the technique that I have used for years. That technique recently was cited as the reason for a one minute delay. In fact, it was not the reason we were late. The DGS system and a slightly delayed ramp clearance to push were the real cause. We were ready and the brakes were released a minute early. These delays are useless and mean nothing when an agent would have never entered it had no delay been incurred. However, the multiple events that occur after door closure still doesn't preclude the agent for coding the delay incorrectly. I would also like to point out I was contacted by my supervisor who was only interested in my holding the 1L door open versus the actual cause of the delay. I continued to be harassed by various phone calls during my layover trying to get me to see the light. All over one minute. It felt like pilot pushing to me.Company has always claimed Safety to be the number one goal. Schedule will never come before safety. It appears in this instance that schedule may be first which is sparking my desire to revisit this very important subject.Company has shown videos during recurrent training cycles highlighting the technique I use. The aircraft was at a foreign station. It was parked at the gate. The cargo doors were open. The Captain allowed the agent to close the 1L door early while cargo doors were still open. The jet bridge was pulled. Slides are armed. The aircraft begins to fill with smoke. The decision is made to evacuate. The 1L door is no longer available, nor is the slide since the jet bridge prevents it's inflation and proper position. The usable exits are opened and slides inflated. Passengers evacuate via the slides. Injuries occur. The working Captain in hindsight wishes he had not allowed the entry door to be closed so early. It would have allowed for a safe and orderly deplaning via the 1L door. After all, the aircraft isn't moving until cargo is loaded and the doors are closed. These seeds were planted during FAA approved recurrent training cycles. I listened. I agreed. My supervisor now tells me I'm out of line. It's a technique that isn't allowed. It's not in the FOM. It's also not in the FOM preventing me from doing this. Captains Authority allows me to address issues that don't exist in any manual.I've been flying airplanes for XX years. I've never had an accident or incident. I operate with safety as my number one goal. I intend on leaving here with that streak intact.I implore all that read this to come to the conclusion that I have. It makes no sense to close and block the 1L door while in the chocks with cargo being loaded. Did we not already learn this the hard way? I could have left 5 mins early but would have still been late due to routing around Tropical Storm Zeta. This is about safety. It's about the talk and the walk being in lock step.Supervisor putting schedule ahead of safety.Let Captains be Captains.
ASRS:1769317.s: A pilot reported a one-minute delay at a foreign gate caused by DGS and ramp clearance issues, not their technique of keeping the 1L door open during cargo loading. The pilot argued this safety practice, supported by training videos, was unfairly criticized by a supervisor who prioritized schedule over safety.

ASRS:1769329.n: Was advised inflight by ZZZZZ controllers that they were unable to contact ZZZ Approach controllers. ZZZ had closed one hour early due to their reduced hours, however, there was no NOTAM in our flight plan that advised of the early closure. In addition to there being no NOTAM, ZZZ had also failed to 'release' the airspace over to the Center before going home. As a result, ZZZZZ could not clear us for an approach into the airspace. We were issued holding instructions until someone in ZZZ returned to the airport to release the airspace. Initially, ZZZZZ seemed unsure if ZZZ was even open or not. I told them that they had indeed closed based off of the remarks section of the AWOS. I knew that ZZZ closed at XA00 local based on recent flights. Plus, the airport itself (Runways and taxiways) would close later due to the construction that takes place at night. However, because there were no NOTAMs for either closure this time, I thought that they would be open. We had no alternate, as the weather was good, and as such had limited time to hold. Fortunately, we eventually got clearance to proceed into ZZZ.ZZZ ATC failed to release the airspace to ZZZZZ prior to signing off for the night. As a result, we were held until the airspace could be released. In addition, there were no NOTAMs noting the early closure of the ATC facilities at ZZZ.
ASRS:1769329.s: The pilot reported that ZZZ Approach closed early without a NOTAM and failed to release airspace to ZZZZZ Center. Consequently, the aircraft was held until ZZZ personnel returned to transfer control, delaying the approach into ZZZ.

ASRS:1769347.n: There was a guest assigned X3, despite the fact the seat is blocked as per social distancing guidelines and safety of FA's.The Customer Service Agent (CSA) refused to reseat the guest, which made me feel very uncomfortable to say the least. A CSA was informed and asked to reseat, however they refused the request, which violated the policy, jeopardizing safety of flight attendants, as well as created a major inconsistency. As a solution there was an option to move a guest traveling by themselves, like anyone from Row X-Y, that was not done by the CSA.
ASRS:1769347.s: A Customer Service Agent assigned a passenger to a blocked seat, violating social distancing guidelines and refusing to reseat them despite crew requests. This action jeopardized flight attendant safety and created policy inconsistencies, though a viable solution to move a solo passenger was available but not implemented.

ASRS:1769357.n: I asked a passenger multiple times to make sure his mask was covering his nose and mouth not just his chin. I made all the required announcements, so I believe 4 PAs were made referring to masks. The pilots also made an additional mask announcement. Once we got in the air the passenger took his mask off completely. We serve so much food on a two hour flight that he constantly had food in front of him. Every time I asked him to put his mask on he would take a bite of food. Every time I looked at him, he would take a bite. I could not really give him a warning because every time I looked at him, he would take a bite of something. But he did not wear his mask the entire flight until we were cleaning up at 10,000 feet. Do we really need to serve so much food. On a two-hour flight we provide several food services. Tough to enforce the mask policy when people are constantly eating. This passenger knew better, but just refused to wear his mask. Reevaluate the amount of food served on a two hour flight.
ASRS:1769357.s: A cabin crew member reported that a passenger refused to wear a mask during a two-hour flight, constantly eating food served multiple times. The passenger only complied at 10,000 feet during cleanup, leading the crew to suggest reevaluating food service frequency to improve mask policy enforcement.

ASRS:1769359.n: Guests sitting at X1 and X3.X1 keeps coughing.X3 is wearing the mask with bottom tie off.X1 stood up and opened the overhead bin when the cockpit door was open during the break. I told him loudly to sit down please. He asked 'Why?' I answered 'Because the cockpit door is open.'X3 said 'Seatbelt sign is not on.'They both say 'That is so stupid.' shaking their heads.Every time X1 coughs, guests at X5 & X6 are concerned and look over to him.Get consents from guests about staying seated during pilot breaks.
ASRS:1769359.s: Cabin crew reported that passengers at X1 and X3 refused to remain seated during a pilot break with the cockpit door open, despite crew instructions. The passengers dismissed the safety requirement as "stupid," citing the seatbelt sign was off, while X1's coughing concerned nearby guests.

ASRS:1769363.n: I am the A Flight Attendant. Passenger X was making a connection. She also needed an aisle chair. My tablet was acting glitchy and I could not pull the station flight service phone numbers. There was not a jet bridge phone and no plane phone numbers. There were 2 passengers trapped at the 1 and 2 seats while the aisle passenger was in the 3 seat. Total of 3 people stuck. Passenger X was getting very restless and stressed. I was not aware, for the passenger's safety, I was not to leave and inform the Agent of the urgency for the aisle chair. I deeply apologize, this will never happen again. Working conditions with COVID, are very stressful.Make sure that every flight has availability to jet bridge phones numbers, to communicate with the Gate Agents.
ASRS:1769363.s: A flight attendant reported that a passenger requiring an aisle chair became stressed while three passengers were trapped in their seats due to a glitchy tablet and lack of jet bridge phones. The attendant admitted to leaving the aircraft to inform the gate agent, violating safety protocols, and requested that jet bridge phones be available for future communications.

ASRS:1769383.n: The aircraft arrived from the hangar for the trip. We were told that the aircraft had surpassed its parking to greater than XX hours. We were told by management to accomplish parking per XX.XX.X that led us to work orders XX and XX1 before its next trip that was due out in the morning, requiring a lengthy delay and out of service condition.The aircraft bill of work was never updated to reflect the parking orders being required before the next flight.Find a way to monitor aircraft ground times and work requiring accomplishment.
ASRS:1769383.s: Management directed the crew to perform parking work orders due to excessive ground time, causing a lengthy delay and out-of-service condition. The aircraft bill of work was not updated to reflect these required tasks before the next flight.

ASRS:1769401.n: The Jeppesen Approach Chart for PVC RNAV 7 lists the pilot controlled lights as 122.8. The correct frequency is 122.85. This resulted in a missed approach at night in IMC. The correct frequency of 122.85 is noted on the airport diagram.
ASRS:1769401.s: A pilot missed an approach at night in IMC due to an incorrect pilot-controlled light frequency (122.8) listed on the Jeppesen Approach Chart for PVC RNAV 7. The correct frequency, 122.85, was only found on the airport diagram.

ASRS:1769409.n: After doing simulated engine failures, we were flying straight and level and we had some misfiring. We then immediately came back to the airport, alerted tower, and landed. The tower had [airport personnel] followed us in. I told them what is listed above.
ASRS:1769409.s: The pilot reported engine misfiring during straight-and-level flight after simulated engine failures. The crew immediately returned to the airport, alerted the tower, and landed with airport personnel following the aircraft.

ASRS:1769477.n: I experienced a near midair collision while flying a glider south of the ZZZ airport. Purpose of the flight was currency since the soaring season is mostly over apart from mountain wave flying. Typically, I take a tow into the mountains to connect with the excellent soaring conditions. The plan was to stay close to the airport and perform a short pattern flight. Before the flight, I thought about the extra vigilance required due to the flight in congested airspace. Flying in the mountains presents it's own set of challenges, but from a traffic perspective it's much less stressful than flying close to the ZZZ airport. Takeoff and climbout were normal, and we were established on an easterly heading in the 'glider box' climbing through 7,200 feet when I released from the tow plane. Normal release procedure is to clear right, release from tow, and perform a slight climbing right turn to deconflict from the tow plane while the towplane performs a descending left turn. This was accomplished, and I kept the turn going to a 270 heading. Once rolling wings level at 270, I was presented with the image of a blue and white Piper Cherokee rapidly filling my windscreen head on. Time from recognition to action was within a second and I dumped the nose to build airspeed/separation and rolled right to deconflict. The Cherokee seemed to pick me up at the last minute, and I observed him making a slightly delayed climbing right turn. I estimated separation at between 100 and 200 feet. It was too close! If I remained on tow on an easterly heading, there is a very good chance the Cherokee would have flown directly into me at my 6 o'clock. Very similar to a fatal midair accident that happened 10 years ago at ZZZ between a towplane, glider, and Cirrus transitioning the area. I was on the ZZZ CTAF with the tow plane, and neither me or the tow pilot heard the Cherokee making position calls. The Cherokee continued it's flight eastbound and I made an announcement about the near miss and called his position to anyone else on frequency. Technically, nobody did anything wrong. The Cherokee was not required to make position calls. However, in the busy airspace around ZZZ this is common sense. See and avoid worked, but just barely. I was squawking 1202 (glider transponder code per Letter Of Agreement with TRACON) with a Mode S transponder. I confirmed the transponder was on during my before takeoff checklist and directly following the incident. I had a FLARM collision avoidance system installed in the glider. This picks up Mode C, Mode S, and other Flarm traffic. In the event of a conflict, there is an audible warning and the screen on the S100 variometer displays the clock position, distance, and altitude above/below of conflicting traffic. Very similar to a TCAS. It does not display resolution advisory/vertical speed required for deconfliction. The FLARM alarm did not activate, and I didn't even look at the instrument. My eyes were outside the whole time and I was very lucky they were. This comes down to solid training and a good scan. The World War II pilots had it right. 'Keep your head on a swivel'. Don't trust your traffic avoidance system to show or alert you to everything out there. TCAS, ADS-B, TIS, FLARM, etc. all offer an absolutely incredible advantage in situational awareness and safety. However, it's not a 100% solution. Many gliders and older powered aircraft don't have transponders, and a traffic avoidance system won't pick up something they can't see. You still need to look outside the cockpit.The FLARM/S100 system has certain configurations that can be set by the pilot on when to audibly and visually alert on a potential conflict. Due to flying in close proximity to the tow plane on tow, I believe it's a possible setting to inhibit warnings while on tow. Since this happened within seconds of release, it's possible that is the reason I didn't receive an alert. I'll need to do some reading of the manual and also investigatethe configuration of the S100/FLARM system installed on Aircraft X to further understand this logic. It's very possible this is my fault, and by configuring the system differently I could have avoided a slice of swiss cheese or two from lining up. It's not the people talking on the radio that will hit you, it's the people that aren't. A good scan is critical. Keep that head on a swivel and outside. When releasing from tow in the future, I'll start clearing not only my 3 to 4 o'clock but all the way to my 6 o'clock. It's unlikely I would have spotted the traffic doing that due to the headrest blocking my view directly backwards, but it's a good idea none the less. The local terrain and airspace setup cause a bottleneck between the mountains to the west and the Class B to the east. You have a lot of airplanes flying VFR in a fairly small corridor. That ups the chances for these types of incidents occurring. More education for pilots that not all traffic will be presented or presented accurately on their traffic displays. This is a perfect example. Many pilots think everything out there that can hit them will show up on Foreflight, TCAS, etc. That's absolutely not the case. Better education about the 'glider box' at ZZZ. There is a note about it on the ZZZ airport website, and in the Chart Supplement. It's buried, and realistically not many pilots read those materials for airports they will overfly. There should be a note on the Sectional about the specific dimensions/locations of the ZZZ glider box.Even better, the FAA should make a database of this type of airspace and it's dimensions and allow it to be displayed as an overlay on tools like Foreflight. Just like they do with TFRs. While the Chart Supplement is an awesome resource, my honest experience is nobody looks at it unless they are taking a checkride. Everyone uses Foreflight these days. By presenting this type of airspace as a graphical overlay on these types of moving maps/apps, you have a much higher likelihood of awareness and compliance from the pilot population. This would increase safety tremendously! This wasn't a causal factor in this incident, but easily could be in a future one. All gliders should be required to have transponders. There are plenty of people flying gliders at 17,999 feet. In busy terminal arrival and departure corridors without a transponder. The battery technology exists for this to not be a problem anymore. I can fly all day with my transponder, radio, electronic variometer, and two moving map displays without running out of battery power.
ASRS:1769477.s: A glider pilot and a Piper Cherokee experienced a near midair collision south of ZZZ airport shortly after the glider released from tow at 7,200 feet. The incident occurred because the Cherokee did not make position calls on CTAF, and the glider's FLARM system failed to alert, requiring visual detection and immediate evasive action to achieve 100–200 feet of separation.
